title: Top US Shippers: Electronics imports hit record high in 2021 despite slower growth
content: Retail electronics sales are expected to tick up 2.8 percent in 2022 after a 9.6 percent gain in 2021, according to the Consumer Technology Association (CTA). Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. US electronics imports grew at a slower pace as the pandemic-induced wave of consumer electronics sales crested last year. But even with year-over-year growth in US electronics imports slowing to 4.1 percent last year from 15.2 percent in 2020, total volumes of everything from computers and televisions to electronic shavers and integrated circuits still reached a record high of more than 1.7 million TEU, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com within IHS Markit, now part of S&P Global. Retail electronics and appliance sales in the US have been relatively flat since dropping 11.8 percent in November and were down 10 percent year over year in March, according to advance retail sales data from the US Census Bureau. That doesn’t mean Americans are unplugging from their multiple electronic devices, but it could signal a deceleration to a more “normal” growth rate in electronics purchasing going forward. Persistent supply chain disruptions contributed to the cooling of consumer demand for electronic devices in 2021, along with a slight return to spending on entertainment outside of the home. Still, US retail electronics sales are expected to tick up another 2.8 percent to $505 billion in 2022, according to a January forecast from the Consumer Technology Association (CTA), following a 9.6 percent gain last year. Strong demand for smartphones, automotive technology, healthcare devices, and streaming services will drive much of that projected gain in retail sales, CTA said in a statement accompanying the forecast. “The consumer technology industry has shown impressive resilience in the face of supply chain challenges that are affecting almost every sector of the economy,” CTA President and CEO Gary Shapiro said in the report. “The pandemic gave people more time to explore new tech that made their lives healthier, safer, and more convenient. We anticipate another year of growth for our industry, based on the enormous demand we see from consumers for tech products and services.” Component supply shortages, especially the global shortage of semiconductors, had a substantial impact on US imports in 2021 and early 2022. For example, global automotive production losses due to the semiconductor shortage totaled 1.17 million units in the first quarter of 2021, according to IHS Markit. US containerized imports of semiconductor devices fell 10.2 percent last year after rising 35.2 percent in 2020 and 127.6 percent in 2019. Not all semiconductors and other electronic products arrive in the US by ocean container, however, which makes it more difficult to track shifts in volume and sourcing. Last year’s gains in containerized electronics imports were also uneven, with some product categories slipping while others boomed. Imports of turntables and record and cassette players, for example, jumped 39.5 percent. That growth was driven in part by a 51.4 percent increase in US vinyl record sales that made 2021 the first year in which records outsold CDs since 1991, according to music industry analyst MRC Data. China remained the dominant source of electronics imports, accounting for 56.9 percent of total volumes last year. That its next-largest competitor, Vietnam, held only an 11.2 percent share of the market underscores the enormous difficulty US and global firms have decoupling from or even reducing the amount of goods imported from China. In other words, despite growing at a faster rate, electronics imports from Vietnam have a long way to go to catch up with Chinese volumes. Imports from Thailand, the third-largest supplier of electronics to the US, increased just 0.6 percent last year after spiking 44.5 percent in 2020. Two of the fastest growing overseas markets for containerized electronics imports, Cambodia and Honduras, increased their volumes 44.7 percent and 40.5 percent, respectively, but off comparatively small volumes. Double-digit growth in volumes from Indonesia, the Philippines, India, South Korea, and Taiwan also reflects attempts to diversify sourcing in the region. In addition to shifting some production out of China, electronics importers also looked to diversify their port routings into the US. Volumes through the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach slipped 0.9 percent in 2021, pulling the busiest US port complex’s share of the market down to 53 percent from 55.7 percent in 2020. At the same time, shipments through major electronics gateways on the East and Gulf coasts grew by double-digit percentages, including increases of 13.5 percent in New York and New Jersey, 19.9 percent in Savannah, 15.8 percent in Houston, 34.8 percent in Charleston, 20.1 percent in Miami, and 22.4 percent in Mobile. The ebb and flow of electronics trade across US ports illustrates importers’ commitment to continually seek new pathways to market for their goods in the face of chronic port congestion and unpredictable supply chain disruptions. title: Lineage targets transportation technology market with Turvo buy
content: Michigan-based Lineage Logistics has an existing partnership with Turvo that includes an integration for its customers and investment into the technology provider. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Lineage Logistics acquired transportation management provider Turvo on Wednesday for an undisclosed sum, the latest in a string of buys this year for the highly acquisitive cold chain logistics provider. The companies have a pre-existing relationship that includes a product partnership that gave Lineage customers access to Turvo’s platform, and Lineage’s venture arm investing in Turvo. Lineage, which secured a $1.7 billion investment in January to fuel the Michigan-based company’s growth in North America and around the globe, has been particularly active in the past three months. It acquired Ontario, Canada-based third-party logistics provider VersaCold Logistics Services in April and Baltimore-based MTC Logistics in March to expand its cold storage capacity footprint on both US coasts. Lineage is the world’s largest provider of temperature-controlled logistics facilities and services. The Turvo acquisition is emblematic of its ambitions to be a vertically integrated logistics provider, seeking to bolster its dominant warehouse network by adding technology to manage inbound and outbound flows to those facilities. “The acquisition comes amid a spike in demand for transportation and warehousing and at a time in which the supply chain faces unprecedented challenges,” Sudarsan Thattai, Lineage’s chief information and transformation officer, said in a statement. “We have a unique opportunity to alleviate the impact of those challenges for customers,” Thattai added. “Driver shortages and port congestion, for instance, are addressable by decreasing the number of trucks or containers required to deliver a product from farm to fork. Turvo’s platform matches customers to truck, rail, or container assets that would otherwise be underutilized.” Aside from the VersaCold and MTC deals, Lineage also acquired three Dutch logistics firms in January, and in 2021 partnered with venture firm 8VC on a path to integrate early-stage startups into Lineage’s ecosystem. The latest deal also speaks to a challenge that Turvo faced in scaling its business independently. The company was an early leader in terms of landing venture capital to fuel development of logistics technology, having landed a $60 million round in 2018 that took its total raised to $91.6 million. At the time, that put Turvo among a select group of providers to raise that amount, along with Flexport, Convoy, project44, and Freightos. Those companies have all either raised substantially more since then, or, in the case of Freightos, announced a plan to go public. Turvo, however, hasn’t raised outside funding since its 2018 round. Instead, the company turned to partnerships with fellow software providers and freight intermediaries to grow usage of its platform. In a 2020 interview with JOC.com, Turvo executives said they were building a transportation management system (TMS) that essentially functioned as a collaborative platform with an attached marketplace for third-party applications that could be easily integrated. That path was designed to attract customers in a crowded TMS market. “Turvo will accelerate innovation with much greater reach and scale than ever before, further advancing supply chain digitization globally,” Turvo CEO Scott Lang said in Wednesday’s statement. title: Top US Shippers: COVID-19 lockdowns, port congestion hampering US ag exports
content: Agricultural exports fell 10.4 percent in 2021, with major markets in Asia unlikely to bounce back quickly. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Despite forecasts for another strong harvest, US agricultural interests expect exports to decline for a second consecutive year in 2022 due to pandemic-related supply chain disruptions in Asia and continued congestion at major US ports and inland rail hubs. Extended COVID-19 lockdowns, particularly in China, have severely restricted labor availability and cargo movement among suppliers, factories, and ports throughout Asia, compromising the ability of textile and apparel producers to receive and process cotton imports, according to William Allen, president of the American Cotton Shippers Association. “All of the [Asian] markets are affected by COVID. The Chinese market is acutely affected by COVID,” Allen said, noting that those disruptions are expected to continue in the 2022–23 marketing year, which for most agricultural products begins in the fall. US containerized agricultural exports dropped 10.4 percent to 1.5 million TEU in 2021, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com within IHS Markit, now part of S&P Global. Asia remains by far the largest export market for US farmers, accounting for 71.6 percent of total agricultural exports last year, down slightly from 71.8 percent in 2020. US agricultural exports to North Asia — i.e., mainland China, Japan, Taiwan, and Korea — fell 6 percent in 2021, while exports to Southeast Asia tumbled 22.9 percent. Mike Steenhoek, executive director of the Soybean Transportation Coalition, said shortages of labor and containers and inland transportation bottlenecks in the US — all attributable to the nearly two-year deluge of consumer goods imports from Asia — have also restrained agricultural exports. Shipments of soybeans, hay, and cotton, which together comprise 62 percent of US agricultural exports, fell a combined 10.1 percent last year following a 20.2 percent increase in 2020. Because they are grown and harvested in the interior of the US, shippers of those commodities rely on a steady supply of empty containers and railroad capacity to get their products to the ports and, in turn, overseas markets. Steenhoek compared the agricultural supply chain with a relay race that is predicated on reliable baton handoffs between legs. “What happens if the runner is limping, or jogging, or has fallen and can’t get up at all? We need this predictability,” Steenhoek said. Agricultural exporters continue to experience difficulties in securing empty marine containers, erratic intermodal rail service, poor vessel schedule reliability, and port congestion and drayage issues in Asia. US exporters have accused carriers of deliberately limiting export bookings and equipment availability throughout the COVID-19 pandemic to return empty containers to Asia and refill them with more profitable merchandise imports. “There clearly is real frustration among exporters,” Steenhoek said. Soybean shippers’ description of their logistical problems range from “dire” to “it’s a problem, although I’m still exporting,” but responses from coalition members have been universally negative, he said. That frustration grew so intense that federal lawmakers are on the verge of enacting new legislation that would expand the oversight of the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) to include, among other things, enforcement of so-called common carriage responsibilities. Currently in conference between the two chambers of Congress, the Ocean Shipping Reform Act (OSRA) of 2022 would allow the FMC to refine and enforce rules governing the “reasonable” refusal of service to US exporters. Although they are supportive of those regulatory efforts, agricultural shippers concede they cannot prove in all instances that carriers’ refusal to carry certain export loads represents an unreasonable or discriminatory practice, Steenhoek said. For exporters able to secure bookings and equipment, unreliable vessel schedules and resulting changes to the earliest return date (ERD) — the window in which containers must be dropped off at marine terminals — have been especially damaging. Due to terminal congestion that has caused chronic vessel backups outside major US ports in 2021 and early 2022, carriers have been making frequent “live changes” to export ERDs that result in delays and added costs for exporters, Allen said. Those issues have been particularly acute at West Coast ports, which handle approximately one-third of US agricultural exports, but gateways on the East and Gulf coasts have also been grappling with vessel bunching as import containers stack up at marine terminals. What’s more, port officials expect congestion and vessel schedule disruptions to continue through 2022 despite a temporary slowing of volumes due to COVID-19 lockdowns in China. The queue of vessels waiting to berth in Los Angeles and Long Beach will likely increase again as already-arriving back-to-school merchandise collides with early peak season goods and an anticipated spike in imports once those lockdowns are lifted, Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, told a virtual press conference in mid-April. “We expect a pretty quick recovery [in volumes],” Seroka said. Griff Lynch, CEO of the Georgia Ports Authority, gave a similar prediction for conditions at the major East Coast gateways. “We fully anticipate vessels to backlog on the East Coast this summer,” Lynch told JOC.com. Global demand for high-quality US cotton remains strong, but to capitalize on that demand, shippers will need to work more closely with their logistics providers to secure capacity and equipment, avoid bottlenecks, and improve shipment visibility to increase speed to market, Allen said. “We are highly focused on executing the timely delivery of our product,” he said. title: project44, FourKites head of visibility class: Gartner
content: The report, which focused on trucking visibility, noted that most vendors are still dependent on customers and carrier connectivity in a limited set of regions. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. A much-anticipated — and controversy-tinged — report by technology analyst Gartner on the state of the real-time transportation visibility (RTTV) market singled out two well-capitalized standalone visibility providers, project44 and FourKites, as leaders in the space. The report, called the Real-Time Transportation Visibility Provider Magic Quadrant (MQ), comes at a time when demand for predictive visibility tools has grown due to global supply chain disruptions that have made product lead times longer and less predictable. The controversy surrounding this year’s report — the second MQ that Gartner has issued on the visibility space — is tied to former Gartner vice president Bart de Muynck leaving the company to join project44 in mid-April. De Muynck was a lead author of the 2021 visibility report, but played no direct role in compiling this year’s version, Gartner said, although he did attend some vendor briefings in advance of the production of the report. The report rates 11 vendors, a mixture of pure-play visibility providers and visibility products attached to larger product suites that include transportation management, control tower, or supply chain planning capabilities. Gartner Research Director Carly West, the report’s author, noted that it sought to contextualize vendors that met certain thresholds for revenue, customer counts, geographic coverage, and business growth. While the report takes into account multimodal capability, it “represents a part of the end-to-end supply chain visibility market that predominantly — but not solely — addresses the domestic road transportation modes.” A number of vendors, who all asked not to be identified, reached out to JOC.com over the past week to voice concerns about the legitimacy of the report given de Muynck’s move to project44. The report was released May 24 to Gartner clients, but made more widely available this week. Gartner, for its part, addressed the controversy in a note to clients. “Two other Gartner experts in the transportation technology area, as well as the office of the ombuds, [reviewed] the research from beginning to end, to uncover signs of bias or other inappropriate content if it existed,” the note in the report said. “None of these individuals found any evidence of inappropriate content or process missteps in the document.” That this year’s MQ differs little from the 2021 version is unlikely to dampen criticism of the report from project44’s competitors, but analysts leaving to join companies in the sectors they cover is not a new development. In terms of the significance of the report itself, it’s clear that Gartner perceives companies that focus primarily on predictive transportation visibility, analytics and insights derived from the data, and carrier connectivity as being in a stronger position to sell RTTV products than companies with more diversified product sets that happen to also sell visibility. While project44 and FourKites were the only two vendors in the “leaders” quadrant, France-based Shippeo, with a similar and sole focus on visibility, was the next-highest rated provider and placed in the “challengers” quadrant. Overhaul, which focuses on providing visibility as a means for shippers to mitigate supply chain risk, saw its position improve the most from 2021 and 2022 within the challengers quadrant. From a geographic perspective, the report cautioned that most providers outside of project44 and FourKites are overly dependent on customers and carrier connectivity within one region. One issue for companies trying to sell visibility within broader transportation or supply chain management product sets is that it can be difficult to justify the cost of continuing product enhancements and sales and marketing efforts to support those improvements, for what amounts to an ancillary offering. That was made clear to JOC.com this week by a provider in the global trade management space, who asked not to be identified, that is seeing demand from potential customers for an integrated transportation visibility solution. The cost to build it internally might overwhelm what the company could get for a non-core part of its offering, but the absence of such a tool is glaring when compared with other platforms that have it. Another option is using an existing visibility tool or tools in a white-labeled arrangement, but matching up the data schema between those tools and the company’s core GTM product is not as easy as it may seem, the provider said. The report did not include a cadre of niche, internationally focused visibility data providers, such as Vizion, Terminal49, Portcast, and OpenTrack. Those vendors, most of whom have received venture funding, are likely too focused on non-trucking modes or lack the required revenue to be considered for the report. title: Turning supply chain chaos into profitable business
content: LAKE BUENA VISTA, Fla. —Manufacturers have generally weathered the past two years of disruption and now are shifting into future-proofing their businesses, incorporating better visibility and supply chain control. That is one of the takeaways from Fictiv’s seventh annual State of Manufacturing report. Released Monday at the Gartner Supply Chain Sumposium/XPO at Walt Disney World’s Dolphin Resort, the report found a majority (59%) of companies said improving supply chain visibility is their top priority. Nearly two-thirds of respondents (65%) also are looking to increase onshoring to protect against future global supply chain shocks. “What stood out to me in this year’s report was the progress that has been made over the last three years,” said Dave Evans, Fictiv CEO and co-founder. “2020 was about seeing the problems, 2021 was about finding the solutions, and now in 2022, we see companies are making progress towards a future-proofed industry. Leaders are demanding major changes from the ground up in order to gain much-needed control and predictability. Fictiv was founded due to the very issues companies are still facing today, and I’m excited to see momentum toward technology-powered transformation.” In an interview with FreightWaves, Evans said the 10-year-old company saw tremendous growth in the past few years as manufacturers looked for flexibility to the global supply chain disruptions. Fictiv matches firms with manufacturers that have capacity to handle custom and on-demand jobs. Evans pointed to the recent shutdown of Shenzen, China, due to a COVID case spike. “In our model, we had 249 [manufacturing] orders in flight that were affected,” Evans said. “In hours, we were able to shift all of those orders [to other locations].” It is that kind of flexibility that Fictiv thrives on, although the company started as a conduit between businesses building new products and those with manufacturing capacity to handle the limited runs. That remains a primary focus of the business today, but the past few years have opened eyes among supply chain leaders about the need to be more agile, Evans said. “We’ve taken a road map that might have taken five years and been doing it in 18 months,” Evans noted, saying that employee headcount has been almost doubling year-over-year, and the company recently closed a new $100 million financing round. “Supply chain has never been as sexy as it is now.” The Fictiv report had several other interesting findings, including that 88% of manufacturers want to streamline production by reducing the number of suppliers, and 93% are looking for technology solutions to increase operational efficiency for new product development. While reducing suppliers might seem counterintuitive to managing disruptions, Evans said many companies simply have too many suppliers. And at a cost of between $40,000 and $60,000 to manage each one, there is money to be saved. “I don’t think you can meet a supply chain officer that thinks they have the right number of vendors,” he said. The report surveyed 234 senior decision-makers in supply chain, engineering, research and development, and technology or business leadership roles at companies that produce medical devices, robotics, automotive, aerospace or consumer electronics. Evans said over the past three years of the report, there was a definite trend of leaders recognizing there is a supply chain problem in 2020, shifting into solution mode in 2021, and finally transitioning into executive mode this year. “That road map would have taken a decade [to accomplish],” he said. Among the top themes identified is the increased use of digital manufacturing technology and analytics and on-demand manufacturing platforms. Over 90% of companies are now using or implementing digital manufacturing tech, and 61% are using supply chain analytics, while 58% have adopted on-demand manufacturing platforms. Leaders said they are facing fewer barriers to innovation overall, but 97% are concerned about security in a more digitized environment. The report also found that 73% of manufacturing leaders view outsourcing positively and 48% increased outsourcing to deal with the effects of the pandemic. Also, customer demand continued to shift, with more emphasis on sustainability, quality and advanced features among the top asks. However, while increased agility (49% of respondents) and more efficient team coordination (48%) were cited as ways manufacturers are responding to this, 75% said engineering and supply chain teams need to collaborate more. Evans also pointed to security and productivity as big concerns among supply chain leaders. More companies are focused on improving productivity, which reached a decadeslong low in Q1, Evans said. Fictiv is unique in that its solutions are product-agnostic, but the companies must be willing to change. “If you are fine with the status quo, it’s probably not a good fit,” Evans said. “But if you are looking for agility [Fictiv can help].” He noted that Fictiv has helped companies of all sizes, from a 20-person robotics company that it helped save $600,000, to Honeywell, where Fictiv worked to address an issue in its $6 billion aerospace division. title: Gartner expert: Supply chains can thrive even amid disruption
content: LAKE BUENA VISTA, Fla. Relationships. Trust. Control. And visibility. These are the hallmarks of a strategy to managing and surviving supply chain risk, said Brian Whitlock, senior director analyst at Gartner. Speaking at the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium/XPO 2022 on Monday at Walt Disney World’s Dolphin Resort in Lake Buena Vista, Florida, Whitlock cited those four items as the call to action during his presentation, titled Logistics Risk and Disruption: Is it in the Past or Forever Part of the Future. Whitlock ran through some survey results from recent Gartner surveys, including that 92% of businesses were impacted by COVID, weather, fuel costs, supply or labor shortages, or some other disruption. “What surprised me was how low these numbers were,” he said. “I can’t think of a single company that wasn’t impacted.” Whitlock said it seems like disruptions just keep “compounding on top of each other,” and businesses maybe facing disruptions for a while still. He broke down the three key challenges facing businesses today: building better relationships, control, visibility. Relationships are important, Whitlock said, pointing to a Gartner survey that found 57% of companies were not considered a shipper of choice. “Companies in this group struggled to get capacity,” he said, pointing to a survey where the three top answers on how to improve “all centered around relationships.” Whitlock cautioned against building only local relationships, saying that doing so could hamper operations if a disruption occurs only on the local level. Control showed up in the surveys as 70% of companies said they wanted to bring some outsourcing back in house. Often, this was around managed transportation, warehousing and fulfillment, and freight and payment solutions. One company that Whitlock said successfully did this was Ashley Furniture, which in 2021 acquired trucking company Wilson Logistics, expanded its North American footprint to pull some overseas manufacturing back to the U.S., and when it had to source goods from overseas, charted vessels to smaller West Coast ports, avoiding some of the backlog that occurred at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Visibility was also a key challenge for companies in the surveys, with 70% saying it was their number-one area of improvement. Whitlock said improved visibility will improve costs through better inventory control and labor management. “Visibility is a journey and takes time to develop,” he said. Ultimately, to overcome the challenges and achieve success, Whitlock said companies should: Whitlock pointed to Dell Technologies as a company that embodies some of what he talked about, noting that Dell leveraged this playbook and in 2021 had record revenues and record profits “in large part due to its supply chain execution.” Click for more articles by Brian Straight. title: Monster leans on US sourcing to lower freight costs
content: Aluminum constraints last year had pushed Monster to import more from cans from abroad. However, relying on more imports brought other challenges: port congestion, a lack of shipping containers, and “significant increases in domestic and international freight costs,” Sacks said in August. Monster is now focused on positioning production closer to customers, adding suppliers and rebuilding inventories within the U.S. Sacks said last month adding the two suppliers, which are now operational, should help Monster decrease its reliance on imported aluminum cans. Still, rising aluminum prices continue to present headwinds for the company. Monster saw a “dramatic increase in aluminum prices,” with costs soaring 65% YoY in Q1, President Hilton Schlosberg said. Although Monster has added more suppliers and co-packing capacity in the U.S., the company is still relying on imports to meet demand. The company estimates $46 million in costs were the result of operating inefficiencies “including the importation of aluminum cans,” Sacks said. Beverage can makers are facing similar pressures and are looking to up production in the United States as a way to lower costs. Ball Corporation, which has also imported more aluminum to meet demand, is investing in new ways to increase production in the U.S. The company expects to announce new investments in 2022 “to support domestic U.S. production of aluminum can sheet to further enable long-term growth,” President and CEO Dan Fisher said in the company’s Q1 earnings call. “We’re starting to see investment in the aluminum supply chain in North America,” said CFO Scott Morrison. “So I think that’s encouraging.”

title: The Light Load: Everybody wants Freightliner CPCs
content: The thefts of common powertrain controller (CPC) modules from parked Freightliner and Western Star trucks feels like a game of Clue minus the conservatory, candlestick, Col. Mustard and, well, clues. Come to think of it, it’s nothing at all like Clue, but I digress. Anyhow, unless Miss Marple clears her schedule, Daimler Truck North America and the authorities are going to have to sort through a passel of suspects, usual or otherwise, to get to the bottom of this high-tech poachery. The purloined modules are rich with semiconductors — you know, those microchips vital for trucks that wish to make the leap from Park to Go. As you may also know, only baby formula and McDonald’s soft serve rival semiconductors when it comes to shortages. There are far too few — semiconductors, not bottles of formula or Oreo McFlurries — to meet demand for new truck production, so fleets are hanging on to older trucks. Or they’re making not exactly less-than-truckload piles of cash selling them. “Everybody Wants You,” Billy Squier once crooned to some lass. I have never been in said lass’s predicament, but everybody sure wants those microchips. Some were even willing to sneak onto the grounds of an auction yard in Pennsylvania, risking a run-in with a pack of corgis or other guard dogs, to indulge their chip-lust. The CPCs go for 1,400 smackers apiece in a legal purchase but nearly six times that on the black market. Putting the number of incidents in the hundreds, Daimler is understandably as mad as an old wet possum about the whole sordid business. “The theft of CPC modules is a crime that threatens the livelihood of customers and disrupts our dealers’ operations,” Paul Romanaggi, DTNA chief customer experience officer, said in a press release. Indeed it does. But where do Daimler and the police even begin looking for the bad guys? Are they primarily lone wolves or part of a syndicate? If we all want semiconductors and we all need semiconductors, then even if there ain’t no way we’re all ever gonna love semiconductors — RIP, Meat Loaf — aren’t we all just so many defendants-in-waiting playing feline and rodent on a dilapidated gameboard from the ’40s? If so, to return to the Clue metaphor that we previously established doesn’t really work in this column, can I put in an early request to be Professor Plum? In the kitchen? With the knife? And a plate bearing one of mother’s fresh-baked chocolate chip pound cakes?* — Do any Pams work at P.A.M.? Reckon they get a special parking spot? — Do actual martens live near Marten Transport? People who make a profession of knowing where martens reside say these distant and more lovable cousins of the common house skunk and rat weasel have put down roots in parts of Wisconsin, Marten’s home base, so I guess it’s possible. If there’s a Marten Museum, does it have both trucks and a petting zoo? I’d make that trip. — If the former Con-way Freight had a theme song, I hope it was, well, you know. *The key to chocolate chip pound cake is miniature chocolate chips. title: Top US Shippers: Apparel retailers ordering early to avoid trans-Pac delays
content: US apparel and footwear imports rebounded in 2021, rising 18 percent after falling 11.4 percent in 2020. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Clothing retailers and wholesalers in the US increased their imports sharply last year and expect demand to remain robust this year, but persistent port congestion and fears of further disruption during West Coast longshore labor negotiations are forcing shippers to carry more inventory and pull orders from Asian suppliers forward. Importers worried about stockouts due to cargo stuck on the water, at marine terminals, or at inland rail ramps are building inventories of back-to-school — and even holiday — apparel and footwear well in advance of the typical trans-Pacific peak season. That’s making it tougher for retailers to forecast how much of a given product they should order and putting additional pressure on their supply chains, according to Nate Herman, senior vice president of policy with the American Apparel & Footwear Association (AAFA). “The holiday season accounts for over 50 percent of sales, so trying to deal with the shipping crisis while making sure that we have product in for the holidays has created difficult situations,” Herman told JOC.com. “Companies are trying to bring in many products early, but also trying to guess what that hot product will be. It’s also created a whole litany of inventory issues trying to store these products, and there are warehouse capacity issues all around the US.” Skyrocketing shipping costs — with spot trans-Pacific ocean freight pricing up nearly 150 percent year over year in early May, according to benchmarking firm Xeneta — are also a major concern for apparel and footwear companies, many of which were already operating on razor-thin margins, Herman said. Some companies have raised prices on products to offset the sharp rise in freight rates, but fierce competition among the vast array of brick-and-mortar and online retailers doesn’t allow much room to recoup transportation costs. “There’s a very low barrier to entry into the industry, and e-commerce has made that barrier practically nonexistent over the last 10 years. There are so many players, and so many options to buy clothes and shoes,” Herman explained. Total US clothing imports jumped 18 percent to 1.87 million TEU in 2021, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com within IHS Markit, now part of S&P Global. Last year’s growth came on the back of an 11.4 percent decline in 2020, leaving 2021 volumes 4.6 percent ahead of 2019, the last full year prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. An apparel and footwear importer who asked not to be named said the company placed orders with Asian manufacturers for holiday season merchandise in January and February, rather than in the spring, to compensate for widespread disruption throughout the trans-Pacific supply chain. Vessels are lining up outside major US cargo ports, and transit times for containers headed inland are being further stretched by inconsistent international intermodal rail service. As a result, shippers are faced with a choice between potentially lengthy delays for boxes moving by rail — whether transloaded or intact inland point intermodal (IPI) — and the extra costs of transporting cargo by truck. “J.B. Hunt used to be able to run their containers from Los Angeles to Chicago in four to five days, but now it’s double that,” the apparel shipper said. “But I’ve seen ocean containers on IPI take 20 or 21 days to get to Chicago. I’ve seen some IPI trains sit in Southern California for two or three weeks, just on their own, and they’re just not moving.” Those choices are made based on the product, the shipper said. For seasonal products that need to arrive within a given time frame, the company hires team trucks able to move cargo from the Port of Los Angeles to Chicago in two days, while other products are transloaded into domestic intermodal containers or moved intact based on how quickly they need to arrive. Some clothing importers are looking to diversify their sourcing to reduce risk and reliance on manufacturing in Asia and a highly disrupted trans-Pacific trade. A second apparel and footwear shipper who asked not to be identified said purchasing more products from Central America has drastically reduced the company’s port-to-port transit times and overall transportation costs. “It’s like four days on the water from Honduras versus two weeks on the water from Asia, so it’s a lot quicker,” the shipper explained. “The cost of trans-Pacific vessels is not going back to where we were pre-pandemic. The new normal on rates will be higher, so it’s a lot cheaper for transportation to use Central America.” Shifting sourcing from Asia to Central America has its own risks, however, due primarily to geopolitical instability and a higher incidence of severe weather events such as earthquakes and hurricanes, the shipper said. As a member of the Coalition for Economic Partnerships in the Americas, a group of companies and associations dedicated to promoting regional trade and job growth formed in November 2021, AAFA is also encouraging its members to consider bringing production back to the western hemisphere. “If you want to try and get everybody out of China, which is what everybody in Washington, DC, is saying, and encourage companies to come to this hemisphere, then this is a good option,” Herman said. “You dramatically shorten your shipping time as well in the process and hopefully address some of the shipping crisis.” Contact Ari Ashe at ari.ashe@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @arijashe. © 2026 S&P Global. title: FMC needs to expand to increase monitoring, meet OSRA mandates
content: Even before the new funding request, the FMC, which is authorized for 128 employees currently, had been struggling to find new hires. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. US maritime regulators are seeking additional funding to handle increased monitoring of the container shipping industry amid persistent disruption, and they may need even more money depending on the scale of the mandate within pending shipping reform legislation. The US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) is asking Congress for a 5.2 percent increase in its fiscal year 2023 budget, to $34.7 million, primarily to expand the agency’s workforce from 115 to 150, with the majority of new hires serving in enforcement and customer service roles. The Ocean Shipping Reform Act (OSRA) of 2022, now in reconciliation between the House and Senate before being sent to President Joe Biden for his signature, promises to expand the agency’s authority further, requiring more people and resources. “This investment is needed. Demand for commission services is not dissipating,” FMC Commissioner Dan Maffei said at an April 27 hearing. He added that the agency has had to prioritize its investigations and that the FMC could handle more if it had additional resources. The OSRA bill includes language that would fund the FMC with $4 million more than the agency requested in fiscal 2023, $43.7 million for fiscal year 2024, and $49.2 million for fiscal year 2025. The federal fiscal year begins Oct. 1. Even before the new funding request, the FMC, which is authorized for 128 employees currently, had been struggling to find new hires, according to Commissioner Carl Bentzel. Despite adding substantial staff over the last couple of years, attrition from an aging work force and hiring and training new hires with the desired maritime expertise has kept the commission tally hovering at too low a number that it’s set the FMC behind on calls. “We’re really looking for personnel, but there are not a lot of experts in [the] maritime shipping world pounding down our doors,” Bentzel told JOC.com in an interview Friday. The last two years brought several million dollars in new funding to the FMC’s budget — thanks in large part to the support of President Biden — to increase salaries, and the next three years could see a potential extra $5 million to $6 million annually through the OSRA to expand the workforce. An increased budget would allow the FMC to hire more investigative and enforcement personnel to keep an eye on ocean carriers, alliances, and fees and surcharges. A larger staff would also help the FMC provide ongoing guidance to shippers bringing complaints to the commission and allow it to review —and potentially investigate — more of the hundreds of correspondences the agency has received during the COVID-19 pandemic. Still, Maffei said the biggest challenge for the industry is not regulating ocean carrier behavior, but a need to expand US ports, inland infrastructure, equipment, and labor supply to keep up with cargo demand. “The availability of intermodal equipment, warehouse space, intermodal train service, trucking — and enough workers in each of those sectors — remain challenges to getting more cargo off our ports and to destination with more certainty and reliability,” he said during the hearing. title: 2022 Shipper of Choice Profile: Tractor Supply Co.
content: Presented by FreightWaves, in partnership with TriumphPay, the Shipper of Choice award recognizes the manufacturers, distributors and retailers that do the best job of keeping the American economy moving by fighting driver detention, providing accessible facilities and understanding what it takes to remove inefficiencies from the supply chain. Among the top 25 Shippers of Choice for 2021 is . . . Tractor Supply Co. Tractor Supply Co. was founded by Charles E. Schmidt Sr., who established a mail-order tractor parts business from his kitchen table at his home in Chicago in 1938. Today, the company has more than 2,000 stores in 49 states and is one of the largest operators of rural lifestyle retail stores in the United States. Tractor Supply’s philosophy on logistics and transportation is centered around trusting a core group of transportation providers, said Erick Osburn, the company’s vice president of transportation. “Our philosophy at TSC is to create long-term strategic partnerships with our carriers,” Osburn told FreightWaves. “We keep the size of our network compact and offer core carriers who have performed well over time the opportunity to grow with us. We do not bid our entire network every year — we prefer to keep incumbent carriers in place when service is strong and pricing is in line with the market. We have found this philosophy to be mutually beneficial and appreciated by our partners.” This year’s Shipper of Choice award winners were chosen out of nearly 400 companies nominated by FreightWaves readers on social media. Nominees for Shipper of Choice completed a survey addressing operational data, including dwell times, overages/shortages and damages, hours of operation, communication protocols and facility attributes, including the availability of showers, bathrooms and break rooms for drivers. “Tractor Supply Co. makes every effort to keep drivers driving by minimizing wait times at our distribution centers and stores,” Osburn said. “We regularly review and update our processes and signage to make getting in and out of our distribution centers as efficient as possible.” Osburn said stores are always ready “for their freight and can usually have a trailer unloaded in under an hour and the drivers do not need to assist with the unload.” He added, “We have also shared the importance of providing a great experience for truck drivers with our entire vendor base since they are an extension of our brand.” Tractor Supply also provides driver-friendly facilities, such as restrooms. “Each distribution center and store has its own spin on driver-friendly facilities and amenities, but drivers are always welcome to use our restrooms, grab a coffee or snack for themselves and can almost always count on a treat for their four-legged co-pilots when in tow,” Osburn said. “We are the Tractor Supply Co. after all.” Tractor Supply sells up to 20,000 products at each of its retail locations, everything from work and recreational clothing to lawn and garden tools, home goods, fencing, truck beds, chicken coops, pet food, and feed for farm animals. With such a diverse product range, shipments can come at different times of day and night. Keeping flexible hours for carriers to complete their shipments is a key focus, Osburn said. “Our distribution center yards and operations are open 24/7,” Osburn said. “We have worked with many of our vendors to support night and weekend pickups and operations as well.” At each Tractor Supply distribution center location, truck parking solutions vary based on physical limitations, but newer locations should include more parking for tractor-trailers. “The company is in the process of opening three new distribution centers over the next 36 months and each will contemplate parking and amenities for our drivers to use while on-site,” Osburn said. title: Elephant in the room: Aim to optimize, not cut, logistics costs
content: LAKE BUENA VISTA, Fla. — Ocean rates are up. Trucking rates are high. Airfreight rates are up. And the global supply chain is in crisis. So why does Greg Aimi believe the answer is to eat an elephant? The Gartner vice president of research and logistics technologies hosted a discussion on Tuesday at the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium/XPO 2022 conference at Walt Disney World’s Dolphin Resort, aptly titled, “If you want to cost-optimize logistics, learn how to eat an elephant.” His point was that many organizations approach cost optimization through cost cutting, but because logistics is so big — like an elephant — that is not the right approach. “Cost cutting things are different than what you do in cost optimization,” he said, noting that companies often look to cut line items or limit spending, which ultimately hurts the overall profitability of the logistics operation. Aimi laid out a strategy to achieve cost optimization that will set up an organization for the long haul. It starts by not cutting costs in a way that hamper logistics, but rather looking to find ways to invest in areas “to set you up for the future.” An example of this would be looking at workflow automation technologies, he said. A majority of companies — 52% in a recent Gartner survey — reduced their logistics costs by increasing their operational efficiency, not cutting. Secondly, firms should implement a plan. This can be short term (three to nine months), medium term (nine to 18 months) or long term (18-plus months) and in many cases involves all three steps. In the short term, the business should work to operate better, whereas a reconfiguration of the business should be conducted over the medium term. Finally, the long term should be focused on transformation. Companies seeking to operate more efficiently can look at budget items, examine their freight and payment operations, tighten lead times and shorten delivery windows, and improve collaboration on order quantities. Once the medium-term plan goes into effect, the business should be focused on organizational change, operational alignment and tightening of logistics polices while forming partnerships with 3PLs and carriers to remove waste from the operation. Over the long term, Aimi continued, businesses should be investing in logistics-specific systems and digital technologies such as robotics that will reduce labor and improve service. Also, now is the time to look at conducting a “cost-to-service” analysis. “[You] don’t want to overserve where the cost analysis is [not positive],” he said. “Good logistics is the ability to service on a consistent basis,” Aimi continued. “Great logistics is the ability to do so while optimizing cost.” Aimi added that companies should not discount upstream changes. Operations in the sales and order departments, for instance, can have an impact on logistics costs. Logistics, Aimi said, is so big that it always appears to be the elephant in the room. “The way to eat the elephant is to break it up into pieces.” Click for more articles by Brian Straight. title: FMC signaling measured approach ahead of OSRA
content: Using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, a measure of market concentration, the FMC’s Bureau of Trade Analysis found the Asia-US trade to be competitive, according to the Fact Finding 29 report. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The findings of a Federal Maritime Commissioner’s investigation into how the pandemic has impacted container shipping suggest a measured approach moving forward, finding no collusion among carriers but recommending greater monitoring of their activities. A sharper mandate and moderately expanded powers likely to emerge from legislation this year amid President Joe Biden’s rhetoric against carriers do not look as though they will shake the FMC. Rather, the independent agency is exercising more of its power ahead of the first US shipping reform in two decades — although not with the speed to please all. The results of the investigation by Federal Maritime Commissioner Rebecca Dye, released May 31, dismiss the idea that container lines manipulated the market to send spot rates soaring to historic highs, concluding — as many in the industry inherently know — that unprecedented demand outstripped capacity. The cost of shipping a 40-foot container from Shanghai to Los Angeles is up nearly 50 percent from a year ago at $8,704, according to Drewry, well above pre-pandemic levels below $2,000. Using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, a measure of market concentration, the FMC’s Bureau of Trade Analysis found the Asia–US trade to be competitive, according to the Fact Finding 29 report. The index measures market concentration through the lens of pre- and post-mergers and acquisitions. That is key given the number of major carriers on the trans-Pacific and trans-Atlantic trades has shrunk from 20 in 2015 to 11 now. Dye’s report found that carriers blanked sailings due to port congestion, not to drive up rates, a sharp retort to politicians and members of the shipping public who accused ocean carriers of engaging in anticompetitive behavior. And while the alliances as highly integrated vessel-sharing agreements control the majority of the trade, the report did not note any violations, in spite of months of allegations. Carriers outside the three major alliances have a larger slice of the market, according to the report, which ended a two-year investigation. During the worst of the pandemic in the second quarter of 2020, the share of non-alliance carriers in the trans-Pacific market calling the US West Coast was just 12 percent; now it’s approximately 29 percent, according to maritime analyst and JOC analyst Lars Jensen. In terms of East Coast routings, non-alliance carriers saw their shares swing from zero to 15 percent in the same period. The FMC “to date, observed no indication that the current prices for liner shipping are a result of collusion or illegal conduct on the part of the major ocean carriers,” according to Dye’s report. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) is investigating Maersk and one other carrier, as tied to a global probe by competition authorities into suspected anticompetitive behavior and collusion with global supply chains. The DOJ in 2019 ended a prior multiyear investigation of carriers without having brought charges, according to carriers including Maersk. A week prior to the release of Fact Finding 29 at a shipper summit, FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei said that despite dozens of complaints about higher spot rates, those complaining can’t or are unwilling to provide enough evidence. In two of the three FMC investigations into improper assessment of detention and demurrage fees, two carriers paid major civil penalties in separate cases. The results of agency’s Bureau of Enforcement investigation into the third carrier have not been disclosed yet. “We’ve gotten so many complaints of shipping lines breaking their contracts,” Maffei said at the National Industrial Transportation League’s virtual conference May 23. “When we do look into them, unfortunately we find that most of the time the carrier, while they may have violated the spirit of the contract, the actual letter of the contract somehow gets them out of it.” Congress could change that by further expanding FMC’s power, even going as far as to charge the FMC with setting rates. But the Ocean Shipping Reform Act (OSRA), which is expected to be passed by Congress and head to Biden’s desk in coming weeks, won’t likely go that far. “We can also reduce the cost of everyday goods by fixing broken supply chains, improving infrastructure, and cracking down on the exorbitant fees that foreign ocean freight companies charge to move products,” Biden wrote in a May 30 Wall Street Journal op-ed titled, “My Plan for Fighting Inflation.” Based on both House and Senate versions, the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 at the very least will grant the FMC more power over ocean carrier detention and demurrage billing practices and export services. Perhaps the version of the OSRA being hashed out in conference by Senate and House leaders, will be more dramatic than anyone expected. Or Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., may be exaggerating the impact of the legislation. “The shipping container market is being manipulated and American business owners know it,” Klobuchar, referring to OSRA 2022, tweeted June 1. “While multinational companies make billions more in profit, our exporters are hurting.” Barring a dramatic expansion of FMC’s purview, the agency will likely continue to seek to clarify existing rules and expand its monitoring. Starting May 5, the FMC began requiring alliances and each member company to show more pricing and capacity information. “Additional agreement changes may be required by the Commission to alleviate competition concerns as warranted,” according to Dye’s report. That could include making it easier for the agency to challenge vessel-sharing agreements and give the agreements an expiry date, as they currently don’t have a shelf life. The Fact Finding 29 report proposes rulemaking to clarify and provide consistency on acceptable practices tied to empty container returns, earliest return dates, and carrier and merchant haulage. The FMC should also investigate how container lines, ports, and marine terminals levy charges through tariffs, the report recommended. The five-member commission would have to approve the recommendations in order to pursue them. More activist commissioners than Dye may want to take a more aggressive approach. FMC Commissioner Carl Bentzel wants the agency to provide partial oversight of rail demurrage, for example. Ultimately, though, these are measured moves aimed at providing more structure to commercial exchanges without stepping directly into them. If Congress expects more, it will likely need another shipping act. Contact Mark Szakonyi at mark.szakonyi@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @MarkSzakonyi. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Supply chain roles become major destination for executives
content: Welcome to the WHAT THE TRUCK?!? Newsletter presented by ODFL. In this issue, why Flexport brought on Dave Clark; sriracha and tampon shortages; fuel is Morbin. Flexport lands Amazon consumer chief as future CEO Kind of a big deal — On Wednesday morning, Flexport CEO Ryan Petersen sent out the tweet heard round the world. The 41-year-old CEO of the $8 billion dollar logistics giant that he founded in 2013 will be transitioning to an executive chairman role by next spring. Petersen told Forbes, “My big fear for Flexport is just that we’re not good enough to reach our potential.” A brave admission for any CEO, especially one who stood out as logistics leading man when freight went mainstream last year. Landing a key Amazonian — Meet the new boss: Dave Clark is a 23-year Amazon veteran who is credited with transforming the e-tailer into a shipping and logistics powerhouse. The same year Flexport was founded, Amazon had a disastrous holiday peak season that put them at odds with UPS service levels. FreightWaves’ Mark Solomon reports, “Clark led the rapid-fire building of sortation centers, acquisition of trailers and recruitment of drivers.” Just last week, Clark shocked the business world with his abrupt resignation from his prime position … now we know why. Flexport is on its way to becoming one of the world’s most important technology platforms for supply chain and logistics. Given the scale of the opportunity ahead of us, Flexport doesn't need another executive. We need another entrepreneur. “In five years, Flexport will be known, hands down, as the best supply chain company in the world.” — Dave Clark to Ryan Petersen during an interview for the role The search for an entrepreneur — Flexport has been very successful, growing from $2 million in revenue in 2014 to over $3 billion last year. So why make a change? Petersen tweeted, “The more we learn about our markets — and learning about the world economy is the best part of working at Flexport — the more we realize the opportunity in front of us is enormous.” Petersen believes Clark can be the entrepreneur they seek to grow and grow big. Roar — Not for nothing, but ever since Ryan Petersen took on the DALL-E lion as Flexport’s unofficial mascot, great things have come. Suckin’ the blood out of your wallet — Trucks can’t move without fuel and moving trucks has gotten significantly more expensive as the year has gone on. While the national average DOE Diesel Price Per Gallon is over $5.70, many areas have reported much higher signs at the pump. Just to add some insult to injury: Dry van spot rates are down a penny this week ::facepalm:: Gasoline prices vs. Biden's approval rating pic.twitter.com/N4dtBVOwhK “Spot gasoline markets pushing higher again, up 8-12c/gal while diesel spots up 13c/gal.” – Gas Buddy’s Patrick De Haan California Screamin’ — Drivers headed through San Francisco were welcomed with gas prices over $7! Rooster reports on Back The Truck Up, “With West Texas Intermediate (WTI) and Brent Sea crude both at or near $120 a barrel (and summer vacation season on full tilt), there’s no logical reason for it to go down.” Baby formula, tampons and sriracha all in short supply If you've never noticed the Great Tampon Shortage of 2022, you probably don't use them. If you have wondered about it, I have answers for you! https://t.co/sDzTUwqMav From bad to worse — We all know about the baby formula crisis by this point, but that’s not the only thing shoppers and women in need can’t find. Redditors, Facebookers and Time magazine have reported tampon shortages across the U.S. According to Time, Procter & Gamble claims that the shortage is due to an Amy Schumer commercial that has caused demand to explode. At least they didn’t blame her Netflix special. In reality, the raw material cost for tampons has gone up 300% during the pandemic and feminine hygiene products are up over 10% from a year ago. Mild sauce — Huy Fong Foods is warning of a sriracha shortage and it has nothing to do with this guy drinking 3 pounds of it. The condiment company has curtailed all orders submitted after April 19 and pushed them to after Labor Day. Why? Weather has led to a severe chili pepper shortage. Looking for a substitute (I know, there isn’t one), Trader Joe’s Chili Pepper Sauce has done well by me. Want to learn more about sriracha? Check out this documentary. Trucking and deathmatches — Get ready to rumble this Friday on WHAT THE TRUCK?!? We’re talking to some of the most interesting and electric people in freight. Alex from The Asian Mai show talks about turning his life as an owner-operator into a YouTube channel with over 300,000 subscribers. Pro wrestler and freight broker Gunner Miller takes the stage a few short hours before his next deathmatch. We’ll learn all about the ins and outs of the squared circle and how those lessons translate to freight. Surge Transportation founder and CEO Omar Singh talks about challenges implementing FreightTech. Plus, all the latest headlines and news of the weird. title: New Blume partnership aims to provide end-to-end visibility
content: Resilinc will support Blume’s Orchestra platform with monitoring, supplier visibility, alerts for delays and price changes, and more. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Supply chain tech provider Blume Global has partnered with a risk-monitoring software company to provide clients with the ability to connect real-time visibility and transportation execution to data about disruptions plaguing the supply chain. The integration will see Blume and Resilinc Corp. equip customers with the ability to assess potential disruptions, and prescribed ways to mitigate them. Resilinc’s resiliency solutions will support the Blume “Orchestra” platform — which allows buyers, suppliers, and logistics providers to collaborate — with monitoring, supplier visibility data, and risk scoring, and a predictive tool that alerts customers of delays, price movements, and supply chain constraints, Blume said in a statement Wednesday. “Visibility throughout the supply chain is simply not enough — it’s also about anticipating problems proactively and assessing the alternatives to fulfill and complete a shipment,” Blume CEO Pervinder Johar said in the statement. Resilinc CEO Bindiya Vakil said the partnership will make supply chain resiliency more accessible and cost-effective for the company’s two sets of customers. “We will be able to make real-time event monitoring, supply chain mapping, supply risk data and analytics, and scenario planning capabilities available to Blume’s clients and enable them to be more proactive about managing supply chain disruptions,” Vakil said in the statement. Other companies are also diving into risk management. Just last month, software provider Everstream Analytics closed a $24 million funding round to expand its reach, a clear signal that more shippers than ever are looking for ways to accurately measure and predict supply chain vulnerabilities. Blume and Resilinc’s partnership comes two months after Blume was hit with a cyber incident that downed part of its Asset Management platform. title: Flexport leadership change suggests lack of market-defining progress
content: Clark has indicated he needs five years to make Flexport “the best supply chain company in the world,” a process that will pit him against his old employer Amazon. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. In a move that sent shockwaves through the logistics community Wednesday, Ryan Petersen said he will step down as CEO of Flexport in March 2023 and be replaced by ex-Amazon logistics chief Dave Clark. While the unexpected leadership change demonstrates Flexport’s lure for heavyweight talent, it may also serve as an acknowledgment of slower-than-expected market share gains despite billions in venture backing. In a long public statement posted on Twitter, Petersen said he believed Clark was the person who could expedite Flexport’s growth by allowing Petersen to focus on its long-term vision while allowing Clark to manage operations, as he had at Amazon. Clark, who resigned Friday from his role running Amazon’s global retail business after a long stint building its logistics and warehousing divisions, will serve as Flexport’s co-CEO with Petersen for a six-month transitional period beginning in September. Petersen, Flexport’s charismatic and outspoken founder, will move into an executive chairman role while Clark will also join Flexport’s board as part of the transition. “As Dave said when I was interviewing him, ‘In five years, Flexport will be known, hands down, as the best supply chain company in the world,’” Petersen said in the last of 21 tweets announcing the change in leadership. “Dave is better [at] the things we need to win at the next stage.” Petersen and Flexport declined a request for comment from JOC.com Wednesday. It’s unlikely the move will have an immediate impact on Flexport’s customers as any changes will likely be incremental. However, one priority Clark will inherit is the need to develop Flexport’s relationships with container lines, which during a time of tight capacity are critical for forwarders similar to Flexport to cultivate as forwarders are not taken seriously by shippers unless they can prove they have secured the capacity to back up their services. The privately held Flexport self-reported topline revenue of $3.3 billion in 2021 when it announced its latest funding round Feb. 7, revenue that includes pass-through freight costs paid to carriers. That $935 million tranche, led by famed venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, valued Flexport at $8 billion. In his announcement Wednesday, Petersen said Flexport is on course for nearly $5 billion in topline revenue in 2022, adding that the company is profitable. He also said at least $1 billion of the $2.3 billion in funding it has raised is “in the bank,” according to a Forbes report on the leadership change. He also said Flexport’s headcount had reached 3,500 globally, far lower than the 78,000 staffers employed by Kuehne + Nagel, for reference. Still, Flexport has yet to achieve a dominant position in its core transportation lane, the eastbound Trans-Pacific, much less globally. According to data from August 2021 provided by PIERS, a sister company of JOC.com within S&P Global, Flexport was the 15th largest non-vessel-operating common carrier on that lane between January and August. Its 37.6 percent year-on-year growth in volume in that period placed it in the middle of the pack relative to its peers on the list. Early concern from other forwarders about the threat of Flexport using software as a true differentiator in a highly fragmented market has waned in recent years. A range of forwarders that asked not to be identified have indicated to JOC.com that they don’t encounter Flexport in the market very often. Interestingly, the comment from Petersen about Clark needing five years to turn Flexport into “the best supply chain company in the world” might be a clue that Flexport’s rise is behind schedule. The company, founded in 2013, has grown its revenue markedly over the past decade, but has yet to deliver paradigm-shifting technology into a market that hasn’t stood still. Flexport has faced not only the rise of Amazon as a tech-enabled third-party logistics provider, which Clark oversaw, but also the emergence of other regional digitally native forwarders, such as Forto in Europe, which has raised hundreds of millions from some of the same venture capital groups that have backed Flexport. The big legacy forwarders have also prioritized technology development in the past decade. The five-year window also dovetails with the time horizon of a typical private equity investment, signaling that Clark was brought in not merely to continue the work Flexport was doing, but to take the company from point A to point B over a defined period. “When you raise a bunch of money, and then there's a CEO change shortly after the raise, the CEO change was likely a condition of the raise,” a logistics technology founder who asked not to be identified told JOC.com. While there is nothing to suggest this was the case with the decision to bring Clark into Flexport, speculation will likely run rampant. Clark’s arrival will be seen by some as a coup, coming off 23 years in building Amazon’s prowess as a global logistics powerhouse, both to serve its own goods movement as a shipper and in serving the needs of its third-party marketplace sellers. More recently, Amazon has become a player in third-party logistics across trucking, ocean freight, and trade compliance, serving shippers that don’t sell on its marketplace. The move can also be viewed as Petersen recognizing there was a limit as to how far he could take the company, which he essentially admitted both in tweet form and in the Forbes piece on the leadership change. That admission will undoubtedly fuel commentary from a horde of industry cynics, who have often derided Flexport on social media as being little more than a well-marketed standard forwarder, which similar to other forwarders must devote massive people-hours to solving problems that can’t be solved through automation. The reality probably lies somewhere in the middle of Petersen’s grand vision to create “the operating system of global trade” and those cynical takes of outsiders. In a decade, Flexport has become a multi-billion-dollar logistics provider, and one attractive enough to lure a true logistics heavyweight in Clark. Flexport has also been a standard-bearer for the logistics technology sector in that time, serving as a reference point for other technology players as well as incumbent forwarders. More than a handful of mid-size forwarders have privately confided to JOC.com that the emergence of Flexport has forced them to increase their focus on technology and on the shipper-user experience. It has also fueled an entire sub-industry of logistics tech providers, such as Logixboard, Shipamax, and Vector.ai, dedicated to helping small and mid-size forwarders automate and thus protect themselves from larger and more tech-enabled forwarders such as Flexport.
