title: Looming copper shortfall threatens business sustainability goals: report
content: Growing demand for copper from key parts of the energy transition — electric vehicles, solar and wind equipment, and power lines — will likely outstrip supply later this decade, potentially putting the goal of net zero carbon emissions in 2050 out of reach, according to S&P Global analysts. The energy transition will help drive the total global demand for copper to about 50 million metric tons a year by 2035 from about 25 mmt today, the analysts said in a report released last Thursday. However, even assuming record levels of mining and recycling, there won’t be enough copper to meet that demand, Daniel Yergin, S&P Global vice chairman, said during a presentation on the study. “This study is a wake-up call,” he said. Copper is the “essential metal” for the energy transition because of its pervasive use in various technologies such as EVs and EV chargers, according to Yergin. S&P expects copper demand from segments in the energy transition will jump to about 21 mmt by 2035, up from about 8 mmt today, with EVs, EV charging equipment and a buildout of the transmission and distribution system driving the growth, according to Olivier Beaufils, associate director, Americas Consulting, S&P Global Commodity Insights. Light-duty EVs, for example, contains about 2.5 times more copper than their gasoline-fueled counterparts, he said. “The 2050 climate objectives will not be achieved without a significant ramp-up in copper production in the near and medium term, which will be very challenging,” analysts said in the report. The United States imports about half its copper, but S&P expects imports to climb to 57% to 67% of its demand by 2035. The U.S. and other countries won’t simply be able to build more mines to meet the growing demand for copper, according to the S&P analysts. On average it takes about 16 years to develop a copper mine, Yergin said, citing the International Energy Agency. “Absent a major policy shift, however, regulatory, permitting, and legal challenges, combined with long timelines for new mines to come onstream, will continue to dampen the pace of supply increases,” the analysts said in the report. The challenge to increasing copper supplies will be compounded by increasingly complex geopolitical and country-level operating environments, including the strategic rivalry between the United States and China, the analysts said. Technology and policy innovations will be needed to cut the copper supply-demand gap, according to the report. That will require partnerships among governments, producers and end users, the analysts said. They called for more study on three key areas, including technology innovations to enable cleaner mining and refining of copper, partly to reduce the carbon footprint of the copper industry and to make it easier to get permits for new production, according to the report. They also urged clearer and more stable policies around permitting timelines and investment as well as a better understanding of the need for other critical minerals. Last month, the United States, nine other countries and the European Commission formed the Minerals Security Partnership to bolster “critical mineral” supply chains, partly to fortify access to key minerals needed for clean energy technologies, according to the U.S. State Department.

title: Oakland port officials push for opening terminal access as trucking protests continue
content: OAKLAND, Calif. — After four days of protests, Port of Oakland officials reached out to a group of owner-operators on Thursday with a letter that, they hoped, would ease the effects of picket lines on terminal operations. Protesters had hoped that the letter would contain some sign that the state of California was hearing their concerns over the landmark AB5 labor law and was considering action. Many, as a result, were optimistic when Desmond DeMoss, safety and continuity officer at the Port of Oakland, arrived at Matson Terminal with five copies of the letter. The letter, which was sent to Transport Dive as well as the protesters, includes a statement from the port director with a commitment to remain a liaison between truckers and the state, a statement from the governor’s office affirming AB5 remains in effect and an order to stop blocking terminal operations as of Monday or face a citation. Owner-operators said the letter was a disappointment and lacked several key details. “At this stage, obviously, we want to try to come to very amicable solutions so we can all get back to work and get this place running again and get you back to work so you can feed your families, we can be profitable and just see great things happen,” DeMoss told the crowd of protesters. After a quick glance at the contents of the letter, Navdeep Ngill, president of Ocean Rail Logistics who was liasing with DeMoss, said: “It is teaching us what AB5 is. But it doesn’t say we will pause it for this time being.” DeMoss replied that neither he nor the port could answer questions about AB5 enforcement on behalf of the government of California. Soon after, he left the visibly upset crowd with more questions than answers. The crowd of protesters then split off to weigh their next steps and waited for more word from Ngill and others, who came back with a question for the group. “Anyone who thinks that this paper [letter] accomplished anything?” The crowd loudly responded, “No, nothing.” Ngill then said, “So it brought us back to ground zero,” with some replying, “Yes.” Finally, Ngill asked the group what they should do on Friday morning, to which the crowd yelled, “Strike!” “Continue the protest!” Stay here!” Harpeet Sandhu, executive director of the American Sikh Caucus Committee, advised the protesters get legal representation. “I suggest you all somehow get a lawyer and respond to this letter.” The letter, Sandhu said, had created a paper trail that could start legal action. Hardeep Grewal, an owner-operator since 2003, closed out the gathering with a call to action for protesters to recruit friends and ensure there was a strong presence on Friday, if they wanted the protests to continue. Dozens of protesters gathered at the port on Friday morning to continue their efforts. Many expect protests will continue through Monday, though they said they would wait to decide until the end of the day.

title: Ocean rates past peak, but will remain elevated: K+N CEO
content: Two-thirds of air cargo handled by Kuehne + Nagel is carried in freighter aircraft, with the rest in bellies of passenger planes. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The highly elevated spot rates on the major ocean trade lanes have passed their peak, but shippers should expect short-term prices to settle at two- to three times pre-pandemic levels for the foreseeable future, Kuehne + Nagel CEO Detlef Trefzger said Monday. “We have seen an extreme peak of spot rates in the past and this seems to be behind us,” Trefzger told analysts on a first-half earnings call. “Sea freight rates in the decade pre-pandemic were historically low. Our scenario is that for this decade on average, those contracted rates will be significantly higher than in the previous decade.” Drewry’s World Container Index fell 2.6 percent last week to $6,820/FEU, which was 24 percent lower than the same week in 2021. Spot rates from Shanghai to Rotterdam at $9,092/FEU as of July 21 are down 30 percent year over year, while Shanghai to Los Angeles rates at $7,280/FEU are down 27 percent, according to Drewry. But even as rates softened through the first half, they remain significantly higher compared with the same period last year, both in air and ocean. This contributed to a record half-year result for Kuehne + Nagel and allowed Trefzger, who retires on July 31 after nine years at the helm, to hand over a highly profitable group to incoming CEO Stefan Paul. In the January through June period, Kuehne + Nagel group revenue rose 55 percent year over year to $21.4 billion, earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) more than doubled to $2.28 billion, and net profit rose 113 percent to $1.63 billion. Ocean and air business drive almost 80 percent of the group revenue, and both segments reported significant year-over-year improvements in profitability. In ocean, despite a 3.4 percent decline in volume to 2.2 million TEU, the average gross profit per TEU of $932 was 53 percent higher year over year. EBIT per TEU through the first half was up 139 percent. In air freight, volume increased 16 percent to 1.14 million tons, with the average gross profit per 100 kg of $220 up 55 percent compared with the first half of last year. Increases were also reported in Kuehne + Nagel’s road and contract logistics segments. Road logistics revenue was up 12 percent to $2.1 billion, although high rate levels pushed EBIT up 48 percent year over year to $81 million. Contract logistics revenue topped $2.5 billion, up 7 percent, while EBIT was up 13 percent to $84 million. Trefzger believes the profitable operating environment will continue, at least through the third quarter, with no easing of disrupted air and ocean markets. “There will be a peak season,” he assured analysts. “We don’t see a turn in the disruption at the moment. We don’t see an escalation, but we don’t see a turn either. There is no major change ... we are where we were a quarter ago regarding disruption.” Trefzger said the problem facing forwarders in air and ocean was not a lack of demand, but a shortage of capacity. Container ships are tied up by congestion in the US, Europe, and Asia, and the belly cargo capacity in passenger planes has not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels. “That has been a characteristic of the market for the last 12 to 18 months. We have a supply problem. We do not have a demand bottleneck,” he said. “Growth will resume as soon as capacity is available again. I believe we will not see a major increase in capacity offered for the next six to 12 months.” In air cargo, Kuehne + Nagel is currently carrying 65 percent of its air freight in freighters and 35 percent as belly cargo, but the amount of below-deck capacity available on long-haul passenger aircraft will decline into the winter months. “Now is the season for passenger planes with the summer vacations, but for the winter season the belly capacity will be reduced,” Trefzger said. “Some major markets are still not offering free entry into the country, like China, which limits the belly capacity into one of our strongest markets.” Contact Greg Knowler at greg.knowler@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @greg_knowler. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Trade groups demand EU review carrier anti-trust exemption
content: Trade groups complain that the benefits of the block exemption enjoyed by shipping lines in Europe are not being shared with the rest of the economy. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Ten trade organizations dependent on container shipping have demanded the European Commission immediately launch a review of carriers’ exemption from competition law to allow time for changes to be made before the block exemption expires in April 2024. The demand for an urgent review of Europe’s Consortia Block Exemption Regulation turns up the heat on the European Commission following a report earlier this month by the International Transport Forum (ITF) that called for greater government regulation of container shipping to ensure fair competition. The trade organizations representing shippers, forwarders, ports, terminals, and intermodal service providers said in a joint statement Monday that the benefits of the block exemption enjoyed by shipping lines are not being shared with the rest of the economy, which is “in itself a compelling reason” to begin an urgent review. “The effects of lockdowns on the production of goods and the shifts in demand due to the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic were certainly significant,” the groups said. “But the ability of the shipping industry to collectively manage these impacts and at the same time generate profits totaling over $186 billion in 2021, at the expense of the rest of the supply chain and ultimately Europe’s consumers, demonstrates that something is wrong.” Signatories to the joint statement cover a wide range of carrier customers, including the Global Shippers’ Forum, European Shippers’ Council, the European Association for Forwarding, Transport, Logistics and Customs Services (CLECAT), and the International Federation of Freight Forwarders Associations (FIATA). The block exemption outlines the conditions under which liner shipping alliances can provide joint services without violating EU antitrust rules. But the statement said the regulation allowed carriers to avoid “many of the checks and balances of EU competition law” and exchange commercially sensitive information to manage the number and size of ships deployed, and the frequency of sailings. “European businesses and other parties in the supply chain have suffered huge disruption to the movement of goods by container shipping since the regulation was last renewed in April 2020, with many sailings being cancelled or diverted to other ports, and ports being bypassed at short notice,” the statement noted. “At the same time shipping rates have more than quadrupled on many routes and continue to remain three to four times higher than in 2019 before the pandemic.” Short-term rates from Asia to North Europe valid for 88 days or less are currently at $5,753/TEU, almost seven times higher than during the same week in pre-pandemic 2019, according to rate benchmarking platform Xeneta. Long-term contract rates on Asia–North Europe of $5,151/TEU are almost six times that of the same week in 2019. On the Asia–US West Coast trade, the current short-term rate of $6,683/FEU and the long-term rate of $7,337/FEU are both six times higher than the rates recorded in the same week in 2019. In their letter to the European Commission (EC), the signatories highlighted the investigations conducted in the US by the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC), which resulted in President Joe Biden in June signing into law the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22), “addressing many of the grievances of users and services suppliers to the container shipping lines.” It was the first major US shipping reform in more than two decades, giving maritime regulators greater oversight over container storage fees and the ability to monitor whether ocean carriers are adhering to revised rules on loading exports. But not all the US probes found in favor of shippers. An FMC fact-finding study (FF29) released in May concluded unequivocally that competition in container shipping was “vigorous” and that rates did not rise to all-time highs last year and remain significantly elevated not because of collusion, but rather “are the product of the market forces of supply and demand.” This was a point highlighted by John Butler, president and CEO of the World Shipping Council, who told JOC.com earlier this month that liner shipping is “a very closely monitored industry” and that carriers actively compete in the global marketplace. While the European Commission has not yet launched a formal evaluation, EC spokesperson Maria Tsoni told JOC.com recently that a “fact finding exercise” has begun to collect information from carriers operating on European trades, which will feed into a review of the block exemption regulation that expires on April 25, 2024. “Before it expires, the commission will evaluate its impact and relevance in order to determine whether it should be prolonged and, if so, under which conditions,” she said. However, the shipper and forwarder groups say a formal review is urgently needed as it will require all parties to submit evidence and arguments on how the container shipping market can operate in a way that is “fair and transparent to all parties in the maritime supply chain.” “This should include consideration of new measures and mechanisms and should allow sufficient time for these to be considered and implemented before the expiry of the current regulation in April 2024,” the joint statement said. title: Falling rates to test shippers’ long-term contract resolve: DSV
content: A solid first half saw DSV almost double its net profit to $1.3 billion. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The strategy adopted by several major carriers of offering attractive rates to lock shippers into multi-year contracts will be tested as rate levels continue to decline, DSV’s Jens Lund said Tuesday. “Carriers invest in their customers to get some of the large accounts on board,” Lund, the COO of the Danish forwarder, told analysts in a first-half earnings call, adding that securing lower rates comes with some sort of commitment in the length of the contract. “We hear customers accept a lower service level because they can only use one shipping line, but the price difference sometimes is significant and that persuades them to move in that direction,” he added. “They will have a fun time if the rates drop off because of course we will phone and say ‘listen, we have a better rate for you.’ That is going to happen.” Spot rates from Shanghai to Rotterdam at $9,092/FEU as of July 21 are down 33 percent since Jan. 1, while Shanghai to Los Angeles rates at $7,280/FEU are down 28 percent, according to maritime consultancy Drewry. The same disrupted markets and elevated rate levels that are driving extreme carrier profitability also served DSV well through the first half. The forwarder’s six-month revenue of $16.9 billion was an increase of 42 percent year over year. Gross profit rose 40 percent to $3.7 billion, earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) were up 110 percent at $1.9 billion, and first-half net profit of $1.3 billion was up 95 percent. DSV reported a 1 percent decline in air cargo volume in the first half, but the 814,000 tons was above the global market that DSV estimates declined overall between 3 percent and 6 percent. In the ocean segment, the forwarder handled 1.35 million TEU in the first six months, down 6 percent year over year against a global market that DSV estimates also declined between 3 percent and 6 percent. Despite a clearly softening freight market, DSV has increased its previous operating profit outlook for 2022 by 8 percent and is now expecting full-year EBIT to be between $3.1 billion and $3.4 billion. DSV CEO Jens Bjørn Andersen told analysts that a drop in rate levels was built into the guidance through a “not so optimistic scenario” at the lower end of the range. “We did not see a drop in yields in Q2, but with the anticipated developments in the market with rates continuing to go down and capacity coming back in, we do expect the yields to come down, but not to anywhere near where they were prior to COVID-19,” Andersen said. This was a point made by Detlef Trefzger, CEO of Kuehne + Nagel, during the forwarder’s first-half results Monday. Trefzger warned shippers to expect short-term prices to settle at two- to three times pre-pandemic levels for the foreseeable future. There will also be no easing of North Europe’s congestion in the foreseeable future, according to DSV, largely a result of infrastructure shortcomings in port and inland logistics that limit handling volume. “There is no help for this because there are no significant investments that will resolve these issues,” Lund told JOC.com in an interview Tuesday ahead of DSV’s results announcement. “There has been no investment across the board at ports in Western Europe. “We will continue to have systematic disruptions of the supply chain,” he added. “There is not enough capacity on trains, and in haulage, there has been a shortage of container vessels. We can do the line haul from A to B, but we can’t get the equipment out of the ports because there is not enough capacity.” That was having a significant impact on inventory levels as importers increased order volume to compensate for delays across disrupted supply chains, filling all available warehouses “We are getting closer to the capacity limits of critical infrastructure, and when you go above what the capacity can handle, you have all the disruptions,” Lund said. “Some importers have bought too much, but others have planned for an unstable supply chain and are holding more stock,” he added. “We also have customers adjusting business continuity plans using several warehouses instead of one. All the warehouses in Europe are full. There is no empty space in the market.” Contact Greg Knowler at greg.knowler@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @greg_knowler. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Shippers seeking outsourced logistics aid despite rise of self-service software
content: Logistics technology vendors have told JOC.com that they have seen an increase in demand for so-called managed transportation or lead logistics provider services this year. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The COVID-19 pandemic has provided shippers with a stark reminder of how quickly and steeply market dynamics can shift. Historically, market upheaval has led shippers to turn to service providers and consultants to help manage key ocean freight processes. And despite a surfeit of logistics technology having arrived on the scene the past decade — tech designed to be cheaper and easier to implement than earlier generations — software vendors have told JOC.com they have seen a rise in demand for what’s commonly called managed transportation services. Managed transportation is where a third-party logistics provider (3PL) or software vendor not only provides a system to a shipper, but also runs the system on behalf of the shipper. The lure of managed transportation services for a shipper generally is driven by three factors: where logistics isn’t considered a core competency, where it lacks the resources or expertise to manage some aspects of logistics management, and where it feels the system provider’s acumen allows it to better leverage the system. Fran Barker, logistics and supply chain procurement practice lead at Accenture, said a shipper outsourcing logistics processes is like “buying maturity.” “You're behind on what it takes to run the process and the tech and you want to learn from experts,” Barker said on a recent webcast about outsourcing ocean freight planning and execution, held by the software vendor BuyCo. In the meantime, a fourth dynamic has become more pronounced during the pandemic: rapid changes to the external supply and demand environment that makes everything more challenging, from finding affordable capacity to the operational aspects of managing bookings. That, to a certain extent, has negated the value of technology intended to empower shipper logistics teams. Even systems designed to be used in-house are seeing a rise in requests for managed transportation from shippers, a service often referred to as lead logistic provider arrangement. For instance, Jonas Krumland, CEO of Germany-based logistics technology provider Logward, told JOC.com the company has seen an influx in demand for such services this year from customers and has added resources to handle those requests. The software provider, spun out of the German forwarder Leshaco, specializes in serving industrial shippers. Barker, meanwhile, said shippers must think of logistics outsourcing on a modular basis, meaning they need to decide which functions they want to handle in-house, and which are better suited to be outsourced. He also said this is not a static consideration, given the speed with which technologies designed to empower in-house management are entering the market. “A lot of shippers, not just ones on the bleeding edge, are examining which processes should be in-house, because the tech has become more accessible,” he said. “Tech that wasn’t available 10, five, or even three years ago.” In terms of ocean freight management, Barker said that shippers that had direct relationships with container lines were able to maintain access to capacity in ways that those who outsourced completely to forwarders weren’t. “Shippers in the range of $10 million to $30 million ocean freight spend struggled to get capacity last year,” he said. “Not only were their forwarders not able to hold on to their negotiated rates, shippers struggled to even get on the vessel.” Ian Kahoro, senior manager of global trade center of excellence at the Hershey Co., provided a good example of how splitting the carrier relationship — the procurement and planning aspects of ocean freight — from operations and execution works in practice. During the recent outsourcing webcast, Kahoro said that Hershey maintains direct contracts with container lines but has outsourced ocean booking to its forwarders. “We have what I call a hybrid model,” Kahoro said. “The forwarder is making the bookings for us, because that used to be a very operational piece for us that got worse the past two years. We were touching bookings three to four times.” By owning the carrier relationship, Kahoro said Hershey can maintain access to capacity for products that need to move according to seasonal promotions. And more generally, because the company’s products have a shelf life, it has enabled it to manage extended supply chain delays. “Forwarders add a lot of value to the table, but you also have to look at where you rank in what they’re doing for you,” he said. “Forwarders are representing more than just us. If it’s your product, you have to be sure it’s going where you need it. You have to own that.” Eric Gauthier, founder of Montreal-based supply chain consultant MyTLA, said the decision to outsource isn’t necessarily cut and dry in “this vast, complex industry.” But he suggested that companies with freight transportation spend of more than $2 million is a decent threshold to consider. “Let’s say a shipper has an annual spend of $2 million across ocean, air, ground, courier and global trade management services,” he told JOC.com. That company will likely have $500,000 in costs, at a minimum, associated with managing those modes, Gauthier said. The costs include $200,000 for an experienced logistics director, including salary, benefits, and expenses. Another $200,000 would be spent on technology, whether a transportation management system (TMS), supply chain portals, vendor and order management systems, configurations, and integration with other key supply chain systems, such as an enterprise resource planning tool. Another $100,000 would be spent on external services that can’t be brought in-house, such as consulting, programming, or customs services. “In that scenario, can the shipper regularly negotiate and maintain service agreements with the carriers that generate 20 percent — $400,000 — worth of savings of overall logistics spend by managing the business in-house?” Gauthier said. “What are the opportunity costs of locking in with contracted rates with one or two carriers? Will the technology stand the test of time? Does the project have the necessary, internal buy-in to get the new department up and running?” Gauthier concurred with Barker on the pace of technological advancement affecting shipper decisions about what can be taken in-house. But he added that “the managed-service industry invests heavily in their operating systems and the customer-facing portal services that make them easier to work with and harder to part from.” “Small and medium-sized shippers should compare the costs of developing these tools in-house against integrating with turnkey, value-added tools developed and maintained by industry experts,” Gauthier added. title: Longshore workers, employers reach tentative deal on healthcare benefits
content: West Coast port employers and the union representing their longshore workers on Tuesday announced they had reached a tentative deal on health benefits as part of ongoing contract talks. The deal, which covers the “maintenance of health benefits,” is subject to “agreement on the other issues in the negotiations,” the International Longshore and Warehouse Union and Pacific Maritime Association said in a joint press release. And while the two parties said they would not discuss the terms of the agreement, they said the deal represented an “important part of the contract being negotiated.” The ILWU and the Pacific Maritime Association have been negotiating a contract that covers more than 22,000 longshore workers at 29 West Coast port since May 10. The healthcare deal is the first official update indicating progress in the talks since the contract expired on July 1.

title: Port of Oakland resumes operations as AB5 protests quiet down
content: OAKLAND, Calif. — The Port of Oakland resumed normal operations on Monday as owner-operator led protests against AB5, California’s labor law, quieted down. “All four of our marine terminals are operating normally today,” Roberto Bernardo, director of communications at the Port of Oakland, told Transport Dive on Monday. Last week, hundreds of owner-operators effectively shut down operations at the port by blocking access to truck gates. But by Thursday evening, many protestors became discouraged after port officials sent a letter threatening a citation for anyone blocking terminal operations. On Friday, protest plans shifted. “We all ended up deciding that we don’t have that much on our side and we all or [a] majority of us will be going back to work,” Japi Samra, an owner-operator for 10 years, told Transport Dive in an email. Some, he added, were also looking to join an association to get better direction, funds, and legal representation. “A lot things are against us, now if we continue only we will hurt ourselves and port of Oakland business,” Samra said. Sunil Kamboj, a driver for CPX, told Transport Dive a lack of money was a big factor for many protesters who decided to return to work. “Everybody pays rent for their home,” Kamboj said. Some truckers couldn’t risk continuing to protest and not work, Kamboj said, as it would hurt their wallet. Still, some remained committed to continuing the protests, though they avoided interrupting operations. Bernardo said the protesters on Monday were in “free speech zones,” set up at a distance from any terminal gates. There were “no more than 40 or so demonstrators at any given time, spread out at four different locations within the ports” on Monday, the Oakland Police Department said in an email.

title: Tive targets cold chain, last mile with cheaper, smaller tracking device
content: When Tive raised a $54 million funding round in April, CEO Krenar Konomi said the cost of tracking devices must continue to fall to make the tech relevant to more of the market. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Freight visibility hardware provider Tive on Wednesday rolled out a lightweight, low-cost tracking device designed primarily for shippers, cold storage operators, and last-mile delivery companies. The product, called Tive Tag, is as thin as a shipping label and adheres to shipments in a similar way to labels, the company said in a statement. The new tag is also half the cost of conventional data-logging devices affixed to truck trailers, shipping containers, or pallets. Tive did not specify the cost of the tags beyond saying they are 50 percent cheaper than existing devices. The tags are designed to last for one year and are safe for air cargo because they don’t use lithium batteries, the company added. The sticker-like tracking devices capture temperature data as well as location, making it particularly suited for perishable shipments and other cold chain applications. Tive CEO Krenar Konomi said it’s been difficult to deliver hardware solutions in the first- and last-mile legs due to the price and reverse logistics burdens of more expensive devices. “Customers have been searching for a last-mile solution, and cost has always been the barrier,” he said in the statement. Tive is one of a number of players in the fast-growing internet of things (IoT) device market in logistics and transportation. The company raised $54 million in venture funding in April, and at that point had more than 300 customers. “We shipped 200,000 trackers in '21 and 75,000 in the fourth quarter alone,” Konomi told JOC.com in an April interview. “The pull and traction is just very real. Fifty-five percent of our customers have never used trackers before. They suddenly realize this is the time to switch to this type of technology.” At the time, Konomi also addressed the company’s goal of lowering the price point and improving the ease of use of the devices it made. One issue that’s weighed down the growth of companies with a hardware-based approach to visibility is the cost of devices and the reality that only certain types of shipped goods are valuable or risky enough to offset those costs. At about $40 per tracker, shippers can bristle at the idea of incurring extra cost on top of freight rates and ancillary charges, especially when they feel such monitoring services ought to be part of the price they already pay. “As trackers go to $20, you unlock more shipments, and then to $10, you unlock more potential volume,” Konomi said in the April interview. “The most globally interconnected system is the financial system. The next most global system is supply chain and logistics. But unlike in finance, what’s missing in supply chain and logistics is data.” Maritime analyst Drewry last month projected that containers equipped with tracking hardware will account for 25 percent of the global box fleet by 2026 — an eight-fold increase over current levels. The rollout of so-called smart containers was accelerated by Hapag-Lloyd's decision in April to equip 100 percent of its dry container fleet with trackable sensors. Tive’s devices can be used across freight modes. Tive’s customers include logistics providers DSV, Geodis, and Crane Worldwide Logistics, and shippers in the retail and pharmaceutical industries. title: Complaints flowing in after FMC adjusts submission process
content: Prior to OSRA-22, FMC complaints could cost shippers hundreds of thousands of dollars and took around three years to resolve, according to AgTC Executive Director Peter Friedmann. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Shippers have already filed a handful of charge complaints against ocean carriers now that new ocean shipping reform provides them an easier path to get the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) to investigate accusations of inaccurate or unfair container storage and usage fees, rolled bookings, and more. Two major shipper groups are applauding the move, saying that eliminating the need for lawyers and hefty filing fees to submit a complaint is making the agency one of enforcement, similar to the Better Business Bureau. With several complaints already filed — and more expected — after the FMC highlighted the process change, the commission will be challenged in investigating them and implementing other parts of the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22). Following an internal review of how to best implement and enforce OSRA-22, the FMC is consolidating its investigative and prosecutorial duties into a newly created Bureau of Enforcement, Investigations and Compliance (BEIC), the agency said July 29. The BEIC will comprise three sections: the Office of Enforcements, the Office of Investigations, and the Office of Compliance, with each having its own director. As a further part of the reorganization, the FMC will convert the roles of area representatives to investigators who will focus solely on enforcement activity. Lori Fellmer, vice president of logistics and carrier management at BassTech International and chair of the National Industrial Transportation League’s (NITL) ocean transportation committee, said allowing shippers to directly file a complaint without having to go through a legal team “removes some of the nonsense” involved with the previous process. “There are certain things that are not up for debate; they’re factually based,” Fellmer told JOC.com last week. “It shouldn’t be an effort of who can withstand the argument longer and spend the most money on a lawyer.” Before President Joe Biden signed OSRA-22 into law on June 16, FMC complaints could cost shippers hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees and generally took about three years to investigate and resolve, according to Peter Friedmann, executive director of the Agriculture Transportation Coalition. In addition, the losing party could be required to pay the winning party’s legal fees, often leading to a David-vs.-Goliath battle in which small shippers with few resources were taking on ocean carriers with large in-house legal teams well-versed in FMC rules. “The process had such a chilling effect that no one wanted to file anything,” Friedmann told JOC.com July 21. Whether the procedural updates will change the workflow for container lines — or lead to more complaints — is still to be determined, John Butler, president and CEO of the World Shipping Council (WSC), which represents carriers, told JOC.com. “There are a lot of options already for how to initiate a complaint with the commission, so I think we’ll have to see how it plays out and if it turns out to be fundamentally easier for everybody,” Butler said. That the FMC hit Hapag-Lloyd with an $882,220 civil penalty and Wan Hai with an $850,000 fine for detention charges two months before OSRA-22 was even passed has not only given shippers more confidence in filing complaints, but assurance they’ll be protected from retaliation, Fellmer said. The FMC is still determining its process for reviewing complaints — and has reserved the right to further amend that process — but as of now, complaints are sent to area representatives for an initial review of shipper-provided documentation, an FMC spokesperson told JOC.com last week. Already struggling to keep up with violations prior to OSRA-22 becoming law, the FMC plans to hire at least seven positions within 18 months of enactment to assist with investigations and oversight. Until then, the agency will continue to be “resource strained,” with one investigator for every $1 trillion of commerce it is investigating, FMC Commissioner Carl Bentzel said during a panel discussion Tuesday. While not all complaints are seeking refunds, and some are groundless, the FMC’s main goal in reviewing each communication is to stay in the loop on what’s going on in ocean trade. To further help the FMC zero in on violations, surveys are being sent out to shippers asking if they have received non-compliant invoices since June 16 and brought them to the carriers’ attention, and if so, what actions carriers have taken. In the meantime, carriers such as Hapag-Lloyd have updated or temporarily ceased how they assess fines while they work out a system that includes the 13 data points OSRA-22 now requires on an invoice, a process stemming from Commissioner Rebecca Dye’s Fact Finding 29 report. The FMC is also looking into claims that certain carriers are forcing shippers to sign a guarantee that they will pay future detention and demurrage charges as a condition for releasing cargo. All this data helps the agency as they continue to make decisions on rulemaking and enforcement in compliance with OSRA-22, according to the FMC spokesperson. Fellmer said as more rules are defined, more shippers are likely to come forward with complaints. “It’s a calculated decision,” she explained. As a shipper, “every time you have a problem, you think, ‘Do I want to be a pebble in the shoe of this important service provider, or suck it up and move on?’ But there comes a point where you can no longer suck it up and move on, and that’s an individual decision for each company to make. But the commission has reassured us repeatedly that they’re there to protect shippers.” Contact Teri Errico Griffis at teri.griffis@ihsmarkit.com. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: BNSF extends westbound shipping embargo into August
content: BNSF’s temporary shipping embargo of food, diesel and other commodities shipments will continue into August, the railroad announced Wednesday. The embargo of many westbound shipments to California was announced last month in a bid to lower congestion that has caused delays for the railroad and shippers, ports and other stakeholders. But BNSF plans to incrementally loosen the embargo due to recent gains in velocity across its southern region. “As we enter the next phase of our service recovery, we must proactively work together to improve the congestion in California by continuing the embargo in August,” BNSF said. “BNSF will continue to carefully review and consider customer circumstances and will increase the number of permits issued weekly as network conditions improve.” The western railroad will issue 30% more permits for the next seven-day period beginning Thursday, after train velocity reached a 90-day high over the most recent seven days, the railroad said in a release. “We will maintain our focus in the weekly permit review process on the number of shipments already in the pipeline headed to California customer destinations and work to mitigate overfilled pipelines while allowing railcars to flow where shortages might exist,” BNSF said. The shipping embargo comes after shippers and other stakeholders have pressed regulators to step in to address lengthy rail delays. BNSF said customers may refer to the railroad’s website to submit permit requests, view the list of commodities exempted and find further information about the limited embargo, which applies to non-intermodal shipments. The railroad is also continuing to reevaluate its network conditions, and as it sees further progress on reducing congestion, “we anticipate that we will be able to stop the current permit embargo structure and continue working collaboratively with individual customers as necessary to manage traffic flows,” BNSF said.

title: Supply chain issues are coming for your beer – WTT newsletter
content: Welcome to the WHAT THE TRUCK?!? newsletter. In this issue, CO2 shortages strike breweries; Senate bill proposes $40K tax credit for electric semis; dog days of the spot market; and more. Somewhat stable — You may be wondering why I haven’t talked much about the dry van spot market lately, and the truth is it’s been in a start-stall slump since May. When you’re getting less than a bottle of Two-Buck Chuck a mile, you gotta look on the bright side of the bottom: stability and normalization which sure beats a steady systematic decline. The spread between spot and contract rates is as wide as the San Andreas Fault at 94 cents. FreightWaves’ Michael Rudolph reports, “While I do not foresee contract rates dropping below linehaul spot rates before Q1 2023 (at the earliest), shippers might be especially aggressive in their Q4 renegotiations.” Speaking of spreads — FreightWaves CEO and founder Craig Fuller recently tweeted, “The spread between retail and wholesale diesel prices is pretty insane right now. Small truckers pay retail, large carriers pay wholesale. Fuel surcharges are indexed to retail. Large carriers are making bank right now.” He isn’t kidding. While that does nothing for small carriers who’ve been crushed by low rates and high fuel for months on end, the silver lining is retail is starting to see steady declines as well. Pump it up — The diesel truckstop national retail average started the month at $5.81 and has fallen to $5.41 today. Now to make you sad again: A year ago at this time dry van spot rates paid $2.58 and retail diesel cost $3.27. If the average semi gets 6 mpg, that’s a difference of $1.09 a mile (subtracting fuel from spot rates) versus $2.03 a mile a year ago. Ouch. And then the supply chain issues came for your beer Cno2 —I’d tell you to go cry in your beer, but those seem to be in short supply as a CO2 shortage is threatening the survival of some small and local breweries. Everett, Massachusetts-based Night Shift Brewing took to Instagram on Tuesday to announce that the CO2 shortfall has cost the company’s 12-person production team their jobs. To Night Shift’s credit, they’re paying those employees through Oct. 1. “Breweries depend on CO2 to make beer, so this was pretty awful news to get. Seems like this will be an issue that impacts a lot of local breweries, so we’re probably one of many breweries facing this new threat to our business.” — Night Shift Brewing on the gram Where’d the CO2 go? — Apparently, the issue stems from contaminated raw gas being sent to CO2 firms for purification. Gasworld reports, “There are a number of ways that CO2 can become contaminated by other compounds, such as oil and grease vapor, rust and pipe scale and plasticiser compounds.” On top of that, there’s less capacity for production as ammonia/fertilizer plants have had to deal with their own shutdowns. “I work at a brewery in Boston and we’re pretty much on emergency CO2 delivery only, there just isn’t that much to go around. — A poster on Reddit’s r/Boston forum Cover story? — How many times have you come across businesses using the supply chain as an excuse for other shortfalls? Good Beer Hunting alleges that Night Shift Brewing’s issues may extend well beyond a CO2 shortfall. The blog lists a failed expansion into Philadelphia, high marketing budget and a brewing facility with no room for growth that led company leaders to propose this move to Jack Abby’s facility back in January. So, all clear on the CO2? — Nope, it is still a big issue that extends well outside of our borders. Brewers in the U.K. and New Zealand have reported similar shortages. Even this splash park had to shut down as it uses CO2 to treat its water. What’s unfortunate is that just like in trucking, it’s the small guys who get canned first when costs soar. Here’s my list of highlights relating to EV tax credit in new Senate bill: • This is a big one: Commercial vehicles that weigh OVER 14,000 lbs are eligible for a $40,000 tax credit or 30% of cost of the vehicle (whatever is less). This means the @Tesla Semi will qualify. 1/10 How’s that BEV semi look now? — Ignoring the fact that the Tesla Semi is in a perpetual state of postponement, this $40,000 tax credit is good news for carriers looking to get battery electric vehicles from other manufacturers. Speaking of Tesla, among changes to the new Senate bill is that Elon Musk no longer has to go goblin mode as the $4,500 bonus credit to union-made EVs that benefited Ford and GM over Tesla has been removed. There are a number of other credits for buying noncommercial EVs, and the program would run until Dec. 31, 2032. For a snappy breakdown of what’s included, check out this thread. I suppose in the meantime, these credits could make dealer markups more palatable, though I think we’d all prefer if inventory availability drove prices down. The CHIPS Act did pass the House on Thursday, and if that goes through that certainly could help with getting all these EVs off the lot. title: DB Schenker pulls parent group back into black
content: Forwarder DB Schenker has joined its European peers in reporting a huge increase in profitability through the first half of the year. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. DB Schenker led its rail operating parent Deutsche Bahn back into profitability in the first half after two years of group losses, with the forwarding unit almost doubling its operating profit compared with the first six months of last year. "The first half of 2022 was Schenker's most successful half-year in its 150-year history as a logistics company,” Levin Holle, CFO of DB Schenker, said in a statement Thursday. “DB Schenker played a major role in bolstering the DB's favorable performance overall." It was the first profitable result for the German state-owned railroad in two years, with the group’s core passenger rail business losing more than $10 billion through the COVID-19 pandemic. "Our turnaround has been successful. Demand is booming and we have returned to profitable business,” DB CEO Richard Lutz said in the statement to investors. The turnaround was due largely to DB Schenker’s robust performance. Of the total group earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) of $1.93 billion, the Essen-based logistics subsidiary contributed $1.22 billion, close to double the profit the logistics provider earned in the first six months of 2021. DB Schenker's revenue was up 36 percent to $14.3 billion. While carriers are enjoying record profitability this year, earnings generated by the big forwarders are not far behind as they take advantage of the heavily disrupted air and ocean markets. Kuehne + Nagel this week reported H1 group revenue was up 55 percent year over year to $21.4 billion, while EBIT more than doubled to $2.28 billion and net profit jumped 113 percent to $1.63 billion. DSV’s six-month revenue of $16.9 billion was an increase of 42 percent year over year, gross profit rose 40 percent to $3.7 billion, EBIT was up 110 percent at $1.9 billion, and first-half net profit of $1.3 billion was up 95 percent. title: A looming graphite shortage could snarl the EV battery supply chain
content: Experts warn that supply of a key component in electric vehicles is hurtling towards a tipping point when global demand will outstrip supply — a moment that could come as early as this year. Graphite is one of the primary components that make up the anodes in a lithium ion battery, yet the state of its supply has gone largely unnoticed for years, even as demand for battery-grade minerals continues to rise with electric vehicle sales reaching record levels. “Graphite has kind of been the poor cousin of the battery minerals and doesn’t get the attention of the other commodities,” said Gregory Bowes, executive chairman of the Northern Graphite Corporation. “But we’re getting very close to an inflection point where demand overtakes supply and this is going to be first page news.” Supply of the key EV-battery mineral is headed for a deficit of just over 20,000 tons this year, a shortfall that will only balloon throughout the next decade, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence estimates. Graphite mines are located in only a few places around the globe, making global manufacturers reliant on limited procurement sources and vulnerable to supply shocks. Last year, China produced 79% of the world’s graphite supply, according to the USGS, compared to just 1.2% in North America — none of which came from the U.S. And China is home to not only the majority of the world’s graphite mines, but also the downstream processing that’s necessary to make the material usable in batteries. “The supply is getting tighter and tighter and the downstream demand for graphite is accelerating really, really rapidly,” said Daisy Jennings-Gray, senior price analyst at Benchmark. Since September 2021, prices per ton of the high-grade graphite mostly commonly used in lithium ion batteries have risen from $530 per ton to $825 per ton in June 2022, according to Benchmark. The group expects that number to top $1,000 per ton in 2025, and to remain at “a high level” through 2030. Higher costs and tight supply have more companies looking to secure supply by diversifying their sourcing or investing in production themselves. Last year, Tesla announced a deal with Australian graphite mine operator Syrah Resources to buy the mineral from one of Syrah’s sites in Mozambique, part of the automaker’s strategy to reduce its supply reliance on China. And Northern Graphite, which currently operates a mine in Quebec, plans to open a second mine in Bissett Creek in southern Canada to up its own graphite production as demand continues to grow. On the U.S. side, the Biden administration has deemed graphite a “critical mineral,” prioritizing it and other battery-grade materials, including lithium and cobalt, for investment. In February, the administration announced nearly $3 billion in funding to bolster supply chains for advanced batteries. Alabama has emerged as home to what will become the U.S.′ first graphite processing plant. Westwater Resources and its subsidiary, Alabama Graphite Products, broke ground on the site in April with plans to be operational by the second quarter of 2023, according to local reports. Westwater President and CEO Chris Jones noted last year that initially the raw graphite processed in the plant will be imported, but “none of it will be from China.” The company also expects to open a new mining operation in the area by 2028. While the move towards a more diversified supplier and processing base is positive, Bowes stressed that solving the problem is not a quick fix, and one that will take billions of dollars to tackle. “The crux [of the problem] is we need a lot more supply and construction has not started yet,” he said. “So there’s going to be a very serious point here where the automakers and battery makers look around and there’s not enough graphite and it can take a few years minimum to build a mine.”

title: Shipper seeks FMC intervention after $3 million in D&D charges
content: A food importer was hit with nearly $3 million in detention and demurrage fees by an NVO handling its reefer container business. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. A food importer is seeking relief from the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) after the company says it was hit with almost $3 million in detention and demurrage fees from a non-vessel-operating (NVO) common carrier at the Port of New York and New Jersey. New York–based Bakerly says Seafrigo, an NVO based in New Jersey, billed it $2,973,475 in fees from October 2021 through March 2022. Of that amount, $2,357,244 was for demurrage, and $616,230 for detention. In reviewing the charges, Bakerly’s account team found multiple invoice billings per purchase order when only one should have been applied, the company said in a complaint to the FMC filed Wednesday. Bakerly put a stop payment on the invoices that had not been paid. The shipper now wants reimbursement for the $973,227 it has already paid and is disputing the remaining charges. “This invoicing negligence prevented Bakerly from paying any of these invoices as Seafrigo has never offered any explanations for any reason that the charges were repetitious even when paid,” the complaint said. A spokesperson for Seafrigo told JOC.com Thursday the company had no comment. Bakerly could not be reached for comment. The invoices were billed prior to the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 being signed into law June 16, under which parties may invoke self-executing provisions to eliminate detention and demurrage charges if the invoices are incomplete or incorrect. Bakerly said in the complaint that it should stand to reason that the invoices, no matter the timing, “do not pass the standards of the Interpretative Rule.” “Failure to include accurate information on D&D invoices with any demurrage or detention charge eliminates any obligation of the charged party to pay the applicable charge based on the current provisions,” Bakerly said. The complaint brought by Bakerly is another in a string of detention and demurrage cases the FMC has investigated of late. The agency hit Hapag-Lloyd with an $882,220 civil penalty in April and Wan Hai with an $850,000 fine a month later, both for detention cases. Bringing attention to violations has gotten easier under OSRA-22 and the FMC’s recent move to nix the need for lawyers and filing fees to submit a grievance with the agency. title: FMC reorganizes enforcement duties in aftermath of OSRA-22
content: The Federal Maritime Commission is hiring more investigators as part of stepped-up enforcement activities driven by OSRA-22. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Amid ongoing efforts to enforce new shipping reform in the US, the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) Friday said it is consolidating its investigative and prosecutorial duties into a newly created Bureau of Enforcement, Investigations and Compliance (BEIC). The reorganization follows an internal FMC investigation to identify ways to increase the effectiveness of the commission’s enforcement and compliance activities as the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022, signed into law by President Joe Biden on June 16, rolls out, the FMC said in a statement. “The review determined a restructuring and merging of enforcement and compliance programs would result in a more efficient, coordinated, and responsive operation from initiation to conclusion of an investigation,” the FMC said. The BEIC will be comprised of three sections: the Office of Enforcements, the Office of Investigations, and the Office of Compliance, with each having its own director. Under OSRA-22, the FMC is required to increase its staff by no fewer than seven positions to assist in investigation oversight; it has requested an increase in funding to fund those positions for fiscal year 2023, which begins Oct. 1. As a further part of the reorganization, the FMC will convert the roles of area representatives to investigators who will focus solely on enforcement activity, the agency said. “This reorganization has the support of all five commissioners and creates a structure better suited to meeting the mandate the President and Congress have given this agency to prioritize enforcement,” FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei said in the statement. “Specifically, it enhances FMC’s capacity to closely scrutinize the conduct of the ocean carrier companies and marine terminal operators to ensure compliance with the law and fairness for American importers and exporters.” The FMC has already filled a few new positions, Maffei said at the agency’s public meeting Wednesday. Although the agency has 18 months to fill the roles under OSRA-22, hiring will be done in fiscal year 2022, which ends Sept. 30. Maffei said in June the agency was already understaffed and his goal was to increase the team of 115 to 150 as soon as possible. The new FMC enforcement bureau will be led by an attorney with regulatory, prosecutorial, and investigative experience. FMC Managing Director Lucille M. Marvin will serve as acting BEIC director until a permanent hire is made. Contact Teri Errico Griffis at teri.griffis@ihsmarkit.com. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: DAT, Convoy embroiled in anti-competition legal battle
content: Convoy’s June countersuit against DAT alleges that DAT puts freight brokers in an “untenable position” by making them agree to exclusive deals with non-compete clauses. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. DAT Freight & Analytics and Convoy, two prominent players in the US domestic truckload market, have been engaged in a legal feud since January over a commercial relationship that soured as Convoy built what DAT alleges is a competitive product to its flagship load board product. The two companies have filed suit against one another, with DAT alleging that freight broker Convoy breached its contract with DAT by using DAT’s proprietary data to build a rival product to DAT’s load board, and Convoy countersuing over what it calls monopolistic behavior from DAT. The case could have major implications in the spot truckload space, as DAT is the industry’s largest load board, while Convoy is a well-known digital intermediary that has raised hundreds of millions of venture capital investment to reshape the truckload market. In a Jan. 19 lawsuit filed in US District Court in Oregon, DAT alleged that Convoy, a freight brokerage, used its relationship as a DAT customer to build a competitive digital load board, an act that breached a non-compete clause in Convoy’s contract with DAT, originally signed in 2016 and amended in 2018. Aside from operating the industry’s largest load board, Oregon-based DAT provides associated rate benchmarking products. The alleged contract breach came to DAT’s attention in early November 2021, two weeks before Convoy launched a new product, Convoy for Brokers. DAT asserts that product is directly competitive to its core load board product and was built based on data obtained through its relationship with DAT, according to its January lawsuit. DAT ended its contract with Convoy after learning of the alleged breach, and it asserts Convoy then quickly moved to introduce its competitive product to the market, the lawsuit alleges. On June 17, Convoy filed a countersuit against DAT, alleging that DAT engages in monopolistic behavior by forcing broker and carrier customers — which pay subscription fees to access the DAT load board — into non-compete agreements that prohibit them from developing more advanced load-matching products and services. What’s more, Convoy alleges in the countersuit that by charging higher subscription fees to its broker customers that want to use other load boards to find available cargo, DAT is engaging in behavior designed to insulate it from competition. “When Convoy did buy itself out of DAT’s exclusivity requirements, Convoy found that competing services lacked coverage and quality because DAT had locked up a substantial portion of the relevant market and denied others access to data,” the broker said in its June countersuit. The lawsuits are still pending. Both DAT and Convoy declined to comment to JOC.com, citing the ongoing litigation. JOC parent company S&P Global has a strategic data partnership with DAT. The case could have implications for the US spot truckload market, as DAT is a primary source of available loads which brokers and carriers use to fill their pools of owned or third-party capacity. In its June 17 countersuit, Convoy claimed that DAT’s load board effectively has a 64 percent share of “the relevant market based on the volume of loads posted to DAT and the understanding that a significant portion of those loads are exclusive to DAT.” “DAT’s 887,000 loads per day would mean that over 40 percent of all full truckloads in the United States are posted to DAT’s load board,” Convoy asserted in the June filing. “This 40 percent is relative to the entire universe of truckload freight, including the volume covered by contract and asset carriers. Thus, DAT’s share of the loads posted to spot freight matching services is far higher.” Convoy’s lawsuit is primarily about the extent to which new freight marketplaces, whether neutral software entities or brokers themselves, can break free from what it has characterized as the industry’s reliance on DAT, and to a lesser extent, its main competitor Truckstop.com. “DAT’s load board, although antiquated in many ways, remains a must-have source of load matching services for carriers and brokers moving spot freight,” Convoy said in its countersuit. “DAT boasts of its dominance. A monopolist is rarely so brazen that it openly directs others not to compete. DAT, however, is not bashful. DAT writes into some of its contracts a provision completely prohibiting its customers from competing with DAT. DAT thus presents broker customers with an untenable choice: either agree not to compete with DAT under any circumstances or lose access to DAT’s load board and to the carriers that use DAT to source loads.” For its part, DAT asserted in the original January filing that Convoy, founded in 2015, essentially used DAT’s load board and benchmarking product, called RateView, to rapidly develop an internal capability that it would ordinarily not have. “Convoy could not have built [and did not build] its pricing algorithm, or otherwise create a functional load board, without using and misappropriating the proprietary data and trade secrets it was accessing for improper purposes on the DAT load board,” DAT said in the January lawsuit. “Convoy independently has no meaningful long-haul history, rate history, lane history, or other data that would be required to develop and operate an automated, algorithmic-driven digital load board like ‘Convoy for Brokers.’” DAT said the only source for “the volume and quality of data and information needed to develop and launch its competing load board” from which Convoy could have developed Convoy for Brokers was its own load board, which DAT says was accessed “under the guise of acting as a broker ...” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Stanley Black & Decker to slash SKUs, footprint in $1.5B savings plan
content: Stanley Black & Decker is transforming its supply chain as it works “with a sense of urgency” to generate cash flow, according to vice president of business development and interim CFO Corbin Walburger. The toolmaker found itself saddled with extra product after easing consumer demand pushed retailers to slow purchases. The company ended Q2 with $6.6 billion in inventory, which is higher than historical levels and a $400 million increase from the prior quarter. Stanley Black & Decker has already begun curtailing production of finished inventory as it looks to normalize inventory levels, according to Walburger, a move that is expected to raise costs over the next three to four quarters. Over time, the company will reposition manufacturing, sourcing and distribution closer to the end customer to shorten lead times and reduce reliance on safety stock. “So, you have a choice: Maintain very high levels of inventory due to the long supply chain, or have your supply chain closer to your customer, elevate your agility and resiliency to better serve those customers,” Allan said. “We believe being closer to the customer is the right answer.” The company is looking to pare down its network of 120 manufacturing facilities, with Allan noting the business plans to “simplify and consolidate our regional footprints around high performing industry core, technology enabled sites.” To secure supply, Stanley Black & Decker will leverage more contract manufacturing and deepen relationships with suppliers. Beyond cutting costs, the transformation plan is meant to insulate the company from long term disruption and position the toolmaker to bring products to market faster. Standardizing components means that products will be built around “common building blocks,” allowing the company to make more high-scale purchases and shorten product cycles. “Our success with this transformation will build a more sustainable, agile and efficient supply chain that is resilient in an ever-changing and dynamic operating environment,” Allan said.

title: Transportation capacity rises again in July, pricing declines, report says
content: Supply chain data released Tuesday showed further cooling in transportation markets. The July Logistics Managers’ Index (LMI) fell 4.3 percentage points to 60.7, the lowest reading in the data set since May 2020. A reading above 50 indicates expansion while a reading below 50 indicates contraction. “While this does still represent a healthy rate of expansion in the logistics industry, it is a far cry from March when the index hit an all-time high reading of 76.2,” the report read. The transportation prices subindex dropped 11.8 points in the month to 49.5. This was the first time in two years the pricing data was in contraction territory. However, the report noted that the exit rate for the month was 8 percentage points higher than in the beginning of the month. Transportation prices logged a 54.7 reading in the last week of July. “We will continue to watch this space to determine whether this late July surge was an aberration, or a sign of breaking from the usual July doldrums and peak season coming over the horizon,” the report continued. A 7.4-point jump in available transportation capacity (69.1) drove pricing lower in the month. This was the fastest growth rate for capacity since April 2019. However, the increase in capacity was “much more muted in the last week of July.” Transportation utilization was up less than a point from June at 59.3, but the index marked 27 consecutive months of growth. Transportation markets were notably tighter for downstream companies, or those closer to the end consumer, than upstream producers. The 12-month forward-looking survey showed respondents believe transportation prices will remain high. The survey returned a reading of 58.7, which was 0.9 lower than June’s reading. The elevated rate expectation supports recent commentary from the C-suites of the nation’s biggest trucking companies. During the second quarter, many trucking executives said they expect rates to remain high as they continue to pass through cost inflation to shippers. Inventory levels (68.8) remained in growth mode, but the pace was 3 percentage points lower than in June. The index has also moved well off the February high of 80.2. “There are signs of a slowdown in what had been out of control inventory growth as the current value is a mere 2.4 points higher than the same time last year,” the report said. “This means that seasonally speaking, inventories are increasing only slightly more quickly than one year ago.” Inventory costs (79), down 4.8 points sequentially, have also pulled back from highs set earlier in the year. The total cost to hold merchandise will likely stay high as available warehouse space is in short supply and interest rates continue to increase. Warehousing capacity continued to contract but at a slower pace. The subindex stood at 47 in July, a 6-point increase from June. “This metric has been in a state of contraction since August of 2020, as high inventory levels and a long lead time on building new space has made it difficult for supply to keep up with demand,” the report stated. “It is likely that warehouse space will remain stretched through the rest of the year as we begin to move into the traditional peak season.” Logistics real estate investment trust Prologis (NYSE: PLD) noted that the market moderated from all-time peak tightness during the second quarter. However, the firm still sees warehouse rents in the U.S. climbing 25% this year. ​Warehousing utilization (68.8) was down slightly during the month, with prices (76.2) slowing 2.2 points. However, both indexes remained firmly in expansion territory. The LMI is a collaboration among Arizona State University, Colorado State University, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rutgers University and the University of Nevada, Reno, conducted in conjunction with the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals. title: Duplicate ocean invoices plague exporter Scoular: audit
content: Audit technology vendor OpenEnvoy said it unearthed $3.7 million in total billing discrepancies for Scoular over the past six months, with container lines the biggest culprit. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Scoular, the second-largest US animal feed and grain exporter, found nearly $2 million in duplicate freight invoices for one segment of its business, according to a case study released Tuesday documenting its freight audit automation process. The case study, released by Scoular’s audit technology partner OpenEnvoy, identified $1.95 million in duplicate invoices over a six-month examination of bills Scoular received from international transportation vendors. The audits, which occur prior to Scoular issuing payment, flagged an overall $3.7 million in discrepancies, including the duplicate invoices. OpenEnvoy said in the case study that identifying potential invoice errors prior to payment allowed Scoular “to resolve issues with their vendor in real-time and prevent credit holds.” The audits found container lines to be responsible for most of Scoular’s inaccurate invoices, OpenEnvoy added. The issue of shippers dealing with duplicate invoices rose to prominence last week when New York-based food importer Bakerly filed a complaint with the US Federal Maritime Commission against New Jersey-based non-vessel-operating common carrier (NVO) Seafrigo. The complaint detailed, among other things, nearly $1 million in duplicate invoices for detention and demurrage charges assessed by Seafrigo. The duplicate invoices that surfaced during OpenEnvoy’s audit of Scoular’s bills were related to the exporter’s feed business. The privately held company had more than $6 billion in total revenue in 2021. Scoular declined to specify to JOC.com its annual transportation spend or the percentage of total transportation spend tied to its feed business. Scoular was the 11th-largest US exporter overall in 2021, moving 69,657 TEU and trailing only DeLong in the animal and feed grain category, according to the 2021 JOC Top 100 Exporter list. The Omaha, Nebraska-based company ships grain, seeds, and ingredients for human, pet, and animal products in more than 80 countries. “Years ago, our merchandising assistants would receive an invoice and physically enter the information into our [enterprise resource planning] system,” Leslie Dieck, controller at Scoular, said in the case study. “There was no automated auditing of the invoices before approval.” Dieck said Scoular scoured the market for third-party systems that automated the process, using the traditional three-way matching method upon which most freight audit and payment vendors rely. The three-way match involves comparing documents that specify the agreed rate and service levels to the invoice sent by the transportation provider. While shippers using systems based on the three-way matching concept generally see a major improvement over manually reconciling bills in-house, the outsourced process generally involves a mixture of technology and services. Dieck said Scoular was looking for a more automated approach that relied less on services. “We also tried to build a solution in-house and found difficulties managing how our vendors would use the system,” she said in the case study. “We wanted to avoid having our team review invoices daily. Manual reconciliation is not fun and does not promote strong employee engagement.” The case study noted that aside from lacking the ability to audit invoices before approvals, Scoular also didn’t capture performance metrics or spend data. But more problematic was that Scoular became bogged down by disputes with vendors that led to difficulty recovering overpayments. “If we fall behind with ocean carriers, they will threaten us with credit holds,” Dieck said. “This means we essentially pay everything up front and have to go back to fight for overpayment or duplicate payment, which is time-consuming and takes employee resources. It was a two-fold problem.” Buy-in for automating the invoice auditing from Dieck and Kurt Shinn, Scoular’s director of finance and accounting, was key to the project, OpenEnvoy CEO Matt Tillman told JOC.com. He said the company has found success targeting those with finance or accounting responsibility rather than those with logistics responsibility. “We focus our efforts on the finance team as the result of overpayment impacts cash flow, and therefore treasury,” Tillman told JOC.com Tuesday. “Finance teams [traditionally] shifted the payment approval process to the freight team in an attempt to transfer accountability. While that workflow resulted in a fast payment, it left treasury with costly clawback periods for overpayment.” Instead of outsourcing the audit function, OpenEnvoy is aimed at enabling finance teams to control the process. Logistics teams use the product primarily for analytics or to access supporting evidence associated with an invoice, such as a bill of lading or customs filing. OpenEnvoy was co-founded in 2020 by Tillman, who previously founded international transportation management system Haven, which was acquired in 2021 by logistics technology provider FourKites. Other providers in the space include Ocean Audit, Intelligent Audit, Martin & Sorbo, and Condata, along with a host of freight audit and payment providers that specialize in domestic transportation invoices but offer services or technology for international modes. The issue of ocean freight invoice accuracy is likely to become more prominent in the months ahead, with new legislation governing the manner in which terminals and container lines can invoice shippers and their representatives around detention and demurrage charges. The Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22), signed into law in June, allows the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) to levy fines against carriers and terminals who are found to have issued inaccurate detention and demurrage bills, and extract refunds for shippers.
