title: Survey: Nearshoring to Mexico happening ‘faster than expected’
content: While the rise of nearshoring to Mexico has been steadily increasing over the past decade, the pandemic and several other recent global disruptions have kicked the trend into high gear. About 88% of U.S.-based small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) will reshuffle their supply chains to utilize suppliers in the U.S. or Mexico in 2023, according to a recent survey from Gartner-owned consultant Capterra. “The switch to nearshoring is happening faster than was predicted in 2021,” the survey said. “Most industry professionals predicted this change would happen very slowly, over five or more years. But even the 2022 numbers we see in the data were stronger than those predictions, and 2023 will continue to see a rapid shift to nearby suppliers.” Capterra, a software consultancy and review site based in Arlington, Virginia, surveyed 300 supply chain SME professionals in the U.S. for the research titled “From Nearshoring to Cooperative Procurement.” While 88% of SMBs plan to switch at least some of their suppliers to ones either in the U.S. or close by, 45% plan to switch all of them, the survey said. Survey respondents said shorter supply chains, the United States-Mexico-Canada-Agreement trade pact, lower labor costs in Mexico and the North American transportation infrastructure as reasons for altering their manufacturing sources. Ben Johnston, chief operating officer at Kapitus, said his firm expects nearshoring of manufacturing to Mexico, which has an established manufacturing base and low tariff trade agreements with the U.S., to become more frequent in the coming years. New York-based Kapitus is a small business and industrial equipment financing company that provides funding for everything from construction firms to health care providers to small manufacturers in the U.S. “There is already a significant manufacturing presence in Mexico, including many precision technology manufacturers,” Johnston told FreightWaves. While automotive vehicle and parts manufacturing, consumer electronics and medical equipment have been a major part of U.S.-Mexico supply chains for decades, Johnston predicts increasingly more production of electrical components related to green technology. “The Infrastructure [Investment and Jobs] Act of 2021 and the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 provide large sums to spur investment in infrastructure and green technologies,” Johnston said. “Many of these incentives require manufacturing of subsidized products to occur in the U.S., or with approved trading partners, of which Mexico is included. In addition, new regulations prohibiting the manufacturing in China of certain items deemed critical to national defense will drive additional high-tech manufacturing toward the U.S., Mexico and other U.S. allies.” The survey also stated that 65% of supply chain professionals are concerned about economic inflation going into 2023, followed by a lack of inventory (43%) and economic recession (42%). “SMBs are hit harder than larger companies who have more resources available to them to absorb higher procurement and logistics costs and to reduce operating costs, such as labor,” the survey said. Johnston said concerns about inflation have already begun to affect how SMB’s will source their supply chain this year. “The trend toward the repatriation of manufacturing to the U.S. will continue in 2023 as long supply chains and geopolitical unrest drive businesses to seek more reliable alternatives,” Johnston said. “Continued cost reduction for U.S. manufacturers is critical as a strong dollar has hurt the competitiveness of U.S. manufacturing on the global stage and is slowing the overall repatriation trend. Inflation also remains an issue for U.S. manufacturers, but we are currently seeing a slowing of both consumer price index and producer price index and expect that trend to continue throughout the year, making inflation less of a long-term concern for manufacturers.” Click for more FreightWaves articles by Noi Mahoney. title: Viewpoint: Inventory management key to stifling inflation
content: While the smart money tries to get into the head of the Federal Reserve and its interest rate strategy, it’s baffling to see that after three years the market makers still do not understand the inflationary pressures each pipe in the supply chain can have on the economy. There is one pipe in particular that will continue to stoke the flames of inflation, and it will last for months to come. The solution is in the hands of the retailers. I’m talking inventory management, which so far is graded at a dismal D. Companies have used a combination of time and cutting back in manufacturing to whittle down their inventories, but it has not happened at the speed they projected. Some companies predicted inventories would be down by the end of the first quarter and yet warehouses are still near 100% capacity, according to WarehouseQuote. While “time heals all wounds” in some areas of life, time has only exacerbated retailer problems. What has materialized is the compounding impact of increased warehouse rates. The ugly unwanted items in storage are still ugly and unwanted. The only difference is the lofty price at which they are stored. This pile of inventory is not going down fast enough, and even with less freight coming in, there is still little room for it to find a home. It is for this reason this pipe of the supply chain will continue to be white hot for inflation. National storage pricing is up 1.4% month over month and 10.6% year over year. This is a reflection of the full warehouses across the nation. And warehouse costs are passed onto the consumer. Until the retailers figure out what to do with the items in these warehouses, the rates will continue to go up and thus be passed onto the consumer. While some of these items are being purchased on the secondary market, they are still in warehouses. The only difference is the owner. “National warehousing capacity remains low and will remain tight for the foreseeable future as U.S. industrial construction starts have fallen considerably year over year due to rising interest rates,” said Chris Huwaldt, vice president of solutions at WarehouseQuote. The ripple effects of the warehouse bloat will also exacerbate future late charges. ITS Logistics is warning of exploding per diem charges in the second and third quarters. It is seeing more items being held in ocean containers on chassis. While some say only truckers pay per diem, that is not entirely true. Shippers can pay per diem. “On the surface, in a lot of cases, it is dependent on the contract the BCO/shipper has with the NVO/ocean carrier,” explained Paul Brashier, vice president of drayage and intermodal at ITS Logistics. “If that contract bills these charges to the trucker, the trucker outlays and then bills back to the BCO/shipper. If the contract bills these charges to the shipper/BCO, the trucker does not have to outlay and those charges go directly to the shipper/BCO.” Brashier continued, “Regardless, shippers pay these fees. In some cases, if the MSA between the shipper/BCO and the trucker has a clause for negligence, the trucker could be on the hook if they did not pull a container from the terminal in time or terminate an empty quickly. If the trucker’s operations are on point, this is very rare and usually happens less than 1% of the time.” Simply put, per diem rates are passed onto the consumer, which stokes inflation. It’s another cost that the Fed has no control over. This comes at a time when imports are still coming in healthy pre-pandemic levels. While the ports are no longer processing at pandemic highs, they are still moving more containers than they have had in the past. Manufacturing disruptions are also still happening. These two challenges are translating into delivery delays. One of my contacts has a client that received its snow tires in January instead of October. These tires will now go into storage. HVAC systems are delayed by 99 weeks for some construction companies. Windows have been delayed a year and large electrical lights used in construction also have been delayed. On top of these postponements, the inflationary bump up on the commodities and equipment needed for infrastructure projects are eating away at how many projects can be done. The cost of capital is so high now that borrowing for projects is also attributing to projects being axed. That impacts not only jobs but the local economies that serve those workers. For college students who want to go into logistics, these last three years have given them a wealth of knowledge. Now they will learn in real time about inventory management. They are seeing challenges on both ends of the inventory spectrum. Inventory management is huge for a company’s survival and we are already seeing some retailers struggling. The increase in the cost of these stockpiles will continue to go up until they can figure out how to get the product out of storage. Donations to those in need around the world? A bonfire? Use sustainable recycling to make something else? Bottom line: The inflation on certain products will not be squelched until this inventory problem is addressed. Past the hype. title: Global shipping in the ‘process of normalizing’
content: This fireside chat recap is from Tuesday, the first day of FreightWaves’ Global Supply Chain Week. FIRESIDE CHAT TOPIC: Examining the current landscape of global maritime DETAILS: A discussion with Gordon Downes, CEO of New York Shipping Exchange, about current trends in ocean shipping. “I think it’s very clear that the market has normalized or is in the process of normalizing. Prices are coming down, close to pre-pandemic levels. The carrier ocean networks are starting to untangle, so the supply chain bottlenecks, which were very prevalent and made headlines during the pandemic, are now largely being removed and we’re seeing normalization in the market.” “What I think is likely to happen, is we’ll see destocking take place and then companies need to reinstate their purchase orders … and that will probably happen at similar times. We will see somewhat of a bullwhip effect.” On the recent capacity cuts from ocean carriers: “We’re seeing carriers starting to rationalize their networks — blank vessels, reduce the number of strings that they are running — because the demand at the moment is suppressed. … There again is another risk of a short-term period where there are bottlenecks, or at least shortages of supply, and that could very well cause freight rates to spike up again.” More FreightWaves articles by Todd Maiden Past the hype. title: How to navigate maritime supply chain logistics post-pandemic
content: This fireside chat recap is from Tuesday, the first day of FreightWaves’ Global Supply Chain Week. FIRESIDE CHAT TOPIC: Post-pandemic maritime trends DETAILS: Jackie Gonsalez, vice president of supply chain business development at Crowley Logistics, discusses maritime industry trends, the impacts of nearshoring, reshoring and what to watch for as the maritime space evolves in the post-pandemic era. “Now, the trend is how do we readjust to the new normal? How do we change the capacity that we did have during the pandemic to now you know, everybody pumped up whether it was vessels in certain areas, equipment in certain areas, trucks in certain areas, and now it’s having to redeploy them to where the needs are today?” “There’s been a lot of things shifting into nearshoring, so closer to the Americas. And so instead of maybe so much coming from the West Coast, maybe now a lot more is coming into the East Coast and into the Gulf.” “How are we shifting all that capacity within the U.S. as well as the vessels in that space and really just looking at everything from a broader picture, instead of just single-handedly [asking]: ‘How do I get freight from Asia?’” Past the hype. title: Reshoring, nearshoring production away from China remains ‘hot topic’
content: This fireside chat recap is from Tuesday, the first day of FreightWaves’ Global Supply Chain Week. FIRESIDE CHAT TOPIC: What do reshoring and nearshoring mean for supply chain strategies? DETAILS: More and more companies are considering reshoring or nearshoring their manufacturing operations back to North America after the global supply chain disruptions caused by the pandemic and U.S.-China trade war. SPEAKERS: Rosemary Coates is the founder and executive director of the Reshoring Institute, a nonprofit and nonpartisan organization aimed at helping companies decide where they should manufacture, with a focus on bringing production back to the U.S. Anthony Smith is FreightWaves’ chief economist. “Reshoring is a hot topic, it’s on every board’s agenda. I saw a survey recently that over 80% of companies in America are considering reshoring. But that doesn’t mean that you’re going to rip everything out of China and bring it all back to the U.S. It’s more subtle than that. What we’re seeing mostly right now is companies that are starting to rebuild their supply chains inside the U.S.” “There’s lots of open jobs in the U.S., somewhere over 2 million open jobs, and there are lots of people unemployed. The mismatch is that the skills that are required now are not the skills that those available workers have. That means that we need to re-skill our workers. So I really think we have an education and skills problem, not a labor shortage problem.” “It’s very difficult to extract your [production] from China. But I’m here to tell you, you better be thinking about it, because the situation in China’s not going to get any better. It’s going to continue to deteriorate.” Click for more FreightWaves articles by Noi Mahoney. title: LA Port director expects ‘real progress’ in West Coast labor talks this spring
content: Talks between port employers and workers represented by the International Longshore and Warehouse Union continue to drag on, with Seroka saying that “we’re at the outer edges of what historically has been the farthest reaching end of negotiations like this between these two sides.” With negotiations in flux, shippers are continuing to move cargo away from the West Coast to avoid any potential for disruption. And although Seroka has crossed the country in an attempt to win back cargo share, the Los Angeles Port director said “there is still trepidation among shippers.” “There are many transportation managers that yet couldn’t go back to their boss for a third straight year and say, ‘I got our cargo stuck in the jaws of congestion out in California,’” he said. Contract uncertainty has only exacerbated a volume slowdown at the Port of Los Angeles. As with other hubs across the nation, the port is contending with dampened demand and extended factory closures in Asia associated with the Lunar New Year holiday. As capacity loosens at other ports, it’s possible even more shippers will take the opportunity to shift cargo away from the West Coast. “Most shippers are seeing a surge in ocean shipping capacity and have already adjusted their shipping lanes to other ports,” Spencer Shute, principal consultant at supply chain consultancy Proxima, said in an emailed statement. “Continuing this practice until the negotiations have completed is the best practice to reduce risk.”

title: Pandemic exposed global pharmaceutical supply chain’s fragility
content: How did generic pharmaceutical wholesalers fare during the COVID-19 pandemic compared to the big three drug wholesalers that control 90% of the market? What is the state of the pharmaceutical supply chain now? What are some of the difficulties of shifting drug manufacturing production from countries like China and India back to the U.S.? These are some of the issues Christina Hultsch, a partner in Benesch’s Healthcare Practice Group, discussed with John Kingston, editor at large at FreightWaves, on Wednesday during Global Supply Chain Week. Hultsch, who represents generic drug manufacturers, said vulnerabilities existed in the global supply chain before the pandemic since three drug wholesalers control more than 90% of the pharmaceutical market. However, the disparity between generic manufacturers and the big three was exposed when the Chinese government shut down the entire Wuhan province, where many of her clients had their manufacturing facilities, in late January 2020. “Initially, we thought, oh, a couple of weeks we’ll get through this, and then it turned into three, six months and not a whole lot was happening coming out of China, so that was the first big problem,” Hultsch said. “Then all the dominoes started falling after that, [and] even if you could get the drugs, you couldn’t really ship it across the ocean. You couldn’t find workers to do this or that, or you couldn’t find trucks to load anything onto.” Shipping costs also skyrocketed during this time, she said, crippling some generic manufacturers used to paying a few thousand to ship a load pre-pandemic to paying anywhere from $20,000 to $50,000 for the same load of drugs. “It resulted in obviously a lot of debt building up for those manufacturers in a business that is already struggling with cash flow,” Hultsch said. She said the biggest issue with generic manufacturers competing with the three largest wholesalers, even before the pandemic, was certain payment cycles. “There’s a different payment cycle on the wholesaler-customer side. and it’s really easy math,” Hultsch said. “If the wholesaler has better payment terms, has more time to pay the manufacturer than it has on the other end with the customer, then the wholesaler never has to come out of pocket and holds all of the economic power. That makes it very easy for them to dictate the terms and makes the generic market a really low-margin market.” However, generic drug manufacturers, already operating on low margins, struggled to survive when the pandemic hit as many were crippled by soaring shipping costs and significant delivery delays. “When the pandemic hits, you are dealing with the actual delays in deliveries,” Hultsch said. “You have late fees in your contract. You have shipping costs that multiplied by 10 to 50%. Then suddenly a low-margin business is really squeezed to the point where it’s getting hard to survive.” This interview is from Wednesday, the second day of FreightWaves’ Global Supply Chain Week. While the pandemic highlighted certain vulnerabilities for U.S. drug manufacturers that depend on countries like China and India — which produce more than 80% of the primary ingredients in medications used around the world — moving manufacturing facilities closer to home is complicated, according to Hultsch. “You can’t build up a facility overnight,” she said. “It’s going [to go] through a long approval process and you’re looking at two years at a minimum if you’re starting to relocate production. So, it’s certainly an effort, but it’s not going to be a quick fix, and what we have found, particularly in the U.S., when we have tried to go with local CMOs [contract manufacturing organizations], is they often have quality issues. We really have been getting better, more reliable quality out of China and India, as opposed to what we’ve seen from some of the U.S. manufacturers.” Past the hype. title: Efficient, tech-driven supply chain management drives HelloFresh’s success
content: During the pandemic, consumers shopping habits changed dramatically toward online channels, pressing companies like HelloFresh to rethink their supply chain operations. “With the shutting of borders and homes and schools, everyone’s coming home and staying home, and we were a lucky recipient of that in some ways,” said Matt Cicinelli, vice president of operations and technology at HelloFresh. “We were set up to be a business of one size, not knowing COVID was coming, and we quickly transitioned into rapid growth.” Cicinelli’s keynote on Wednesday helped kick off the second day of FreightWaves’ Global Supply Chain Week three-day event. Cicinelli discussed how HelloFresh is upgrading its approach to customer attraction and retention while handling the supply chain challenges that have arisen in a post-COVID world. HelloFresh was founded as a startup meal kit company in Berlin, Germany, in 2011. Since then, the company has managed to scale into a global food solutions group, operating six different brands from the meal kit and ready-to-eat sectors in 16 countries on three continents. In 2021, HelloFresh delivered 1 billion meals and currently has about 7.5 million active users. The company employs 20,000 globally. “When we look back at 2021, year over year compared to 2020, we grew 53% in the U.S. in terms of box count,” Cicinelli said. “We invested a lot in 2021. We had to keep up and fulfill those needs, while reacting to what was unknown at the time, such as how the disease was spreading, social distancing pressures, which ultimately reduced everyone’s capacity.” The pandemic helped HelloFresh expand its customer base, which the company is now focused on retaining moving through 2023 and beyond. The pandemic disrupted supply chains around the world, compelling companies like HelloFresh to expand their transportation and fulfillment networks. One of the challenges for the company during the pandemic was sourcing the ingredients and foods that go into the meal kits. “If you look back into Q4 of 2020, transportation capacity was definitely a challenge for everyone, the labor market was a challenge for everyone,” Cicinelli said. “At HelloFresh, it was compounded by the consistent challenge we have, a constantly rotating origin of a lot of our suppliers. When you’re trying to chase a product that’s moving from its origin in a capacity constrained area, it’s obviously a big challenge for us.” HelloFresh was able to grow during the pandemic by reconfiguring its supply chain through technology and hard work, according to Cicinelli. “We were talking earlier about the size of business we are equipped to be when the pandemic hit,” he said. “We are very fortunate to be a bigger business than we planned to be at that point in time. But it was powered by people, and we’ve been trying to now supplement those people with tools and technology so that we can stop doing so much on one spreadsheet, then they can invest those people into the product development that’s going to lead to the retention and the growth of our products that we want to see.” On the commercial transportation side, Cicinelli said HelloFresh went through a massive expansion of its partnerships with carriers during the pandemic. “In 2022, it’s been a reconciliation of that and investing in partners who are going to be there for you,” he said. “At this point, the pendulum of price is swinging, and so price and quality are table stakes. What we’re really looking for now are the suppliers and the partners who are there when we need them. And we’re very lucky to have some of those.” Click for more FreightWaves articles by Noi Mahoney. title: FedEx Express pilots union leaders approve strike authorization vote
content: The labor union representing FedEx Express pilots says contract negotiations with the company have stalled, moving the union closer to holding a vote to approve a strike. The union leader for FedEx Express pilots has been granted the ability to call for a strike authorization vote among its members in a special meeting Friday, according to a resolution from the FedEx Express Master Executive Council, which is part of the Air Line Pilots Association, International. The ALPA’s president, Jason Ambrosi, also backed the measure. “FedEx pilots are committed to reaching a deal with management, but we will not waiver in our commitment to deliver a contract that rewards pilots for their sacrifices to build FedEx into the global leader it is today,” Chris Norman, Master Executive Council chair, said in a statement. “Although a strike authorization vote has not been called at this time, our customers and shareholders should be aware that the pilots may be headed in that direction shortly.” The approval for such a vote to be called comes after nearly six months of federally mediated negotiations between FedEx Express and the union. The current contract became amenable in November 2021, and the two parties went to the National Mediation Board in October in a bid to expedite the contract talks. FedEx Express and the union have made progress during the talks, as a union representative noted in January that the two sides reached an agreement on retirement issues. The representative, First Officer Brian Baldwin, said terms regarding pay and contract duration were still being negotiated. “The items that remain between the Airline Pilots Association, Int’l (ALPA) and FedEx are so few, they can fit onto a single sheet of paper,” according to the Master Executive Council’s website. Since pilots are covered under the Railway Labor Act, they must be released by the National Mediation Board and have a 30-day cooling-off period be exhausted before they can strike, per the Master Executive Council. The strike authorization vote also has to be held. “If management does not show up at the table, we must send a very clear message that FedEx pilots are unified and ready to strike,” Norman said in a message to union members. FedEx said in a bargaining update that the decision has no impact on its service, adding that strike authorization votes are a common union tactic during negotiations under the Railway Labor Act. It also said negotiations with its pilots remain productive. “FedEx is fully committed to working with our pilots and the National Mediation Board to reach a comprehensive agreement,” the company said. “We are confident that we can do so, while also delivering the best possible service to our customers, without any disruptions to our operations just as we have done in each previous bargaining cycle.”

title: US to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing after global shortages during pandemic
content: This recap is from Thursday, the third day of FreightWaves’ Global Supply Chain Week. FIRESIDE CHAT TOPIC: The state of the semiconductor supply chain. DETAILS: Radford University’s Zach Collier discusses the state of the semiconductor industry with FreightWaves’ Eric Kulisch after chip shortages roiled the global economy during the pandemic. They discuss new U.S. policies that were implemented to better control this key technology and avoid future shortages. On the fragmented supply chain: “The life cycle of a chip is really complex. So there are people that design the chips, and then typically, the people that design the chips are different than the ones that end up manufacturing the chips, and that’s due to a number of reasons. But the supply chain is very fragmented for chips. So one group designs them and then another group might manufacture them and then other people might then assemble them and package them and test them, and so these chips go all across the United States, all across the world, before they end up in the things like our smartphones and laptops and whatnot. On factors that led to the chip shortage: “When the pandemic happened and all the lockdowns started, there was a spike in the demand for chips and the demand was already going up for chips before the lockdowns occurred. And so that’s an important part of this. Part of the story is that things like electric vehicles and the Internet of Things was already causing an increase in demand for these chips. And then, when everybody had to work from home, the demand just spiked from there, which led to some shortages are things like automotive and pretty much all across the board for chips. On the CHIPS and Science Act: “The CHIPS Act that passed last year was sort of an answer to some of these questions about bringing back some of the manufacturing and other parts of the supply chain domestically here in the States. We only produce, in terms of the manufacturing side of things, about 12% of the world’s chips, even though we demand anywhere between a quarter and a third depending on who you talk to. So that imbalance means that we are in some sense vulnerable or sort of at the mercy of the supply chain.” Past the hype. title: GSBN, Navis partner to help exporters track ERD changes
content: Exporters have seen an increase in changes to earliest return dates (ERDs) during the pandemic, as port congestion affected vessel departures. Photo credit: Aun Photographer / Shutterstock.com. A consortium of container lines and marine terminals is partnering with terminal operating software provider Navis to provide information for a new app that helps exporters track earliest return date (ERD) changes at terminals. The partnership, unveiled Thursday between Navis and the Global Shipping Business Network (GSBN), entails moving ERD data from terminals using Navis software to a new GSBN app via a product called Execution and Visibility Platform (EVP) that was developed by Kaleris, which acquired Navis in 2021. EVP acts as a layer that connects all terminals using Navis products. “If you wanted to work with a terminal that deployed a Navis [terminal operating system], you needed to go into each individual terminal,” Rene Alvarenga, director of product management at Kaleris, told the Journal of Commerce this week. “The difference here is that the EVP sits on top of every terminal we have. So the GSBN will have one single point for every terminal that uses [Navis].” ERD is the earliest an exporter or its transportation provider can in-gate an export load. The ERD is generally decided by the terminal, even though it has no direct role in the contractual relationship between an exporter and container line. The Kaleris-GSBN partnership is meant to resolve longstanding ERD issues stemming from that process, specifically the lack of clarity about when a container should be sent to a terminal, which results in detention and demurrage billing disputes with carriers. A lack of real-time information on ERD changes also creates drayage trips where export loads can’t be in-gated, resulting in transportation and storage costs for exporters. While changing ERDs are an operational and financial nuisance for exporters, the resulting billing disputes also hamper carriers, GSBN CEO Bertrand Chen told the Journal of Commerce. Chen said the data exchange between the GSBN and Karelis could flow in the other direction as well, with carriers providing information to terminals using Navis to help them update ERD information. “ERD data is not a simple data set,” he said. “By working with Navis and their deployed [terminal operating systems], we can leverage their deployed base.” That deployed base of container terminals is looking more broadly at ways it can serve shippers directly through technology, Alvarenga said. That’s a departure from the pre-pandemic mindset, where the focus of container terminals tended to be centered around efficiency within the terminal. “Times have changed,” he said. “COVID caused disruption. Terminals have different views to connecting to the outside world. Whereas before a terminal would have said ‘the data is mine, don’t touch it,’ now, to survive in a volatile world, they have to integrate with the landside.” Chen said the ERD app is only the first opportunity the GSBN and Kaleris plan to tackle. “Long term, the goal is to go beyond the [terminal operating system],” he said. “Terminals are more inclined to look at data they can actually share. Terminals have built their own portals, but the reality is you’re not going to have 50 portals that shippers need to access. And the software vendors don’t want to have 15 platforms they need to connect with.” Chen often touts GSBN’s non-profit structure as a benefit because it allows the consortium to serve as a neutral conduit of data and solutions. “We’re not taking the side of the shipping line or the [beneficial cargo owner],” he said. “Potentially we can solve the dispute [around ERDs] because the shipping line is not going to fight every single invoice for the customer.” Navis software is used by more than 500 container terminals globally. GSBN members include Cosco Shipping, Cosco Ports, OOCL, Hapag-Lloyd, Hutchison Ports, and the Shanghai International Port Group. title: BlueCargo will use new investment to expand container platform nationwide
content: Importer customers led BlueCargo, which previously only served the key US container gateways of Southern California and New York-New Jersey, to branch out to other ports. Photo credit: Steve Estvanik / Shutterstock.com. BlueCargo, a software provider that helps US importers manage container pickups and returns, has landed an $11 million funding round from venture investors, cash it will use to expand its platform nationwide, it said Thursday. Los Angeles-based BlueCargo, founded in 2018, has until now served only the ports of Los Angeles, Long Beach, and New York-New Jersey. CEO Alexandra Griffon told the Journal of Commerce that customers have been seeking a way to manage containers at any US gateway using BlueCargo’s software. “We have been focusing on the biggest gateways, where there are the most [detention and demurrage] issues,” Griffon said. “But the feedback was, ‘this is great, but let us know when it’s nationwide.’ It’s hard for them to use it for some containers and not others. The funding is enabling us to focus on product that can serve the needs of bigger importers.” BlueCargo’s system allows importers to scour a single site for available appointments at terminals for import pickups, empty returns, and so-called dual transactions, instead of having to check individual terminal websites. Crucially, the system also allows importers and their drayage partners to document attempts to make appointments, a key auditing step in disputing detention and demurrage (D&D) charges from container lines and terminals. Aside from shippers, BlueCargo also serves logistics services providers (LSPs), while more than 1,200 drayage carriers use it to schedule pickups and empty returns. “BlueCargo’s audit trail and documentation process [helped] cancel for us and for our customers $5.2 million in unreasonable detention and demurrage charges in [Los Angeles, Long Beach, and New York-New Jersey] in 2022 alone,” Vincent Fasso, president at BlueCargo customer Forrest Logistics, said in a statement. Other customers include furniture retailer Living Spaces and the drayage division of XPO Logistics. Griffon said BlueCargo’s growth was tied to a greater need during the pandemic to control D&D costs, as port congestion wreaked havoc on container flows through Southern California and New York-New Jersey. “We weren’t targeting enterprise customers before, but now we’re looking at top 100 importers,” she said. “Any large shipper now has an objective to reduce D&D that they didn’t have before. So its been the right timing in terms of customer awareness and us getting the tool on the market.” Griffon said managing D&D costs has moved from being an operational issue to a finance issue, with BlueCargo working with importer finance teams to forecast and track free time. At one importer customer, the finance team projection for what it would pay in D&D in 2022 was off by 35 percent. “Their goal now is to get that down to 5 percent off, and that’s an area we can help with,” she said. “Importers can track what they’ve paid across the whole year, but getting accurate numbers on D&D costs right now, that’s what we first help them determine.” BlueCargo has grown from four employees two years ago to 35 today, and will use the funding to double the size of its engineering department, the statement said. The funding announced Thursday brings the total amount invested into BlueCargo to $15 million. title: Slync investors double down on beleaguered company with new funding
content: The new funding for Slync will be used to build out the company’s existing product lines. Photo credit: MNBB Studio / Shutterstock.com. Existing investors of troubled logistics software provider (LSP) Slync.io have pumped $24 million in new funding into the Dallas-based technology company, it said Thursday. The funding round comes a week after Slync co-founder and former CEO Chris Kirchner was arrested and charged by the US Department of Justice and Securities and Exchange Commission with defrauding investors and funneling company funds into personal accounts. The new funding, led by previous Slync investor Goldman Sachs with participation from Blumberg Capital, ACME Ventures, and Gaingels, also comes four months after Slync hired logistics veteran John Urban as CEO and chairman to resurrect the company’s brand. “Our customers recognize the power and potential of the Slync platform, and our investor partners do as well,” Urban said in a statement announcing the funding. The funding will be used to build out the company’s existing product lines. One, called Intelligent Carrier Management, helps LSPs and shippers automate the freight booking process. The other, known as Intelligent Order Orchestration, automates order-related processes between emails and spreadsheets and the order management systems LSP and shippers use. “Every day, millions of emails, spreadsheets, PDFs, and messages are exchanged as part of the logistics management process, yet most existing systems only capture a fraction of them, and that’s a big, expensive problem,” Urban said. Slync said in the statement its customers include several global enterprises and large LSPs. “These companies will be making separate announcements about their use of and success with the technology in the coming months,” it said. The new funding round is likely to raise eyebrows within the logistics technology given Slync had already raised more than $72 million in venture capital, the lion’s share in a Goldman Sachs-led $60 million round in February 2021. Slync, and Kirchner in particular, have become an easy target for those who believe that logistics software isn’t well-suited for venture capital funding because of slow sales cycles and a fragmented provider landscape. Part of the SEC’s investigation into Kirchner’s activities included what the agency alleges were misrepresentations of Slync’s revenue. title: Negotiators say longshore contract talks continue, hopeful of deal soon
content: Thursday’s joint news release marks the first official update from the two parties since September, when a labor dispute involving a marine terminal employer and another union complicated negotiations. The intra-union dispute centered around the assignment of cold ironing work at Seattle’s Terminal 5, and whether SSA Marine could assign the work to the International Association of Machinist and Aerospace Workers. In September, the machinist union filed a dispute over the matter with the National Labor Relations Board. At the time, the longshore union alleged the dispute was coordinated by SSA Marine as a means to stall coast-wide contract negotiations. “This action by SSA, which it will pretend is necessitated by another workforce’s threat of job action, forces the ILWU to focus its attention, otherwise spent in bargaining, on defending the preservation of ILWU work in Seattle,” the longshore union said in a September news release emailed to Supply Chain Dive. Though the intra-union case is not yet resolved, negotiations are still ongoing. Whether the contract talks will end before the National Labor Relations Board resolves its dispute, and the bearing the case has at the bargaining table, remains unclear. The two parties have declined to comment publicly on the issue. Over the past months, several industry stakeholders have guessed at when the contract talks will conclude. Just last week, Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka said he expects the two sides will make “real progress” on the talks during the spring. In the meantime, shippers facing uncertainty have taken matters into their own hands and diverted cargo away from the West Coast as they avoid any risk of labor disruptions at the West Coast ports. In their joint news release Thursday, the two parties in the longshore labor talks emphasized West Coast ports have continued to operate during the negotiations, which began May 10, 2022.

title: TPMTech23: Retailers seek to make supply chain visibility data more useful
content: Shippers seek to make better use of the supply chain visibility data they are receiving by turning to predictive analytics, speakers at TPMTech23 said. Photo credit: Zapp2Photo / Shutterstock.com. Shippers who survived the disruptions caused by the global pandemic did so by achieving visibility throughout their supply chains. But to improve their performance going forward, shippers must better manage the data they receive from transportation vendors, technology providers say. “Everyone wants visibility, they value it, but they want to make it more useful. It’s just a tool,” Gene Gander, general manager of global sales at logistics software provider WiseTech Global, told the Journal of Commerce's TPMTech23 conference Thursday in Long Beach. Supply chain visibility became the biggest challenge for importers during the pandemic because many retailers ordered more merchandise than they needed to ensure they had enough inventory on hand given the ocean and inland transportation disruptions, said Matt Elenjickal, founder and CEO of freight visibility provider FourKites. That inventory was housed in their warehouses, the warehouses of their vendors, and also in trailers and containers scattered throughout their networks. Retailers found they did not have real-time visibility into all of the locations where their inventory was housed, Elenjickal said. “Everything was turned upside down,” he said. Some retailers and other shippers may seek a technology provider with a single platform that collects all the data needed to track shipments throughout the supply chain, but the reality is that the data generators are the ocean carriers, truckers, non-vessel-operating common carriers (NVOs), and warehouse operators moving or storing their cargo. “There is no company out there that can do it all,” Elenjickal said. Shippers are the biggest users of predictive technology, said Tim Sensenig, chairman and CEO at shipping and supply chain management provider TMSfirst. They use technology to track data for purchase order management, route optimization, and supply chain visibility. However, each shipper must rely on its own staff to integrate that data so it benefits the entire enterprise, he said. “You need visibility, clean data, and people to implement it,” Sensenig said. “It’s really about integration.” Julie Gerdeman, CEO of Everstream Analytics, a predictive analytics firm, said the transportation industry in 2023 must manage diverse risks. Those include delays in shipments coming from China given COVID-19 disruptions, uncertainties that come from diversification of sourcing to countries other than China, insolvencies of smaller service providers and vendors that could occur due to wild swings in the economy, cyberattacks that could upend logistics operations, and labor disruptions such as a potential breakdown in contract negotiations between marine terminal employers and the International Longshore and Warehouse Union on the West Coast. Shippers learned over the past two years that addressing disruptions after they occur is waiting too long, so they are looking to information service providers to help them predict when disruptions in the supply chain are likely, Gerdeman said. “Use what is provided to make better, faster decisions,” she said. “We’re on a path to prescriptive analytics. Everything we do is prescriptive.” Elenjickal said true supply chain visibility allows the shipper to go from reactive to proactive to predictive to being prescriptive. “It’s transportation management,” he said. “Push everything down to the execution level.” Contact Bill Mongelluzzo at bill.mongelluzzo@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @billmongelluzzo. © 2026 S&P Global. title: More investment headed to US last-mile delivery market
content: Changes in consumer behavior are driving greater interest and investment in last-mile carriers and technology. Photo credit: Aria Logistics. US consumers may be buying fewer appliances, swing sets, and sofas at the moment, but shippers and their transportation providers aren’t taking their eyes off last-mile delivery. Most are betting that last- or final-mile delivery will become increasingly important as e-commerce sales expand, despite a US economic slowdown. And as e-commerce grows, shippers continue to push for end-to-end shipment location visibility and better management of that final delivery. “Some changes in consumer behavior that were made during the pandemic are enduring,” said Geoff Muessig, chief marketing officer at regional LTL carrier Pitt Ohio. More shipments that once went to stores are going to homes, even as consumers buy fewer goods, Muessig said. Shipper demand is pushing companies from Maersk to Pitt Ohio to take greater interest in the last mile, even if their core business is closer to the first or middle-mile. Technology companies such as visibility providers FourKites and project44 are investing in last-mile software and partnering with developers. Pitt Ohio last week made an undisclosed investment in New York-based Aria Logistics, which handles home delivery for major US retailers in markets across the US. Aria, led by founder and CEO Arelis Bonilla, specializes in the delivery of appliances, furniture fitness equipment, and electronics. Pitt Ohio expects home delivery of larger items to continue to grow at a double-digit rate. “People have learned it’s easier to have a large-format item delivered to your home as opposed to wrestling it into your SUV,” Muessig said. “You may go to the store and order there, but still have it delivered.” The Pittsburgh-based LTL provider — which currently handles a “couple hundred” home deliveries a day from the Midwest to the Northeast with its own equipment — acquired a minority stake in Aria, not a controlling one, said Muessig. The LTL carrier will have an advisory role in Aria’s business. “Being an entrepreneurial company, we’re always looking for opportunities, and Aria provided an opportunity to invest in a company that may be able to help us create solutions for our customers and grow to scale,” Muessig said. “We’re looking at new technology, and we’ll look at what Aria does.” That’s a unique approach for an LTL carrier, said Satish Jindel, president of SJ Consulting Group, which advised both companies on the deal. “You don’t need to be in the last-mile business to tap into it,” Jindel said. Pitt Ohio’s approach shows there are many routes to residential delivery. The last-mile market is highly fragmented, with many small carriers focused on single markets and a few large players. That makes it difficult to enter the market through acquisition. Maersk, for example, acquired Pilot Freight Services, a US-based forwarder, last year in part to strengthen its final-mile services. There are relatively few final-mile companies with that scale and scope of services, even if they would consider a sale. Another option is partnering with a logistics company that specializes in final-mile delivery. RXO, which inherited LTL carrier XPO’s last-mile division in its recent spin-off, is one example. And some companies, such as Estes Express Lines, have built their own last-mile divisions. Most large LTL companies have their own last-mile divisions or partner with third-party logistics providers. Investing in an existing final-mile provider is another option, and Pitt Ohio found one that fit its long-term growth strategy. In recent years, the carrier has expanded its reach by investing in other regional LTL trucking companies, notably Dohrn Transfer in the Midwest and Ross Express in New England, although Pitt Ohio has also acquired smaller companies, such as Teal’s Express in New York. Pitt Ohio will be able to use its relationship with Aria to develop best practices in last-mile delivery, and Aria will have access to Pitt Ohio procurement, safety, and technology expertise. Most importantly, the companies will be able to integrate the flow of information from LTL to the final mile. “The biggest breakdowns today aren’t in the physical movement of goods, but the flow of information,” Muessig said. That uninterrupted flow is needed to feed information to the final customer, in this case a consumer, in multiple digital forms. That includes frequent texts or emails updating delivery times, alerting customers to a shipment’s arrival, and post-delivery quality surveys. For many retailers, the last mile doesn’t necessarily lead to a customer’s front door. Delivery methods such as curbside pickup and “buy online, pick up in store” are becoming more common. Walmart now does more than $1 billion in in-store pickup business a year, the company said Tuesday. Those rapidly evolving delivery options require a higher level of connectivity between companies, enabled by technology. Increasingly, larger US shippers expect data from all their transportation and logistics providers will be visible within a single workflow. “Some companies are very good at integrating the information flow all the way through with the final-mile carrier,” said Muessig. “That integration is the value of our investment with Aria.” Contact William B. title: Kuwait government orders Agility to vacate logistics parks
content: Agility, the second-largest shareholder in logistics giant DSV and new owner of global airport services company Menzies, will absorb a significant financial hit from the Kuwait government’s decision not to renew five contracts for huge warehouse properties. The government intends to rebid the contracts, which a source in Kuwait says will allow the state to maximize revenue on distribution centers that were leased 20 years ago at rates far below today’s market value. The loss of the contracts is noteworthy because they represent Agility’s most lucrative, highest-margin logistics properties, according to the source. Agility, with roots in logistics real estate, filed suit to remain the incumbent master lease holder for the state-owned logistics parks, but a Kuwait court recently dismissed the case. “Agility believes that the … contracts of the sites that the Public Authority of Industry requests to be vacated have been renewed, since Agility has sent notification to the PAI with its willingness to renew those contracts as per the terms of the contract,” the publicly traded company said Jan. 3 in a statement on its website. It plans to appeal the court ruling. Agility is one of the largest private owners of industrial real estate in the Middle East and Africa. It started in 1979 as the state-owned Public Warehousing Co. providing basic storage services and was privatized in 1997. Over the years it acquired many logistics companies — including Geologistics, Transoceanic Shipping, and Global Express Line — and unified its services under the Agility brand in 2004. Agility Logistics became a major global contract logistics provider, managing warehouses and supply chains for multinational corporations. In 2021, Agility sold its global logistics business to Denmark-based DSV, the third-largest logistics service provider in the world by gross revenue, for an 8% share in the company. Today, Agility’s holdings include companies involved in fuel logistics; customs clearance consulting, inspection and digitization; remote camp site operations for mining and other purposes; property and parking management at Kuwait’s airport; commercial real estate; defense and government logistics support; e-commerce logistics technology; and metal recycling. The most recent figures show the company had $590 million in net revenue during the first nine months of 2022. Last summer, Agility acquired Menzies Aviation, a provider of ground, fuel and air cargo services at 250 airports worldwide, for about $928 million. Menzies is now the world’s largest aviation services company after combining with Agility’s National Aviation Services, which grew from its home in Kuwait to serve other airports in the region. Kuwait’s Public Authority of Industry late last year announced it was not going to renew contracts with Agility to manage nearly 38 million square feet of warehouse space, citing new procurement laws that require expiring contracts to undergo an open bid process for all interested parties to submit proposals. Under the concession agreements, PwC/Agility built and operated the warehouses on public land and then must transfer them back to the government if the contract is not renewed. Agility has continued to manage some blocks of logistics property after its contracts expired in recent years while Kuwaiti officials considered their strategy and the company’s request for an extension. Changing leadership at the top of the Industry Authority also may have contributed to the delay in taking back the land. The government recently ordered Agility to vacate the property. Agility warehouse contracts were priced years ago, at rates that are now extremely beneficial to the tenant, when demand was limited, according to the source, who asked not to be named because of the political sensitivity of the situation. The government has been raising rent on new industrial properties offered in recent years because it wants better returns to further its goal of diversifying national income away from oil. Officials are under pressure to follow the new procurement law after public criticism that expensive warehouse rates have contributed to higher consumer costs. “The government doesn’t want to run anything. They just want a bigger chunk of the pie,” the source said. The Kuwait government will manage the properties relinquished by Agility until it conducts a bid and transfers them to new lease holders, according to notices published in local newspapers. Agility subtenants have been instructed to simply switch payments to the government while it temporarily serves as their landlord. They are not expected to experience any impact from the transfer of control. Agility is eligible to participate in the bidding process for the logistics parks it previously managed. title: TPMTech23: ‘Purchase order management’ the new catchphrase in logistics
content: The challenge that retailers face today in managing purchase orders is that supply chains have become much more complex and dispersed, attendees at TPMTech23 were told. Photo credit: Rawpixel.com /Shutterstock.com. The wild swings in supply and demand over the past three years, and the supply chain disruptions they generated, have renewed interest among retailers in using technology to manage a document vital to supply chain logistics — the purchase order that importers present to overseas factories for the production and delivery of their products. Purchase order management declined in importance in the pre-pandemic world because trans-Pacific supply chains had generally become reliable. That all changed when congested ports in Asia and the US, poor carrier on-time performance, and blank sailings disrupted trans-Pacific supply chains. Now, retailers are devoting as much attention to the first-mile move of the product from the Asia factory as they had been devoting to the last-mile delivery in the US, according to Rob Garrison, CEO of Mercado Labs, a purchase order management platform. “That same product they speed to your door [in the US] takes six months for them to get it to the US,” Garrison told the Journal of Commerce’s TPMTech23 conference in Long Beach Friday. The challenge that retailers face today in managing purchase orders is that supply chains have become much more complex and dispersed as retailers source product from multiple factories and ship the goods under contracts with multiple shipping lines and non-vessel-operating common carriers (NVOs). At each step in the supply chain, data on the shipment is being generated by the carriers and NVOs that touch the product. Trojan Battery Company, which sources from five factories, uses purchase order management to share shipment data with the factories so they can integrate their production schedules with the shipment of the batteries, said Holly Pearce, director of materials and logistics for C&D Technologies and Trojan Battery Co. “When I initiate a tender, I demand integration with my service providers,” Pearce told the conference said. Managing the flow of data among multiple factories and transportation providers requires the use of technology because emails and electronic data interchange (EDI) will no longer meet the demands of today’s increasingly complex supply chains, said Jim McCullen, chief information officer at Century Supply Chain Solutions, a technology-focused logistics service provider. “You have to get the data into the right hands to get that product moved,” McCullen told TPMTech23. “You have to manage this with technology and people.” Each retailer has multiple departments charged with ordering and purchasing the products, shipping and storing the goods, and final-mile delivery. “On the six-month journey of the product, where are you focused? It depends upon which sector of the company you are in. Each person in the organization has a different need,” McCullen said. “This brings operations and technology together ever so sharply.” Contact Bill Mongelluzzo at bill.mongelluzzo@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @billmongelluzzo. © 2026 S&P Global. title: TPM23: MSC putting ocean shipping first after ending 2M Alliance: Toft
content: MSC CEO Søren Toft told TPM23 global container fleet growth will be mitigated by scrapping and IMO emissions rules. Photo credit: Caught in the Moment Photography. Mediterranean Shipping Co. CEO Søren Toft said Monday the huge number of ships the company will take delivery of in the coming years prepare it for future global trade growth, adding that the world’s largest ocean carrier is on a different “trajectory” than Maersk as they wind down their 2M Alliance. Toft told attendees at the Journal of Commerce’s TPM23 conference in Long Beach that the company’s orderbook — totaling some 1.6 million TEU, or 40 percent of its current fleet — signals to customers that the carrier will be with them in the long term and that its commitment remains chiefly to ocean shipping rather than selling an integrated supply chain service that Maersk is now looking to do. “We have strong commitment to shipping,” Toft said. “We are hopefully a long-term partner with our customers and our investments in new vessels demonstrate that.” The January announcement that MSC and Maersk will wind down the eight-year-old 2M Alliance by 2025 should not have any major impacts on customers or the industry as a whole, Toft said. He said the decision to not renew the alliance for another 10-year term was mutual and the result of diverging strategies between the two carriers. “The trajectory of Maersk is different than the trajectory of MSC,” Toft said. “We could have seen ourselves extending [the 2M Alliance], but not under just any circumstances.” Toft said that vessel-sharing agreements, including 2M and the earlier P3 Alliance that also included CMA CGM, enabled an era of mega-ships entering the global fleet and helped reduce overall shipping costs. He said that even with the eventual end of 2M, MSC may yet enter space-sharing or other agreements with Maersk. But with most of the alliance efficiencies already having been realized, MSC had to rethink the value of the 2M offering. “The world looked very different 10 years ago, and a lot has happened since then,” Toft said. “The alliances were a response to years of price pressure and the need to get larger economies of scale and deploy bigger ships. And indeed, we have passed most of those efficiencies on to customers and lowered their costs.” Toft acknowledged that overall new ship deliveries, with the global fleet growing 7 to 9 percent annually over the next several years, will outweigh market demand, which is returning to more normalized growth of 2 to 4 percent annually. But he said that fleet growth will be mitigated by older, less fuel-efficient vessels leaving the market. Starting this year, shipping companies will need to measure the carbon dioxide output of their ships under the International Maritime Organization’s Carbon Intensity Index (CII). The requirement under CII for lower carbon dioxide output over the coming years could result in 7 to 9 percent of the global fleet being scrapped, Toft said. As it moves back to being an independent carrier, Toft said MSC aims to hold on to its dominant market share in ocean shipping. He said MSC is looking to beef up its offers in surface transportation and inland logistics through its Medlog subsidiary, but those other services will be ancillary to providing customers with ocean capacity. “We are not an integrator,” Toft said. “We are first and foremost a shipping company. We let customers choose what they want.” Contact Michael Angell at michael.angell@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @michael_angell. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: TPM23: US can’t quit China, but trade needs to de-risk: Petraeus
content: Outside of future pandemics, retired Gen. David Petraeus said geopolitics and demographics mean further risks for US sourcing from China. Photo credit: Caught in the Moment Photography. The era of unfettered growth in international trade is coming to an end as geopolitical tensions and trade barriers arise across the world, particularly between the US and China, retired US Gen. David Petraeus said Monday. Petraeus, now a partner at private equity firm KKR, told attendees during the opening keynote of the Journal of Commerce’s TPM23 conference in Long Beach that trade will increasingly shift to new countries such as Southeast Asia, India, and Mexico as US businesses look to hedge the risks they face with China. Yet switching to those new countries carries risk as well, he said, meaning China will remain a key trade partner for years to come. “The barriers to the movement of capital, goods, and labor were all going down during the era of globalization,” Petraeus said. “Globalization is not over by any means, but it is now become ‘slowbalization.’” The shift away from China has seen some slow progress. China accounted for 40.7 percent of all US imports last year, according to PIERS, a sister product of the Journal of Commerce within S&P Global, down 1.7 percentage points from 2021 and the lowest level since 2006. Apple started manufacturing some iPhones in India last year to avoid the type of disruption it saw at its main factory in central China during the COVID-19 pandemic, Petraeus said. The pandemic highlighted a host of risks that shippers now need to be aware of and prepare for in their supply chains, he added. Globalization coincided with many US companies switching to “just-in-time” inventory management, which was further aided by the approximately two-week ocean transit from China to the US West Coast. But Petraeus said the risk of overseas factory shutdowns or shipping delays means companies are more likely to hold higher inventories and require more warehousing. “Just-in-time logistics may not be as solid an idea as it used to be, and we’re not back to just-in-case logistics,” Petraeus said. Outside of future pandemics, Petraeus said geopolitics and demographics mean further risks for sourcing from China. New trade barriers such as restrictions on microchips and technology that can be used for military goods further hinder US trade with China. The Inflation Reduction Act signed last year also favors US manufacturing, Petraeus said. Likewise, a shrinking workforce in China due to an aging population also raises labor costs, once one of the country’s main advantages, he added. “You keep adding all of this up and you see dramatic transformations in the supply chain," Petraeus said. Those factors will drive more US product sourcing to other countries such as Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Mexico, he added. However, those countries present their own risks, Petraeus said. India and the Philippines still lack the roads and rail networks to get products quickly to market. Bureaucratic hurdles in those countries also need to be lowered to grow their share of global trade, Petraeus said, adding that recent actions by Mexico’s government to reduce election oversight are a concern about the country going in the wrong direction. Petraeus said those factors will mean that China, while likely being seeing some trade move away, will continue to underpin trans-Pacific trade with the US. “None of these other countries can replace China, none of them has the kind of colossal capacity that’s built up many decades in China,” Petraeus said. “We can’t decouple from China. There’s selective decoupling taking place, on both sides.” Contact Michael Angell at michael.angell@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @michael_angell. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: TPM23: Resilient US economy may avoid recession in 2023: economist
content: Investments by shipping and logistics companies and ports have made the global supply chain more flexible, reliable, and resilient, former IHS Markit chief economist Nariman Behravesh said Monday. Photo credit: Caught in the Moment Photography. The US economy may avoid a recession this year as key elements such as consumer spending prove more resilient than widely expected, economist Nariman Behravesh told the Journal of Commerce’s TPM23 conference in Long Beach Monday. “Despite dire predictions last year of an imminent recession, we’ve seen the global and US economies shrug off some of these shocks,” including inflation, volatile stock markets, and widespread supply chain disruption, said Behravesh. The “dramatic easing” of supply chain disruption helped empower that “shrug,” he said. “Investments by shipping and logistics companies and ports have made the global supply chain much more flexible, reliable, and resilient, and plunging shipping costs have benefited world trade,” Behravesh said. “The very, very good news is that the multiple crises we’ve seen in the last two years have not derailed the US and global economies, but the level of uncertainty remains at near record levels, so we’re not out of the woods yet,” said the former chief economist of IHS Markit, now part of S&P Global. A year ago, Russia had just invaded Ukraine, sending oil and fuel prices rocketing worldwide. The Omicron variant of COVID-19 was spreading rapidly in China, leading to lockdowns. And fears of a US recession were climbing as the Federal Reserve raised interest rates to fight inflation. “Compared with a year ago, things seem a little less scary, so I’ll take that as a positive,” Behravesh said. Meltdowns in crypto currency and the high-tech sector grabbed headlines, but consumer and capital spending and trade were resilient, said Behravesh. “We are probably going to be able to avoid a deep downturn in 2023,” he said. “A lot of pessimists have started using terms like ‘soft landing.’” Behravesh expects inflationary pressures to gradually ease. Growth will slow he said, “but recessions are far from inevitable, and soft landings are possible.” World trade will slow, but will be helped by supply chain “decongestion,” which will also help reduce what he called supply-driven inflation. “Last year global inflation was about 7 percent, this year so far about 5 percent, and next year will be 3 percent, which is still above the 2 percent that central banks want to see,” Behravesh said. “As supply chain issues have been resolved both headline and core inflation have begun to fall, maybe not fast enough, but they are falling,” he added. “The big decline has been in goods prices, so that’s very positive. The decline in service prices, unfortunately, has been much slower.” Behravesh noted that the US had two consecutive quarters of economic contraction in the first half of 2022, “but there was no recession. How can you have a recession when unemployment is at its lowest point in 50 years?” And US gross domestic product expanded in the last two quarters of 2022. “Robust household and business finances are keeping the US very resilient and will continue to sustain growth in consumer and capital spending and trade,” Behravesh said. “We’ve had high-tech layoffs, but these have been more than offset by strong employment growth in the service sectors.” Contact William B. title: TPM23: CN focusing investment on capacity growth: CEO
content: The pandemic altered traditional methods of shipping, Canadian National CEO Tracy Robinson said. Photo credit: Caught in the Moment Photography. Canadian National Railway is focusing on building capacity to enhance on-time performance throughout its North American network, build resilience for cargo surges, and offer alternative options to the US West Coast, where a lack of a labor contract has pushed some cargo away, CEO Tracy Robinson said Tuesday. The pandemic altered traditional methods of shipping, forcing shippers to switch ports, terminals, and regions in the past few years as they battled congestion and West Coast diversions, Robinson told attendees at the Journal of Commerce's TPM23 conference in Long Beach. “I’m a believer that supply chains can pretty much do anything if you give them enough time and enough notice as to what’s coming next,” Robinson said, adding that the industry hasn’t had that luxury in the past few years. “But the worst thing that we can do is revert to making sure that we’re protecting our own piece of the supply chain, because the supply chain only works if all it works,” she said. To address growth needs, CN is investing in facilities in Milton, Ontario, and at inland terminals to increase capacity in the Midwest and on the East Coast. Robinson said CN is also looking to enhance operations and provide incentives to truckers and beneficial cargo owners (BCOs) to encourage cargo moves on the weekends. “Our big role is to facilitate growth in the economy,” she said. CN, she added, is focused on maintaining strict schedules, which has been better for planning and serving customers more profitably while moving assets faster. Robinson said she can see clearly where capacity opportunities are, investing in the Prince Rupert and Vancouver corridor in the west, as well as in Halifax in the east. CN’s Halifax terminal grew with record volumes last year, but at 600,000 TEU is still only at 50 percent capacity despite being the quickest Canadian entry to Chicago, the CEO noted. CN will grow its capacity based on the assumption that China will remain the biggest sourcing country for North America while acknowledging the sourcing shift under way into Southeast Asia, India, and potentially Africa that could fuel cargo through eastern Canada, Robinson said. “If you can imagine where that capacity is, where that demand may take us and where we need capacity, we want to make sure that all of us on this continent are positioned well to take advantage of that,” she said. title: TPM23: Sustainability should be collective, not competitive: ONE’s Nixon
content: The cost of decarbonizing shipping will be about $3 trillion, ONE CEO Jeremy Nixon estimates. Photo credit: Caught in the Moment Photography. Decarbonizing shipping should not be a competitive issue, but rather a collective effort between carriers seeking the fuel of the future, Jeremy Nixon, CEO of Ocean Network Express (ONE), said Tuesday. Nixon told attendees at the Journal of Commerce’s TPM23 conference in Long Beach that carriers need to collaborate “as quickly as possible.” “There is no point in us all having our own R&D silos, trying to reinvent the wheel individually,” he said on a panel addressing the route to carbon-neutral shipping. “This is a collective call. If we move forward quickly to decarbonize shipping, we can decarbonize the world.” But Nixon said decarbonizing shipping would also depend on equalizing the price differential between fossil fuels and green alternatives. He said on headhaul trades, the average cost of using current carbon fuels was about $1,000 per FEU, while alternative fuels such as methanol, ammonia, or synthetic liquefied natural gas (LNG) were likely to be two or three times more expensive. “As individual carriers, we will pioneer new green solutions, but if our competitors are running at $1,000 per FEU and we are running at $3,000 per FEU, we can’t survive,” the Singapore-based CEO said. The cost of decarbonizing the industry will be about $3 trillion, Nixon estimated — and that cost burden would need to be passed on. “In terms of the operating costs, if we had to absorb green fuel costs, that would add about $2 billion to our [operating expenditures], and we can’t do that individually,” he said. “We all have to pass on our costs in a logical, transparent way through the supply chain, right to the end-customer, so when we go in a store, we can see what the price and what the CO2 [carbon dioxide] footprint of a product is, and we have all contributed towards trying to minimize it,” Nixon added. Paolo Montrone, head of global trades for Kuehne + Nagel, told panel attendees although there was demand for sustainable options offered by service providers, “there needs to be a big spike” in that demand to drive the investment required. “We can’t wait for the asset owners to make this problem go away,” he said. “Most companies should have decarbonizing the supply chain close to their hearts and part of their budgets should go to into trying new solutions.” Montrone said the transport emissions data that was available to the market was precise enough to be executable for companies wanting to lower their carbon footprints. “Yes, there is a cost, but the counter argument is that first movers will have benefits,” he said. “Companies that decarbonize will have higher ESG ratings and will benefit in capital markets and with consumers.” Katarin van Orshaegen, commercial lead and spokesperson for GoodShipping, an organization involved in the decarbonization of shipping, agreed that the benefits of implementing sustainable transport solutions outweighed the additional costs. “Our customers were not afraid to pay premiums because they saw the costs of not doing anything,” she told the TPM23 panel. “Being the frontrunner gives you access to consumers that are getting more educated, sustainable buying is increasing, and by not doing anything, you would lose all this.” An end-customer that has made the move into green shipping solutions is Julia Bedanova, COO of nursery furniture retailer Million Dollar Baby. “It is non-negotiable for end-consumers and for brands, and the more they ask for carbon-free shipping, the quicker we will get to a level playing field,” she said. “Shippers and the brands need to come to the table and say they want a reduction in carbon, and they are willing to pay a premium.” But Bedanova told the panel it is critical that emissions data is consistent and reliable. “There needs to be a global agreement in how this is calculated and maintained so the shippers and end-consumers can trust and rely on [it],” she said. title: TPM23: Flexport’s new CEO puts focus on building ‘next-generation’ tech
content: “We can double our tech team in six months in this environment, where we couldn’t do that a year ago,” Flexport CEO Dave Clark told TPM23 Tuesday. Photo credit: Caught in the Moment Photography. Former Amazon supply chain executive Dave Clark takes on his new role as the sole CEO of Flexport on Wednesday determined to expand the digital forwarder’s technology platform and customer base — and not so concerned about claims his company plays a “polarizing” role in the freight market. Flexport entered global freight forwarding in 2012 as a digital company determined to disrupt an old-school, low-tech industry, drawing $2.3 billion in investment over 10 years, including a $935 million funding round last year. Similar to other so-called disruptors, it’s been a magnet for criticism. “I spent 23 years at Amazon, so ‘polarizing’ is not new to me,” Clark said at the Journal of Commerce’s TPM23 conference in Long Beach Tuesday. “Any time you’re trying to do something different, people tend to be skeptical, and if they weren't skeptical, I’d be a little surprised, frankly. “ Flexport is “going to do new things,” Clark added. “And I think people should be skeptical until we deliver. When I talk with our customers, they’re really happy with what we’re doing, and they’re happy with our direction, with where we’re going. And that’s the voice that matters the most to me.” Clark joined Flexport last year as co-CEO alongside founder Ryan Petersen, who said he believed Clark was the person who could expedite Flexport’s growth. That was before a slowdown in global trade that led Flexport to announce a 20 percent reduction in its workforce, about 650 jobs, in January. “We had a phenomenal team, but we had too many people given where volume was going,” Clark said, adding there were too many people in the wrong seats. “We had too many salespeople. We had done a big transformation, regrouping our talent to drive more operational execution.” Flexport, which had more than $3.3 billion in revenue in 2021, said at the same time it announced the layoffs that it would hire more engineers this year. “We trimmed back on the roles that were not the right fit for where we need to be and we added roles that were really important for us,” Clark said. What’s important to Clark as he takes the CEO’s seat is accelerating the development of Flexport’s technology platform. “We’re taking the opportunity in this little sort of ‘air gap’ in manufacturing and inventory globally to put our resources toward building our next-generation products,” he said. An example of those products is an app Flexport launched on Shopify earlier in February to help online retailers get access to instant quotes, booking, tracking, and customs clearance services as it aims to deepen its reach with US importers, especially small to mid-sized businesses. “I really liked building and I love supply chain,” Clark said. “[But] I get up every morning and the supply chain is a daily mess. It’s a real opportunity to bring technology into this space, and to help make it easier and make it easier for customers and to pull a lot of waste out of the system.” He sees Flexport’s role as “bringing all these transportation [modes] to a single pane of glass and using our levers to connect capacity at each one.” “We can pull those levers with partners around the world and enable people to actually run their supply chains in an efficient way,” Clark said. Technology not only enables those multimodal connections, it enables Flexport and its partners and customers to scale their operations, he said. “Most companies will never have the opportunity to roll up the kind of scale we’re talking about,” said Clark. “Our mission is to make that easy for everybody.” Contact William B.
