title: Global supply chains not quite back to pre-pandemic norms: analyst
content: Transportation providers should recognize that the impact of bottlenecks are likely to differ across industry verticals, says analyst Jason Miller. Photo credit: hxdyl / Shutterstock.com. The Federal Reserve Board Bank of New York’s Global Supply Chain Pressure Index (GSCPI) for February 2023 indicates that supply chain issues had receded to normal levels, a theme picked up by many outlets. However, a variety of other data sources suggest it is premature to conclude that supply chain bottlenecks have reverted to their pre-COVID levels. As such, a more apt evaluation is that supply chain bottlenecks are resolving, yet issues continue to be more pervasive than before the pandemic struck. The first piece of evidence is data from the Bank of Canada's Quarterly Business Outlook Survey, which directly asks a representative sample of Canadian firms the extent they are experiencing supply chain bottlenecks (a far more direct measurement approach than used in constructing the GSCPI). Whereas GSPCI started showing substantial relief in Q3 2022, the BoC’s index did not start to show much easing until Q4 2022. Moreover, in Q4 2022, BoC's supply chain bottleneck index still had ~22 percent of firms citing supply chain bottlenecks, compared with just 9.4 percent for Q1 2017 to Q4 2019. This suggests we are not back to pre-COVID levels of bottlenecks. The second piece of evidence is a series of monthly business outlook surveys for the manufacturing sector conducted by the Federal Reserve Board Bank of Philadelphia. Starting in 2022, the Philly Fed began asking manufacturers in the third month of each quarter the extent their capacity utilization was being impacted by various factors, including supply chain bottlenecks. The December survey showed ~45 percent of respondents citing supply chains as moderately or significantly constraining capacity utilization, which was down substantially from the September iteration where the corresponding statistic was 68.2 percent. In comparison, the June statistic was 72.1 percent, while March 2022 saw a staggering 85.4 percent of respondents indicating supply chain bottlenecks were moderately or significantly impacting capacity utilization. This provides a second data point indicating bottlenecks are easing but have not returned to pre-COVID levels. The third data set pointing toward disruptions easing but not being back to normal is the Census Bureau's Quarterly Survey of Plant Capacity Utilization data regarding the percent of plants citing insufficient supply of materials as affecting their capacity utilization. While improving in Q3 2022, this issue was cited about three times more frequently than before COVID. As shown, this data tends to track closely to the BoC data, suggesting improvement in Q4 2022 but still worse than pre-COVID levels. The last dataset concerns data from the Institute for Supply Management regarding short supplies of semiconductors, electrical components, and electronic components. This data indicates the number of components in short supply has declined substantially from early 2022 and especially from mid-2021 levels, yet multiple components have been in short supply for 25+ months. Additionally, the number of components cited in short supply still exceeds 2019 levels by a substantial degree. This again speaks to supply chain bottlenecks not having returned to normalcy. For transportation providers, the fact that supply chain bottlenecks are easing but issues have not returned to pre-COVID levels just yet holds several implications. First, for sectors where demand is expected to be strong in 2023 such as agricultural equipment and commercial aircraft, easing supply chain bottlenecks suggest there could be a ramp up of production as we move into 2023 which should be planned for accordingly. Second, the fact that there are still ongoing bottlenecks creates an added degree of uncertainty about manufacturers’ production schedules and timelines for projects, which may face unforeseen slowdowns due to ongoing material availability. Third, transportation providers should recognize that the impact of bottlenecks are likely to differ across industry verticals. For example, while chemical producers reported sharp declines in raw material availability issues in the latest Census Bureau QCEW data, the same did not occur for transportation equipment manufacturers. As such, providers should not assume bottleneck issues are the same across the different industries they serve. Contact Jason Miller at mill2831@broad.msu.edu. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: FMC outlines $44 million budget request to enhance market oversight
content: The FMC’s remit has increased with the passage of OSRA-22. Photo credit: MOLPIX / Shutterstock.com. With new shipping laws to enforce and increased demand for market oversight, the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) is seeking a 14 percent increase in its fiscal 2024 budget request, the agency revealed Monday. Its proposed $43.7 million spending plan would include the hiring of 23 new employees. The 2024 fiscal year begins Oct. 1. FMC chairman Daniel Maffei is scheduled to appear in late March before the House of Representatives’ Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, where he is expected to make a formal budget request. While the FMC’s current fiscal 2023 budget saw a larger increase of $5.8 million over the year-prior budget, agency spokesperson John DeCrosta told the Journal of Commerce the 2024 budget represents “one of the biggest increases in recent years.” The bulk of the budget increase will be for more personnel. Net of retirements and regular turnover, the FMC expects to have 163 full-time employees by 2024, up from 140 currently. The agency added 20 full-time employees in fiscal 2023 as it dealt with supply chain issues that arose during COVID-19, DeCrosta said. Since then, the FMC’s remit has increased with the passage of the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22). Likewise, the FMC is having to keep up with “a large number of foreign-based NVOCCs (non-vessel owning common carriers) entering into the market” since the pandemic, the agency said in its budget justification. In 2022, there were 4,145 non-US-based NVOCCs, up from 1,860 in 2020, the FMC said. “Enforcing OSRA-22 will be among the things the new employees do, but it’s not the only thing,” DeCrosta said. “It’s about helping exporters, consumer assistance, making sure market participants behave according to the law, and that there’s no market collusion occurring.” Contact Michael Angell at michael.angell@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @michael_angell. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Microsoft unveils AI tool to mitigate supply chain risk
content: Copilot, which can also be applied to other Microsoft business applications, aims to help busy supply chain managers quickly make sense of massive amounts of data, Smith told Supply Chain Dive. When you’ve got large volumes of data and busy supply chain managers, AI is needed to help elicit problems and risks, and propose mitigation plans, he added. “A lot of people in the supply chain would say they don’t have time … to look at dashboards if there’s potential data there, let alone engage the suppliers in something that potentially may happen,” Smith said. “The generative AI — the email, communications and business contexts — allows us to really expedite that mitigation and the engagement with the suppliers.” First, the AI algorithm scans news articles and takes other steps to identify any potential risk that may impact suppliers or partners across a network, such as geopolitical or financial risk. From there, an AI-drafted message can be sent to suppliers asking whether they expect any disruption and to confirm if purchase orders will be impacted. “The supplier can then close the loop by replying back, and collaborating,” Smith said. Microsoft initially launched its Supply Chain Center in November as a command center that unifies data across ERPs and third-party management solutions to help solve existing supply chain challenges. Other players in the tech space have also been looking to pool and utilize data to promote supply chain visibility. That includes Amazon Web Services, which launched a cloud application in November. More recently in January, software company Oracle launched new updates to its Transportation Management and Global Trade Management platforms, part of its Oracle Fusion Cloud Supply Chain Management application. The company, which updates its SCM capabilities every quarter, intends to further enhance its sustainability features in the second half of 2023.

title: Freightos’ 2022 financials reveal losses amid improving operating margins
content: Freightos went public in January, seven months after being acquired by a special-purpose acquisition company that injected $82 million into the technology provider. Photo credit: small smiles / Shutterstock.com. Freightos is on a path toward improving its operating margin despite widening losses in 2022, according to CEO Zvi Schreiber. The logistics technology provider released its first financials Monday since going public in January. While still a private company last year, Freightos took a $14.6 million operating loss on $19.1 million in revenues. “We enjoy a high and increasing gross profit margin and our unit economics are improving,” Schreiber said in a statement Monday. In a subsequent earnings call Monday, Schreiber went further about Freightos’ potential. “The power of a two-sided marketplace is the flywheel effect. Buyers attract sellers and sellers attract buyers,” he said. “This flywheel can create decades of sustainable, defensible growth at a very low cost of growth. “We’ve actually taken it a step further,” Schreiber added. “Freightos is a three-sided marketplace, connecting carriers, like airlines and ocean liners, freight forwarders, and importers or exporters.” That three-sided marketplace refers to one part of the business, Freightos.com, connecting forwarders to importers and exporters, and another part of the business, WebCargo, connecting air carriers to forwarders. Freightos’ core businesses involve software and marketplaces that enable forwarders, airlines, and ocean carriers to transact with shippers and logistics companies. The company, in its financial statement, refers to itself as a booking and payment platform. The 2022 operating loss, measured in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), was larger than the $12.4 million loss in 2021. But the company said its EBITDA margin improved from –111 percent in 2021 to –77 percent in 2022. Since Freightos announced its purchase by a special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) in mid-2022, the technology provider has emphasized what it calls gross booking value (GBV) as a key metric upon which to judge the business. GBV refers to the total amount of freight volume transacted across its products, and so is not Freightos’ revenue, but rather a measure of transaction volume growth on its platform. “Our sustained growth in gross booking value leads directly to sustained growth in revenue and gross profit, which at scale is expected to generate a healthy net profit,” Schreiber said in the statement. In reply to an analyst query Monday about how depressed freight rates are impacting Freightos’ fee collections on marketplace transactions, Schreiber said the company’s “take rate will be largely similar this year [to] last year, [in terms of] order of magnitude. But that actually hides that the underlying take rate is actually improving in both parts of the marketplace.” More than half of Freightos’ revenue in 2022 came from software-as-a-service (SaaS) solutions, not its marketplace. But Schreiber told the Journal of Commerce in January, prior to the company’s public listing, that he expected the vast majority of Freightos’ revenue would eventually be derived from its marketplace, not SaaS products. During the earnings call, Schreiber also addressed the issue of what he considered an inflection point for margins, meaning the point at which the scale of the marketplace would overcome fixed expenses related to running the company regardless of the size of the marketplace. “We've always been able to grow our team less quickly than our gross bookings and number of transactions,” he said. “The cost of goods sold pretty much grows together with the revenue. Where we break even is when 65 percent of the revenue covers our expenses.” The company’s net cash used for operating activities was $14.9 million in 2022, compared with $17.3 million in 2021. Freightos’ public listing helped the company reel in $82 million in funds, primarily by unlocking committed capital from the investors behind the SPAC, Denver-based Gesher I Acquisition Corp. Schreiber told the Journal of Commerce in January that funding will be used to help Freightos grow by adding people and making acquisitions. Freightos’ share price closed at $4.05 Tuesday, down from $10 when the company first listed Jan. 26. Its market capitalization is $64.3 million. Freightos estimates its fiscal year 2023 revenue will be between $22.3 million and $23.6 million, with EBITDA losses hitting $21.2 million to $24.6 million. The company expects GBV to rise between 31 percent and 43 percent over the $611 million in GBV recorded in 2022. title: Wan Hai faces $950,000 fine under revised FMC settlement over detention charges
content: The Wan Hai case involves shippers that were unable to return containers to the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach due to congestion. Photo credit: Teri Errico Griffis / Journal of Commerce. Ocean carrier Wan Hai would pay a $950,000 fine under a proposed settlement involving claims it wrongfully charged US shippers detention penalties on 21 occasions in the spring of 2021, according to a revised agreement submitted to the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC). The penalty amount — up from an original $850,000 in May — comes after a 14-month investigation by the FMC’s Bureau of Enforcement, Investigations and Compliance (BOEIC). The new agreement was filed Monday with the FMC; the agency has 30 days to review the settlement. Under the agreement, Taiwan-based Wan Hai would also be forced to pay undisclosed restitution to the shippers in question and be limited from assessing any detention charges when containers cannot be returned. The commission’s decision to seek a higher civil penalty sends a message to other carriers that the agency will wield its awakened investigative power with force. BOEIC initially investigated Wan Hai in December 2021 for alleged shipping violations stemming from 21 detention charges it levied against shippers that were unable to return containers to the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach due to congestion. An initial proposed settlement in May 2022 between the carrier and the BOEIC called for an $850,000 fine and for Wan Hai to cease collection attempts on those 21 invoices. But the FMC rejected the settlement. Among the reasons for rejection, the agency said that asking shippers to take screenshots of available time slots to return containers contravened the provisions under shipping laws that shifted the burden of proof to the carrier, making them responsible for establishing the reasonableness of any detention and demurrage (D&D) charge. The updated settlement would further set limitations on Wan Hai’s assessment of detention charges, and the carrier must “cease and desist from knowingly assessing detention charges” in situations when it fails to provide an equipment return location, identify a return location that is not accepting chassis, or where appointments are unavailable for equipment return. Carriers are under “constant investigation” by the FMC, Chairman Daniel Maffei said at the Journal of Commerce’s TPM23 conference in Long Beach last month. “They’re constantly monitored, moderated, and I really do think it’s more akin to a permanent investigation,” he said. Maffei told TPM23 attendees that while D&D cannot be eliminated, the FMC is working on a rule that will help restore the system’s credibility in order to incentivize cargo movement. “I think in many ways [detention and demurrage] had lost so much credibility with shippers that... [they started] just throwing up their hands and going, ‘It doesn’t matter what I do. I’m gonna get these charges,’” he said. In April 2022, the FMC ordered Hapag-Lloyd to pay $822,220 in civil damages — upped in June to $2 million — after the carrier was found to have improperly assessed detention charges to a California drayage provider. title: Shipper group wants more FMC action on dwell fees, ERDs
content: NSAC recommended in December that shippers should only be invoiced 25 percent of detention and demurrage costs or a universal fee for government holds that are outside of the shipper’s control. Photo credit: SNEHIT PHOTO / Shutterstock.com. An advisory group formed by the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) and consisting of several major shippers is asking the FMC to address why earliest return dates (ERDs) for containers still aren’t adequately communicated despite carriers pledging nearly a year ago to mitigate ERD issues. The issue is one of six matters the National Shipping Advisory Committee (NSAC) has asked the FMC to take up since last June, including seeking clarification on why charging storage fees on government-held cargo is reasonable. NSAC has made six formal recommendations to the FMC in a bid to have the regulators address the issues. Regarding proposals related to dwell fees and establishing a new advisory subcommittee and a uniform data-sharing system, FMC referred NSAC to ongoing FMC rulemaking and investigations. The FMC shut down a recommendation to expand its oversight, saying only Congress can legislate that. NSAC, launched in the spring of 2021 and made up of FMC-appointed shippers from Target, DuPont, IKEA, and other companies, meets voluntarily to flesh out recommendations from experts within the industry. Three members of the group have expressed frustration privately that the agency isn't giving their proposals the appropriate attention. NSAC recommended in December that shippers should only be invoiced 25 percent of detention and demurrage costs or a universal fee for government holds that are outside of the shipper’s control and can lead to months of detainment and millions of dollars in surcharges. The FMC, which has 60 days to respond to recommendations, said last month that reasonableness for accrued storage fees on government holds, just as any other cargo, is evaluated under the interpretive rule and whether the charges incentivize the movement of cargo. The agency added that when two ongoing charge complaints regarding similar storage fees are resolved, they “may be instructive in further interpreting the commission’s interpretive rule as it applies to government holds.” FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei, expressing his personal views, said at the Journal of Commerce’s TPM23 conference in Long Beach last month that, “If customs has your box, you can’t return it no matter how high that fee is. That’s not incentivizing you to return your cargo. So they can’t charge you that fee. In my view, that’s unreasonable.” Another major issue NSAC is pushing to resolve on behalf of exporters is the continued lack of adequate and reliable communication on ERDs on the part of carriers and the need for a cohesive notification system for when a full container can be dropped off at the terminal. FMC pointed the NSAC to Commissioner Rebecca Dye’s Fact Finding 29, which last May reported “all carriers claimed that they communicated vessel schedule or ERD information to their customers,” although some admitted they did not directly share changes. Following the FMC investigation, carriers vowed last spring to mitigate export demurrage or detention charges caused by changes in vessel schedules and ERDs, which account for about half of all detention and demurrage assessments, according to the report. Most carriers assured the FMC they would extend free time by the same number of days the vessel schedule is delayed, while other carriers agreed to preemptively extend free time or waive D&D without issuing an invoice. title: US regulators approve CP-KCS merger to form first US-Canada-Mexico rail
content: The STB approved the merger despite concerns that the estimated 136,000 intermodal loads traveling on the new single-line service between Mexico and the US Midwest is an inflated forecast. Photo credit: Ian Dewar Photography / Shutterstock.com. US regulators on Wednesday approved the closely watched USD $31 billion (C$42.5 billion) acquisition of Kansas City Southern by Canadian Pacific Railway, saying the single-line rail service between Mexico and the US Midwest will increase competition by providing new options for shippers to route their cargo. The vote by the US Surface Transportation Board (STB) was 4-1 and came despite concerns from the STB that forecasts of 136,000 intermodal loads annually by the combined CPKC through the new rail options may be artificially high. CP can take control of KCS as soon as April 14. “On balance, the merger of these two railroads will benefit the American economy and will be an improvement for all citizens in terms of safety and the environment,” STB Chairman Martin Oberman said during a press briefing after the agency’s vote. “One of the underlying factors that we found in this merger is that putting these two small railroads together will provide a stronger competitive landscape in the rail industry because separately CP and Kansas City Southern do not have the same ‘oomph’ power as they do together.” Oberman noted the newly merged company would have about 20,000 “route miles,” putting it up against “western US giant railroads” that have more than 32,000 route miles. STB’s wide-ranging 212-page decision covers several concerns about the impacts of the merger on US ports, longshore workers, and intermodal shippers currently using other North American Class I railroads to move their containers. STB members rejected claims from the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC), BNSF Railway, Norfolk Southern Railway, and Union Pacific Railroad that the transaction would harm shippers. Three FMC commissioners had urged the STB to reject the CP-KCS deal, claiming it would divert cargo from US ports toward Canadian and Mexican ports and rail networks, and harm US port authorities, longshore workers, and rail workers. The STB rejected that argument. “[The merger] will benefit US shippers and receivers, given the availability of new single-line routes from the Port of Lázaro Cárdenas in Mexico to the interior of the United States, especially in times when western US ports are congested,” the STB wrote in its decision. Oberman said the competition from the CPKC routes will put pressure on US ports and railroads to do a better job handling import surges in the future. “It's not exactly like during the pandemic the US ports were functioning well, so every US citizen could have benefited from better movement of goods from the ports,” he said. “Hopefully this will cause the US railroads to up their games at our US ports.” BNSF and UP had expressed concerns that CPKC would increase fees to interchange freight in Laredo and Robstown, Texas, something that would encourage shippers to stop using the western US rail providers between Mexico and the US Midwest, thus reducing competition rather than boosting it. “BNSF and UP fail to adequately explain why the intermodal, automotive, and grain traffic about which they have expressed the greatest concern cannot move via other competitive options,” the STB wrote. “Intermodal traffic is highly competitive and intermodal customers could switch to trucks in a matter of hours if a rail carrier fails to provide a competitive service.” Norfolk Southern expressed concern about the Meridian Speedway, an NS-KCS intermodal gateway through the Gulf Coast that connects the US East Coast to a terminal in Wylie, Texas, outside of Dallas. NS argued that the CPKC railroad will flood the route with bulk traffic, harming intermodal shippers who depend on the Meridian Speedway to move containers. “There is not sufficient evidence that intermodal traffic would be adversely impacted by the transaction,” the STB wrote. “CPKC will remain incentivized to maintain fluid, efficient operations over the Meridian-Wylie route, given KCS’s 70 percent ownership in the Meridian Speedway ... Norfolk Southern has not shown that the impact on intermodal traffic will be as severe as it alleges.” Oberman said while he understood the concerns expressed by the competing railroads, there was “no [factual] basis to credit any of the fears ...” Nevertheless, the STB will grant a seven-year overview period of the entire transaction during which shippers or other railroads can raise concerns about how the combined CPKC operates. title: PepsiCo asks suppliers to avoid buying palm oil from major producer in Indonesia
content: PepsiCo is among the latest consumer goods companies to ban palm oil from Indonesia-based conglomerate Astra Agro Lestari in its supply chain. AAL, which owns palm oil plantations in Indonesia, was accused last year of human rights abuses and land grabbing. In an open letter, the International Federation for Human Rights asked several major consumer goods companies, including PepsiCo, to cut AAL from their supply chains over its “sustained role in forcibly grabbing communities’ land, contributing to environmental destruction, negatively impacting communities’ livelihoods, and criminalizing land and environmental human rights defenders.” Other companies addressed in the letter include Hershey’s, Kellogg, Unilever, Nestlé and Procter & Gamble. An investigation from earlier in 2022 by the environmental group Friends of the Earth alleged that subsidiaries of AAL illegally occupied 16,000 acres of local farmers’ land. After the report came out, AAL said it would appoint a third party to investigate the allegations. In a statement, PepsiCo said that it was reviewing the allegations against AAL through its established grievance process. “While PepsiCo does not source directly from AAL, we are engaging with suppliers who continue to source from them and have asked that they suspend the mills identified as being potentially linked to the grievance and underlying allegations,” the company said. PepsiCo uses palm oil primarily in its packaged food business and is one of the largest buyers of the ingredient in the world, though its purchases still represent less than 1% of the supply, according to the company. The company’s goals around palm oil include having 100% of its supply covered under “No Deforestation, No Peat, No Exploitation” principles or a time-bound initiative showing progress toward that sustainability goal. According to Reuters, which earlier reported on PepsiCo’s suspension of AAL palm oil from its supply chain, Nestlé, Procter & Gamble and infant formula maker FrieslandCampina have also suspended sourcing from AAL. AAL has said in the past that it is committed to upholding human, community and labor rights, and that it cooperates with farming communities in its supply chain. Palm oil is widely used in food, cosmetics and other consumer products, as well as biofuels. AAL is one of the top five producers for the global market, which is projected to grow from $48.6 billion in 2022 to $70.2 billion by 2029, according to HTF Market Intelligence. Environmental groups have long put pressure on companies over palm oil sourcing, as production of the oil has been linked to deforestation and human rights abuses. Retailers as well as consumer goods companies are also alert to the sustainability issues tied to the commodity. As part of its sustainability goals, retail giant Walmart plans to use only palm oil with no deforestation links by 2025 in its private label products. Anbinh Phan, Walmart’s director of global government affairs and business diplomacy, noted that much of the world relies on palm oil from Indonesia, a country rich in biodiversity. According to the Yale Center for Business and the Environment, Indonesia and Malaysia produce over 85% of the global supply. Phan, speaking at a panel hosted by the American Apparel & Footwear Association earlier in March, said that Walmart is beginning to invest in NGOs and place-based initiatives that address the needs and rights of local communities and as well as issues including deforestation in palm oil sourcing. But the executive acknowledged that the company’s efforts can’t make a lasting difference on its own. “Even as we invest in these critical landscapes and address these issues around regeneration,” Phan said, “we really need government participation and action so that these projects last beyond the scope of our investments.” Editor’s note:

title: Can tech startups make food delivery less chaotic?
content: The average person living in a big city can get almost anything delivered in about 30 minutes: toilet paper, tacos or even tequila. While the pandemic solidified shoppers’ need for speed (and convenience), delivery businesses are starting to leverage technology to ease some of the headaches rapid delivery has caused, from underpaid gig workers to congested curbs to increased traffic emissions. At last week’s Curbivore conference, businesses in the delivery space opined on how to improve rapid delivery in the panel “Going the Extra Mile – Building A World Designed for Delivery.” Yummy, a Los Angeles-area grocery delivery service, promises that busy consumers can get their groceries in about 30 minutes. Its delivery workers are employees, not gig workers, and they pull groceries from Yummy’s own physical storefronts instead of dark stores. According to co-founder and CEO Barnaby Montgomery, this investment in communities and workers has paid off. Other companies in the delivery space have focused on improving metrics for delivery drivers, who are often part-time gig workers. Over 85% of the delivery drivers for Pico Mobility, a merchant platform and e-moped subscription service operating in the Los Angeles and San Diego areas, work less than 20 hours per week. The company says it works to reduce barriers to employment. “Sixty percent of the people who would like to make money [doing] delivery do not have access to a vehicle,” said Pico co-founder and CEO Emre Ucer. Pico gives delivery drivers access to e-mopeds on a subscription basis. The e-mopeds are right-sized for food delivery, which decreases the congestion caused by larger delivery vehicles and makes delivery a more eco-friendly option, he said. Pico’s delivery platform also gives drivers a dedicated delivery zone, making their income more predictable and cutting down on travel time and distance. Meanwhile, last-mile location company Beans.ai is working to reduce the headache drivers face trying to find a dropoff point with Google Maps alone. “We all want our customers to get the delivery with one click. There should be no interaction with the driver,” said Akash Agarwal, founder and chief business officer. “The driver should not be calling you: ‘Where are you? I can’t find you. Where is your apartment? What’s your gate code? Do you have a dog?’” With Beans.ai, specific delivery data lives in the app for drivers to access, maximizing their time and income and minimizing idling, circling and parking. Currently, venture capital money subsidizes many delivery businesses, but new pricing models might replace free and cheap delivery as the market matures. This right-sizing of consumer expectations might also reduce the delivery burden on cities. “It is pretty difficult right now to find that sweet spot with the super-high expectations that you have of getting free delivery,” said Maria Shapiro, partnerships lead at delivery platform Nash.

title: US draft legislation seeks to update OSRA-22, boost China scrutiny
content: A California congressman is drafting a bill that would revise the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 less than a year after it was made law by President Joe Biden. Photo credit: Jaxport. A congressman who helped spearhead passage of the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22) is helping to draft new legislation that would update some aspects of the law, including publicizing more broadly penalties imposed on marine terminals and ocean carriers as a result of shipper complaints. The legislation, authored in part by Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., also aims to draw a sharp line on the involvement of China-based entities in US shipping. Once the bill’s text is finalized and introduced in the House of Representatives, Rep. Dusty Johnson, a Republican from South Dakota, will be the sponsor, with Garamendi as the original co-sponsor. Reached for comment on the legislation, Jazmine Kemp, deputy chief of staff and communications director for Johnson, told the Journal of Commerce the draft was not yet “final.” Dubbed the Ocean Shipping Reform Technical Act of 2023, the draft bill, seen by the Journal of Commerce, would heighten transparency into regulatory penalties levied against ocean carriers and marine terminal operators (MTOs) by ordering all sanctions be publicly posted online. Under OSRA-22’s interim charge complaint process, the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) only publicizes certain cases, and many are settled confidentially. The bill would call more attention to all complaints made against carriers and terminals by shippers, drayage providers, and consignees and the course of action taken by regulators. Establishing a more permanent and transparent complaint process has been pushed by groups such as the Agriculture Transportation Coalition (AgTC), which has been pressing for more clarity around a permanent charge process and certainty that when a complaint is brought to the FMC, it will be investigated. “We are helping AgTC members submit complaints, but the solution we seek is for carriers to comply with the law,” the AgTC said in a letter to its members Feb. 28. “OSRA sponsors aren’t happy.” OSRA-22 was signed into law last June by President Joe Biden. The draft bill also calls for the creation of a National Seaport Advisory Committee appointed by the FMC that would consist of 16 port authority representatives and eight marine terminal operators. The recommendation echoes FMC Commissioner Rebecca Dye’s Fact Finding 29 report, published last May, which also suggested formation of a National Seaport, Marine Terminal, and Ocean Carrier Advisory Committee to help the agency monitor with ongoing industry issues. The legislation calls for the seaport advisory committee to be created within 120 days of the bill’s passage. The legislation also recommends including freight forwarders on the existing National Shipper Advisory Committee (NSAC), a group of 24 importers and exporters that provides expertise to the FMC about conditions within freight markets. The draft bill would also heavily limit China-based entities and their ties with US shipping. The legislation seeks to ban all US port authorities from receiving federal funding if they use the China-sponsored National Transportation Logistics Public Information Platform (LOGINK). The bill also reiterates the need to add ocean common carriers that are owned by the Chinese government to the FMC’s list of “controlled” carriers, which are held to a higher standard for rate reviews. Currently, the FMC has Cosco Shipping and its OOCL subsidiary on the “controlled” list. The heightened scrutiny of China comes amid US government concerns over Beijing spying on the US, including fears that cranes manufactured by market leader and Shanghai-based ZPMC — which are used in 120 ports worldwide — could be tracking container moves at US terminals. title: New IMO rule at odds with practical realities: breakbulk executives
content: Certain types of general cargo ships are exempt from the energy efficiency existing ship index (EEXI) and carbon intensity indicator (CII) regulations for the time being. Photo credit: Harren & Partners / SAL. New environmental regulations will cause upheaval in the project and breakbulk shipping market, with the potential to affect commercial relationships and operations, reduce available tonnage, and drive freight rates higher, according to industry executives. The multipurpose/heavy-lift (MPV/HL) shipping segment may, in some instances, be able to avoid these new regulations, but it will not escape the larger pressures of decarbonization, nor requirements to collect emissions data. The new rules, the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO's) energy efficiency existing ship index (EEXI) and carbon intensity indicator (CII) regulations, went into force as of Jan. 1 but won’t be fully implemented until data has been collected for a year. The EEXI measures an existing ship’s energy efficiency against baselines set by the IMO and is relatively straightforward to calculate. The CII is a ratings system that measures how efficiently a ship transports goods or passengers as measured in grams of CO2 emitted per cargo-carrying capacity — i.e., deadweight (dwt) — and nautical mile. Data collected during 2023 must be reported in early 2024 and will be used to give ships a CII performance rating from A (major superior) to E (inferior). Vessels with low ratings will be required to take corrective actions, and rating thresholds will become increasingly stringent over time. The EEXI and the similar, older energy efficiency design index (EEDI) regulation, “are balance sheet issues,” Sam Norton, president and CEO of New York-listed Overseas Shipholding Group (OSG), told the Journal of Commerce. “There’s a one-time test or adjustment. You pass or not, you get your rating, and that’s what you are. From an industry point of view, these are easy.” The CII, on the other hand, “is an income statement issue,” he said. “It’s a flow — it changes and gets more stringent over time.” The CII rating is created by the trading patterns of the vessels, which is controlled by the operator, rather than the owner; and yet, the owner bears the consequence of the CII grading, he said. The CII focuses strictly on capacity and does not take the type of cargo carried by a given vessel into account. Instead, vessel speed, port congestion, bad weather, voyage lengths, and excess fuel consumption are among the factors that affect a ship’s CII rating. As such, industry stakeholders say the index offers a distorted picture of a given ship’s real-life emissions efficiency. “If we look at the IMO framework here, the CII is not fit for purpose,” Thomas Damsgaard, head of Americas for ship owner association BIMCO, said during a Jan. 26 Journal of Commerce webcast. “And that's really what it comes down to. Are we trying to create a greener planet for the next generation? Are we trying to reduce carbon and greenhouse gases? The CII rules do not address those issues. “There is a total disconnect, and this is where a lot of this frustration comes from, because I think there’s a general willingness within the industry to decarbonize,” he added. BIMCO Deputy Secretary General Lars Robert Pedersen said the CII, as currently written, creates unrealistic expectations for vessel operators. “The most CII-efficient ship is empty and never calls a port,” he told the Journal of Commerce. “If we were to change the metric and make it better matched to the intention of the whole concept of decarbonization, it would be the ship that carries cargo and comes into port that would get better ratings. The most suitable metric would actually reflect the commercial imperative. “Whether this will become possible will depend on the actual formulation and analysis of the data,” Pedersen added. Henning Rebnord, environmental, social, and governance and decarbonization manager at general cargo and multipurpose (MPV) carrier G2 Ocean, said the CII rules will significantly impact the MPV market and could incentivize shipping companies to implement measures that increase emissions in other areas to improve their vessels’ CII grades. “To ensure a positive CII rating, carriers may prefer ballast voyages over laden voyages as time spent in port loading or discharging cargo will negatively impact the CII rating,” Rebnard told the Journal of Commerce. “This is not a sustainable solution.” “Other non-eco-friendly measures carriers may consider are using feeder vessels and road or rail transportation to collect cargoes in hub ports,” he added. “This will reduce the number of port calls for the vessels and the time spent in port, consequently leading to a better CII rating, but these are not environmentally friendly solutions.” CII ratings are dependent on trading patterns, which are in turn dictated by the vessel charterer, who has chartered or contracted the ship from the vessel owner. During the webcast, both Norton and Damsgaard said the influence charterers will have on a vessel’s CII rating through the type and duration of a charter and the way a ship is operated signals a fundamental shift in the owner-charterer relationship. The charterer is responsible for determining the speed and duration of any voyage. But if the vessel violates regulations or fails to meet requirements and is subsequently prohibited from trading, the vessel owner is responsible for addressing the affected CII ratings. As such, the CII regulation has the potential to “create an environment where charterers and owners are in real conflict,” Norton said. Charterers taking a ship on a single voyage or short-term time charter of three to six months, for example, may not be interested in maintaining a vessel’s CII rating by sailing at a slower speed or maintaining operational efficiencies, Norton and Damsgaard explained. If that vessel’s rating slides to a D or an E, the owner could be forced to accept lower rates to secure vessel employment, Norton said. On the other hand, charterers who take a ship on a long-term charter of two or three years will be incentivized to maintain a ship’s high CII rating, especially if they sublet the vessel at potentially a higher freight rate than the original charter with the owner, Norton and Damsgaard said. Owners who operate their own ships have a vested, long-term incentive to maintain a good CII rating. Against this complicated background, BIMCO has released a new operational CII clause for time charter parties to help create a more equitable relationship between vessel owners and operators, Damsgaard said during the webinar. Existing charter party terms tend to incentivize moving vessels — and the cargo inside — from one port to another as quickly as possible, OSG’s Norton said during the webcast. For example, the economics of the demurrage clause or provisions for who pays for waiting time are all contingent upon when the ship arrives and when it departs, irrespective of operational circumstances such as port congestion, he said. The BIMCO CII clause does not address regulatory compliance. Rather, it is an operational clause that invites collaboration and cooperation between time charterers and the owners of the vessel, Damsgaard said. “The collaboration is really about collecting [data], and also sharing and working on the voyage planning. It's about creating transparency,” he said. “There’s scope for expanding beyond charter-owner cooperation to port cooperation, to try and get from just-in-time delivery a much more efficient use of [voyage time],” he added. “I think that's a really important point that needs to be pursued as well.” According to Jost Bergmann, business director for multipurpose and general cargo ships at ship classification society and maritime consultancy DNV, baseline requirements for the EEXI and CII rules differ by ship type. Based on IMO analyses of historic emissions data, tankers and bulk carriers are subject to the most demanding requirements, followed by general cargo ships, roll-on/roll-off (ro/ro) vessels, and container ships. Owners must work toward compliance for their assigned ship type, but Bergmann said many are now wondering if they can switch to a less-demanding category. General cargo ships include a mixed “grab bag” subset of specialized vessel types that don’t fit neatly into the general cargo category, differ wildly in emissions performance, and are exempt from the EEXI and CII regulations, he said. This subset of ships, which includes nuclear fuel carriers, livestock carriers, yacht carriers, and heavy load carriers, is not required to comply with the CII and EEXI regulations because they are designed for special purposes and measuring them against their deadweight capacity would be unfair, Bergmann explained. These types of ships are optimized as volume carriers rather than deadweight carriers, which creates a handicap when deadweight is the baseline for compliance measurements, he said. In certain cases, more technical multipurpose, heavy-lift, and heavy-load carrier can be considered members of this general cargo subset as well, giving those vessels a commercial advantage, at least in the short term, Bergmann said. Still, all ships must collect and report their emissions data, BIMCO’s Pedersen said. Pedersen said the IMO could revisit the general dry cargo subset and decide to include it in the CII and EEXI regulations in the future, but the exemption is “not a huge problem” given that the group represents a relatively small portion of the global shipping fleet. “There are limited cross-trading possibilities where you would try to evade CII by using this subset of general cargo,” he explained. “You wouldn't build an MPV ship to transport containers in order to evade CII.” Industry members are less sanguine, however. “The IMO has been criticized for being slow and too tentative with its emissions strategy and is discussing a tightening of requirements such that shipping reaches complete sustainability, or net zero, by 2050,” Bergmann said. “Ship owners are feeling more and more pressure to be sustainable, and this pressure will only increase,” he added. “These exemptions [to the CII and EEXI rules] help carriers and their customers in the short term, but in the long term, it will not save them. It gives them a few more years to trade existing vessels, but eventually the industry will have to demonstrate that it is doing its utmost to reduce emissions.” Contact Janet Nodar at janet.nodar@spglobal.com and follow her on Twitter: @janet_nodar. title: IEPs file brief siding with ocean carriers in FMC chassis dispute
content: The US’ three largest chassis providers are not a named party in the FMC complaint, but filed a brief as an outside party siding with the ocean carriers. Photo credit: Ari Ashe / Journal of Commerce. The three largest chassis providers in the US, siding with ocean carriers, have filed a brief asking the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) to overturn a February ruling by its chief administrative judge that gives shippers and truckers final say on what brand of chassis to use for certain inland moves. The independent equipment provider (IEPs) — DCLI, Flexi-Van Leasing, and TRAC Intermodal — argued that upending the current business model — in which ocean carriers dictate the chassis required on carrier haulage and some merchant haulage business — would create additional equipment shortages and invoicing problems that would do more harm than good to cargo owners. Erin Wirth, the FMC’s chief administrative judge, ruled in February that while ocean carriers can dictate which chassis to use under a carrier haulage agreement — also known as a “door-to-door move” — liners cannot force chassis decisions in any merchant haulage deals, or “port-to-port moves.” The Ocean Carriers Equipment Management Association (OCEMA) appealed Wirth’s decision earlier this month. The filing by the IEPs is an “amicus brief” because the chassis providers are not a listed party in the dispute. The IEPs wrote in the brief that Wirth’s decision would reduce chassis availability because DCLI, Flexi-Van, and TRAC would no longer be privy to sufficient information on cargo movement to know how to allocate equipment within the US, leading to more supply chain disruptions in the future. “It would require the IEPs to restructure chassis pools and operations to the disadvantage of the shipping public, increasing their costs and overriding the IEPs’ right to use and deploy their own assets,” the three companies wrote. “[It would] force a highly disruptive and inefficient restructuring of the [chassis] Pool of Pools at Los Angeles-Long Beach and could well force its demise.” The “Pool of Pools” is a shared pool of chassis covering the ports in Southern California in which DCLI, Flexi-Van Leasing, TRAC Intermodal, and others supply chassis. The chassis providers argued that the trucking lobby that filed the case with the FMC — the Intermodal Carriers Conference (IMCC) — have ulterior motives that are not in the best interest of the cargo owners, but rather benefit the North American Chassis Pool Cooperative (NACPC). NACPC’s owners are also members of IMCC and its parent group, the American Trucking Associations. “IMCC seeks to advantage itself and not the shipping public,” the chassis providers wrote. “It does not want lower rates for merchant haulage prices to the end-user; it just wants NACPC to get a bigger piece of that business than it can get by competing in the marketplace without regulatory help … [and] to replace the results of a competitive marketplace with Commission-imposed rules that would benefit IMCC and NACPC, but not the shipping public.” The chassis providers argue importers and exporters have not been involved in the complaint because they sign annual contracts with ocean carriers which can include or exclude chassis choice in the terms and conditions. The IMCC is due to respond to Wirth’s ruling in April and then FMC commissioners will decide whether to uphold or overturn the ruling. title: Proactive approach to ISPM 15 progressing despite roadblocks
content: Since being discovered in North America in 2002, the emerald ash borer (pictured) has killed tens of millions of ash trees in the US and Canada. Photo credit: USDA APHIS. Breakbulk shippers and logistics providers say they have made significant headway in designing a multi-pronged approach to preventing the infestation of dangerous insects in packing materials used in breakbulk transport, thanks to monthly meetings between stakeholders and enforcement officials. Violations of the International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15 (ISPM 15), triggered by the discovery of certain species of invasive, wood-boring pests in wood packaging material (WPM), can result in hefty fines and, in some cases, the immediate re-exportation of an entire shipment, which can be more costly. Breakbulk importers in the United States have reported an uptick in pest discoveries in recent years, even in WPM that those shippers and their logistics providers believed to be ISPM 15-compliant. The WPM-Dunnage Coalition, a Houston-based group of project and breakbulk logistics executives formed with the goal of reducing inadvertent ISPM 15 violations, is looking to move forward with plans that include new training and procedures to prevent infestation of WPM at their overseas sources and new mitigation processes for infested WPM discovered after entering a US port. Those plans are currently awaiting approval from the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (USDA APHIS), which oversees ISPM 15 enforcement. “We’ve made an extreme amount of progress over the last year, and quite a bit compared to the past three or four years,” Diana Davila, project director at forwarder UTC Overseas and a founding member of the WPM-Dunnage Coalition, told the Journal of Commerce in early March. Robert Hawn, vice president of maritime affairs for the West Gulf Maritime Association (WGMA), which represents carriers and terminal operators, said an ongoing source of frustration for breakbulk importers and logistics providers has been the discovery of invasive pests in WPM that seems to have been properly treated, inspected, and stamped prior to loading onto a vessel. “It appears the problem is not so much noncompliance by the carriers, but [that] the options available to us to treat the dunnage are either not being successfully done, or the treatment is not sufficient — meaning it doesn’t work,” Hawn said. In response, the WPM-Dunnage Coalition has created a training program for overseas WPM inspectors modeled after the inspection practices of the US Customs and Border Patrol (CBP), which enforces ISPM 15 regulations on behalf of USDA APHIS. The coalition hopes to introduce the program sometime in 2023. The Partnership for Environmental Security of Trade (PEST) program would be housed and managed within the WGMA, which would act as a neutral party to coordinate training and maintain certification records. “I think we will have a training session this year, I’m hoping in the second quarter; it’s just getting all the details aligned,” Davila said. “It’s a very long process to get approval.” Jon Daniels, national policy manager at USDA APHIS, said APHIS is also producing a series of educational videos on inspection processes and other information relevant to ISPM 15 regulations. “While the program has been very successful, APHIS continues to work with our trade partners to identify gaps and priorities in our plant health safeguarding work,” he said. That progress comes despite a few setbacks, including the unexpected death of a key scientist who served as a liaison between industry and environmental protection interests. At present, the only way to prevent the re-exportation of a shipment found to contain invasive pests is to incinerate the packing material, but this option is only available for dunnage — not other types of WPM — and only at a small handful of locations. Scott Johnston, an attorney at customs and international trade law firm Givens & Johnston, explained that enforcement agencies are typically reluctant to allow importers to separate cargo from the non-compliant WPM in which it is packaged. Instead, both the WPM and the cargo generally sits on the dock in quarantine until it can be re-exported to a port where the offending WPM can be destroyed and the cargo re-packaged and returned to the US, a costly and time-consuming process, particularly when it requires the importer to charter a new vessel. “Legally, nothing much has changed for the importers; they still have the same obligations,” Johnston said. “If they bring in merchandise that has associated WPM, and Customs finds indications of a live infestation” of the wood-boring pests, re-exporting is generally the only option. Daniels said the agency has been working to develop other options for mitigating non-compliant dunnage, wood used to brace breakbulk cargoes in ship holds, in addition to incineration and/or re-exportation. “For example, one promising alternative is mechanical destruction via wood-chipping and hammermilling,” Daniels told the Journal of Commerce. “We remain open to other novel treatment ideas.” But Johnston said even if chipping becomes an option, ports would then have to decide whether it’s worth their while to purchase specialized wood-chipping equipment, which could cost upwards of $500,000. “Who’s going to invest in the solution? And how are they going to charge for it?” Johnston said. Peter Svensson, senior vice president with bulk and breakbulk carrier Clipper Americas, also a founding member of the WPM-Dunnage Coalition, said APHIS specifications might dictate that the wood be pulverized down to a certain size and that the process take place in closed chambers to prevent pests from escaping, Svensson said. The equipment would also need to be mobile enough to be moved directly to a given port berth or cargo quarantine area. “You can’t just go down to Home Depot and buy a wood-chipper,” he said. “It would have to fulfill certain government requirements.” Efforts to mitigate ISPM 15 violations in the US suffered an unexpected setback in December, when Gary Lovett, a forest ecologist and senior scientist emeritus with the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies, passed away in a skiing accident. Prior to his death, Lovett had become a primary liaison between the WPM-Dunnage Coalition and government officials. Those who worked with Lovett described him as a “translator,” communicating the concerns of importers and carriers to the government. “He was the glue that put it all together,” Svensson said. Josh Ginsberg, president of the Cary Institute, told the Journal of Commerce the institute remains committed to the work Lovett started with ISPM 15 initiative. “What Gary was able to do was bring the lens of good science to people who wanted to do the right thing,” he said. The Cary Institute in July delivered a petition with over 1,700 signatures to the US House and Senate Agriculture Committees requesting a Congressional hearing on invasive forest pests. The petition was an initiative of Tree-SMART Trade, a trade advisory committee Lovett had been leading. The current status of the petition is unclear. Lovett had been working with lawmakers to address importers’ often severely limited access to data and information related to ISPM 15 violations. To file a claim with their insurance carriers or pursue legal action, parties affected by a violation must collect information such as the WPM vendor, the port where the WPM was stamped, and other details. However, importers typically must file a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request to obtain that information, a process that can take months. For example, an engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) firm that asked not to be identified said the re-exportation of about 650 freight tons of breakbulk cargo after pests were discovered in the shipment’s WPM put the company three-and-a-half months behind on a project for a multi-billion-dollar client and ended up costing the EPC more than the client had paid it to procure and transport the cargo. Even though the EPC had already paid 80 percent of the cost of the materials, it did not own the goods outright, which meant CBP couldn’t release information on the violation to them. Daniels explained that certain information included in an emergency action notification (EAN) is confidential because of privacy laws governing personal data, which is why submitting a FOIA request is necessary, adding that APHIS plans to release approved data on non-compliant WPM before the end of the US federal fiscal year in September 2023. In the meantime, importers and carriers are doing what they can to lessen the cost of re-exportation. Johnston, for example, has been advising clients to send non-compliant shipments to Mexico for remediation, which generally takes two to three weeks, as opposed to months if cargo is returned to an overseas origin. “This is probably the number one method for dealing with [re-exportation] when time is a factor,” he said. Others are making up-front investments to stay ahead of the issue. Svensson said Clipper Americas has invested over $1 million in artificial dunnage to avoid violations. In addition, the carrier purchases high-quality wood and pays for extra heating to treat WPM. Svensson said that can cost $35,000 to $50,000 per shipment, but that’s a fraction of the $100,000 to $150,000 it would cost to incinerate the WPM. And it’s nowhere near the $250,000 to $1 million it can cost to re-export cargo. “The more you can do to prevent it, the better off you are,” Svensson said. “But it does come at a cost.” Contact Autumn Cafiero Giusti at autumn@autumngiusti.com. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Maersk going it alone, so far, on policy changes to free time billing
content: The US Federal Maritime Commission has until mid-June to issue final rulemaking around changes to how carriers and terminals assess detention and demurrage on US shipments. Photo credit: ricochet64 / Shutterstock.com. A looming change in how Maersk assesses demurrage and detention fees on US import and export shipments has not yet been matched by other container lines. Maersk earlier this month announced that, beginning April 1, it will stop assessing excess free time fees when customers are not able to pick up or return containers due to those locations being closed. That’s a major shift in free time billing policy, but one that dovetails with the direction of the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC), which is due to issue new rules about detention and demurrage assessment by June 15, a process mandated by the passage of the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22) last June. Mediterranean Shipping Co. and CMA CGM declined to comment to the Journal of Commerce on whether they would take similar steps, while a Hapag-Lloyd spokesperson said, “we have not fully decided this yet, however we should have a viewpoint in a few weeks as we are still evaluating.” The changes to Maersk’s billing practices, which include billing consignees and not drayage providers for detention charges, are part of an effort to get ahead of the new FMC rulemaking process, a Maersk spokesperson told the Journal of Commerce March 8. “Maersk will assess import demurrage, import detention, and export detention charges with respect to US shipments only on days when the pickup or return location for equipment is open for the pickup or return of equipment and cargo,” the container line said in its March 3 customer advisory. “These updates will streamline and simplify our approach to demurrage and detention and provide greater transparency to customers.” Maersk added that “for the purposes of calculating free time, we will consider Monday through Saturday as working days provided the pickup or return location is open." Detention refers to when an empty import or loaded export container is returned to a terminal after contractual free time expires, and demurrage is a storage fee assessed when a loaded import container dwells on a terminal or other storage facility beyond its contracted free time. Container lines have historically charged their customers those fees even on days when a terminal or container storage facility is closed, such as on a weekend. In the case of demurrage fees, container lines generally collect the fees from importers or importers’ logistics partners before passing those fees through to terminals or other storage locations. The demurrage situation is particularly fraught, as importers can’t get their cargo released until fees have been paid, leading to a process where importers then need to claw back those fees if they feel they have been assessed in error. Efforts to alleviate the detention and demurrage burden off importers, exporters, and their landside logistics partners are not, however, straightforward. Port of Houston Authority Executive Director Roger Guenther on Tuesday cautioned that regulators have to be careful about preventing ports and terminals from assessing demurrage over weekends or other times when gates are not open. If a shipper doesn’t have to pay demurrage over the weekend when a terminal is closed, “you’re basically guaranteeing they won’t pick up their containers on Friday and will wait until Monday,” Guenther said at the S&P Global World Petrochemical Conference in Houston. Houston, which experienced a massive spike in import container volumes in 2021 and 2022 during the peak of pandemic-driven supply chain congestion, also saw corresponding container dwell times more than double. title: A lunch break dispute at Los Angeles, Long Beach ports shows the risks of long contract talks
content: A worker and employer dispute over lunch breaks has once again raised fears of port disruption, despite being limited to a chapter of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union. ILWU Local 13 workers at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach are taking lunch break all at once, thereby limiting terminals’ ability to operate continuously, the Pacific Maritime Association said in a statement. The group, which represents shipping lines and terminals that employ longshore labor, is one of the parties in the ongoing West Coast port labor contract talks that has shippers on edge since May 2022. Its counterpart in the coast-wide negotiations, the ILWU, said in a statement workers remain compliant with their contract. Disputes over issues like lunch breaks can be led by local chapters, rather than the greater union, and therefore have little bearing on overall negotiations. Often, as was the case at the Port of Oakland in November, local chapter actions may even disrupt operations without the effects spreading to other ports. While actions from ILWU Local 13, so far, have yet to have a broader impact, the lunch hour issue highlights how the lack of a longshore contract has left the door open for small disputes to raise national attention, alter shipper behavior, and escalate into targeted disruptions. On the surface, last week’s issue at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach appears limited to lunch schedules. In a statement, the PMA said that as of Wednesday, March 15, longshore workers at the two ports stopped accepting “staggered shifts” that would allow terminals to continue operating through lunch hours, instead taking their lunch break between 12 and 1 p.m. on the first shift, and 10 p.m. and 11 p.m. on the second shift. But the issue is deeper than that, as PMA noted longshore workers’ decisions on shifts also affects broader port operations, and may be a breach of contract. “The West Coast longshore contract provides employers the right to assign staggered shifts during meal periods to ensure labor is available at all times to deliver and receive containers. Beginning last week, ILWU Local 13 has stopped complying with that contract provision,” the statement reads. Willie Adams, ILWU’s International President, responded directly to those claims in his own statement, saying: “The ILWU-PMA contract allows dockworkers to take a lunch break just like everyone else. Longshore workers in Los Angeles and Long Beach are working every day according to the terms agreed upon with the PMA.” In its email to Supply Chain Dive, the PMA also shared three pictures of truck back ups at two terminals — Los Angeles’ Fenix Marine Services and Long Beach’s ITS Terminal — saying the long lines were caused by the longshore lunch break actions. The ILWU cast a shadow on those claims, noting “trucks line up outside the terminal gates year-round for various reasons, but the employer highlights these lines during negotiations in an effort to influence public opinion.” A Supply Chain Dive analysis of Port Optimizer data, which tracks truck turn times at Los Angeles and Long Beach terminals, found average monthly truck turn times at Fenix Marine Terminals did not fluctuate much, whereas the figure has inched up slightly for ITS Terminals since the lunch hour actions began March 15. But Adams’ statement also put the responsibility for inefficiency back on terminal operators, saying they “open and close their gates at will, and limit their hours of operations when they are supposed to be open around the clock – 24/7.” The lunch hour dispute could potentially be resolved if the two parties had a contract, according to PMA. “Because the contract is not in place, there is no option for PMA to arbitrate the matter and require the union to man the terminals continuously without interruption,” the statement reads. Longshore workers and their employers had been working for years on the conditions set by a master contract that was put in place in 2014. When that contract expired without an extension in July 2022, so did the ability to resolve some disputes. The lack of arbitration has been cited as an issue behind other disruptions in the past. When Oakland’s longshore clerks walked out of the job over wage claims last November, ILWU Local 34 President Sean Farley told SFGate the action had nothing to do with the negotiations for a master contract. But absent a master contract they also could not take employers to arbitration. “It doesn’t seem to get any better unless we directly confront the employers,” Farley told SFGate at the time. It’s part of the reason why shippers, mindful of any logistics disruption, are diverting cargo away from West Coast ports. Without a contract, the threat of labor action looms large on the 29 ports covered by the ILWU-PMA talks. “Many cargo owners want to see a labor deal before they bring more volume back here. So if we get a contract soon those importers will take notice,” Gene Seroka, executive director at the Port of Los Angeles, said in a media briefing Friday. Negotiations to update the master contract, which started May 2022, are still ongoing both coast-wide and at the local chapter level. In February, the two sides issued a joint statement saying they hope a deal will come soon. Editor’s note:

title: US House duo pledge OSRA fixes to boost FMC power
content: FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei said his biggest focus is on implementing rules that have already been passed through 2022’s ocean shipping reform. Photo credit: Teri Errico Griffis / Journal of Commerce. Two members of the US House of Representatives have called out the Federal Maritime Commission’s (FMC's) lack of authority to carry out its own orders, confirming plans to introduce legislation next week to amend shipping reform passed in June. At a Congressional hearing Thursday, Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., pointed out that the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22) passed last year left out key elements, namely that the FMC lacks the authority to enforce the orders that its law judges are working on. FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei, a witness at Thursday’s hearing, confirmed he would be in favor of updating OSRA-22 to give the agency more autonomy and authority when it comes to enforcement. Co-sponsor Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-SD, said the legislation seeking changes to OSRA-22 would be introduced in the House next week. In leading the House’s effort to reform shipping law last year, Johnson and Garamendi sought even tougher regulation than was ultimately passed and signed into law by President Joe Biden. “Your agency seems to be the only independent agency in the entire federal government that does not have the authority to implement its decisions about unfair practices,” Garamendi said, noting that when the FMC determines a company is acting unlawfully, the agency must then go to court to get a federal injunction. FMC Commissioners Max Vekich and Carl Bentzel in December proposed to House members that Congress increase the agency’s power so that it can legally block vessel sharing agreements between ocean carriers if they find them to be anti-competitive, rather than having to seek an injunction via a federal court. Maffei said he supports his fellow commissioners’ proposal. In his formal request to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee hearing for more funding to boost enforcement Thursday, Maffei said the agency was pushing on with new rulemaking required by OSRA-22 The FMC is working on final rules covering detention and demurrage billing with a deadline of June 15, but Maffei said the rulemaking around when it is reasonable for ocean carriers to refuse vessel bookings has gone “a little slower” than he wanted. “The issue here is we’re trying to maximize the benefits for US exporters while minimizing any unintended consequences that might harm them,” Maffei said. “I would say that is the trickiest rulemaking we have done, but I think we’re making very good progress.” The Agriculture Transportation Coalition in a letter to the House on Wednesday urged the committee to increase the agency’s budget, arguing “the continuing massive public responses from US agriculture, manufacturers, retailers, truckers, freight forwarders” shows new rules and stronger enforcement is needed. title: FMC querying carriers, terminals on free time billing practices
content: A trio of major container lines contacted by the Journal of Commerce either declined to comment or said a decision had yet to be made on whether they would amend their detention and demurrage billing practices. Photo credit: Joseph Creamer / Shutterstock.com. The US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) on Thursday said it is asking terminal operators and the 11 largest container lines calling the US to confirm whether they are charging shippers demurrage and detention fees when port facilities are closed. The request is a signal that the FMC’s ongoing rulemaking around detention and demurrage billing is likely to mandate that parties billing for D&D refrain from doing so when a terminal or storage facility where containers are picked up or dropped off is inaccessible to shippers or their landside service representatives. Thursday’s announcement cites a December 2022 decision by the FMC requiring Evergreen Marine to refund $510 to a trucking company for detention fees the trucking company was charged on a container when the Port of Savannah was closed over Memorial Day weekend in 2020. The Evergreen case was a precedent for “unjust and unreasonable” fees, the commission said. The queries to shipping lines and terminals are being conducted via the FMC’s Vessel-Operating Common Carrier Audit Program. FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei said during a Congressional budget hearing Thursday that beginning in the first quarter of 2022, billed and collected detention and demurrage began declining, and in the second quarter 2022, the rate of waived charges began to rise. "We believe that data will continue to show reductions in billed and collected charges," Maffei said in prepared remarks at the hearing. "Nonetheless, continued progress must be made in changing what I believe has become a practice of using demurrage and detention as a revenue center as opposed to strictly an incentive to pick up cargo and return equipment." Earlier this month, Maersk announced it would refrain from assessing excess free time fees when customers are not able to pick up or return containers due to those locations being closed. A trio of other major container lines contacted by the Journal of Commerce either declined to comment or said a decision had yet to be made on whether they would amend their billing practices. Detention refers to when an empty import or loaded export container is returned to a terminal after contractual free time expires, and demurrage is a storage fee assessed when a loaded import container dwells on a terminal or other storage facility beyond its contracted free time. The FMC’s notice Thursday said a May 2020 rule on detention and demurrage practices gives the commission the authority to determine if fees have been charged in an unjust and unreasonable manner, or if they are “serving their intended primary purposes as financial incentives to promote freight fluidity.” The commission has until mid-June to issue new detention and demurrage rulemaking, a requirement that was part of the passage of the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 (OSRA-22) last June. title: German strikes over pay dispute cripple transportation network
content: Members of the German transport union EVG walked out Monday in a pay dispute that has effectively shut down the country’s rail network. Photo credit: EVG. Strike action by unions representing transport workers in Germany brought the country to a standstill Monday, with rail operator Deutsche Bahn canceling all trains and Frankfurt and Munich airports stopping all scheduled flights. Rail and transport union EVG and trade and transport union Verdi are staging a 24-hour walkout of members over a pay dispute, affecting a wide range of industry sectors and logistics operations, including airport security and ground handling. “This will affect all German rail operations, as employees from all areas of Deutsche Bahn and other rail companies have been called on to walk out,” DB said in a weekend statement. “The long-distance traffic of Deutsche Bahn is therefore completely discontinued.” Flights are being grounded at some of Germany’s busiest airports. “On, Sunday, March 26 and Monday, March 27, there will be no regular passenger traffic at Munich Airport due to all-day strikes,” the airport said in a customer advisory. Frankfurt Airport said in its own statement that “airport operations will be heavily disrupted ... there will be no regular passenger flights” during the strike action. While the strike is only for one day and confined to Germany, the knock-on effects are being felt outside the country’s borders as incoming trains are being delayed or canceled. “The transport of our trains in the direction to and from Germany, and trains transiting through Germany, will be limited and there will be significant delays at the beginning of the week,” Metrans, a subsidiary of container terminal operator HHLA, noted in an advisory ahead of the Monday rail strike. “We expect that the strike will significantly paralyze the entire transport infrastructure.” Austria-based Rail Cargo Group said 50 of its trains to and from Germany were canceled, and all main lines and corridors were affected by the strike action. Maersk warned customers to expect delays for shipments moving by rail and through inland terminals from the beginning of this week. “Maersk planners are working closely with our service providers to understand the overall impact on our inland operations and pre-load containers on rail and direct truck transports where possible,” the carrier noted in a Monday advisory. EVG represents 230,000 workers at Deutsche Bahn rail and bus companies and is demanding a 12 percent pay increase. The United Services Union, known as Verdi, expects 120,000 workers at most of Germany’s airports, as well as transport and port workers, to be in the walkout and is demanding a 10.5 percent pay increase. The German inflation rate is currently at 8.7 percent. Kristian Loroch, collective bargaining board member at EVG, said bringing the country’s transport network to a standstill was a clear message of the importance of maintaining a functioning bus and rail network. “If it is not possible to make bus and train jobs financially attractive again, [a] standstill will not become the exception but the rule,” Loroch warned. The rail and airport strike comes just a week after a strike by Verdi workers effectively closed the vital Elbe River access to Europe’s third-largest container port at Hamburg.
