title: US shipping interests want FMC to regulate rail storage fees
content: Over the last few years, rail demurrage charges “have resulted in costs to US businesses in the hundreds of millions of dollars,” a group representing shipping interests told House leadership. Photo credit: Norfolk Southern. Rail storage fees assessed against ocean containers moving on so-called “through bills of lading” should be overseen by the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) to close a regulatory gap that is ripe for “abuse,” a group of more than 70 shippers, forwarders and transportation interests have told leadership of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. In a letter dated May 2, the group called on the committee to push legislation that would make rail storage charges assessed as part of through bills of lading invoiced to importers by ocean carriers, rather than railroads. That would then give the FMC oversight of such charges, given the agency’s regulatory authority over container shipping. “While we do not suggest that railroads themselves would or should be regulated by the FMC, the railroads’ storage charges under through bills of lading should more appropriately be invoiced through the ocean carriers,” the letter read. “Rail storage charges assessed against containers moving in international commerce, an as-yet unaddressed abuse of demurrage charges, should clearly and formally fall within FMC authority through an act of Congress.” A “through” bill of lading involves an ocean carrier contracting for rail service to ensure a container is delivered from origin to an inland destination in the US. Currently, there is no regulatory agency with direct authority to oversee application of rail storage fees under ocean carriers’ through bills of lading and to determine whether those charges are assessed properly. Over the last few years, rail demurrage charges “have resulted in costs to US businesses in the hundreds of millions of dollars,” the group wrote. Those charges must be paid directly to the railroads — who shippers have no contractual relationship with — to release their cargo, the group said. Furthermore, they argue that rail storage fees do not serve the incentive principle to keep cargo moving fluidly and that allowing railroads to invoice those charges to shippers violates US shipping law. Neither the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 nor the proposed Ocean Shipping Reform Implementation Act directly address rail storage, a muddy middle ground in the US supply chain. “We ... ask Congress to clarify that rail storage charges assessed under ocean bills of lading for through transportation should be billed through the contracting ocean carrier and subject to the OSRA-22 demurrage and detention invoicing requirements,” the group said. The Surface Transportation Board (STB) has exempted intermodal transportation from its jurisdiction and the FMC’s authority remains unclear despite individual commissioners saying the agency has jurisdiction over inland charges on through bills of lading. “[New legislation] would more clearly establish that rail storage charges assessed as part of through international ocean transportation are under the operational authority of the FMC and that any unreasonable charges would be governed by the requirements of OSRA22,” the group said. This isn’t the first group to push for resolution on who should regulate rail storage. In March, the National Shipping Advisory Committee urged the FMC to step in and regulate “abuse” of the storage fee system, asking that rail operators invoice ocean carriers directly for storage. title: Bed Bath & Beyond owes over $95M to these 14 vendors in its supply chain
content: When Bed Bath & Beyond filed for bankruptcy late last month, the retailer lacked the means to keep its shelves stocked while making its loan payments. That liquidity crisis followed months of supply chain struggles ultimately tied to — and exacerbating — its spiraling sales and profits. Now the company is in Chapter 11 and trying to conduct an orderly process of winding down its physical retail business, selling assets and repaying its creditors. The group of companies Bed Bath & Beyond owes money to includes many in its supply chain, who might never be made whole for what the retailer owes them. Some, such as Ryder, have already disclosed publicly that Bed Bath & Beyond’s bankruptcy have affected their own business. The retailer’s largest unsecured creditors include merchandise suppliers as well as vendors for parcel delivery, trucking and other services from across the supply chain, according to court documents. title: FMC post-OSRA complaint process secures $1 million in relief for shipping interests
content: The FMC is expected to publish a final rulemaking on detention and demurrage billing by mid-June. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. US shipping interests who sought relief from the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) over disputed fees have won back just over $1 million since new shipping reform became law last June. Since June 16 when the Ocean Shipping Regulation Act of 2022 (OSRA-22) was signed into law, a total of $1,045,953 has been refunded through the FMC’s interim charge complaint process to shippers, consignees, truckers and third parties who sought the agency’s help to contest charges levied by ocean carriers. “The charge complaint process continues to drive informal settlements and waivers of mainly detention and demurrage billings,” FMC Managing Director Lucille Marvin said at the agency’s bi-monthly meeting Wednesday. As of May 1, 287 charge complaints involving more than $5 billion in disputed fees have been brought to the FMC, Commissioner Carl Bentzel said at the meeting. Of those complaints, 115 met the requirements to launch an investigation; 33 investigations were resolved by the FMC and 60 were voluntarily resolved between the two parties. The remainder are in progress. Marvin said the FMC’s Bureau of Enforcement, Investigations and Compliance will continue to pursue cases against major carriers with a focus on detention and demurrage. OSRA-22 not only gave maritime regulators greater oversight into monitoring ocean carriers’ adherence to the Shipping Act of 1984, but also provided shippers with the so-called charge complaint process — a way to dispute violations of the law without having to go through formal processes of paying filing fees or hiring an attorney. The FMC is expected to publish a final rulemaking on detention and demurrage billing by mid-June. As of March, the agency was still collecting data, including asking terminal operators and container lines if they were charging fees when port facilities were closed. A permanent process for submitting charge complaints is also in the works, with Marvin saying it will be completed through a formal notice of proposed rulemaking and public comment. title: Ex-Slync CEO indicted over alleged misappropriation of company cash
content: Chris Kirchner, who co-founded logistics software provider Slync in 2017, was suspended as CEO last July before being fired in August. Photo credit: Tada Images / Shutterstock.com. Chris Kirchner, the former CEO of logistics software provider Slync, has been indicted over allegedly defrauding the company’s investors of more than $25 million. A federal grand jury indicted him Tuesday on five counts of wire fraud and eight counts of money laundering, the US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas said in a statement Wednesday. The indictment stems from a Feb. 14 criminal complaint alleging that Kirchner, 35, funneled money intended for Slync into his personal accounts. The indictment also alleges Kirchner, who co-founded Slync in 2017, attempted to cover up those activities and fired employees who raised questions about them. “Between April 2020 and March 2022, Mr. Kirchner allegedly initiated nearly 100 wire transfers moving money from Slync’s Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) account into the company’s account at JPMorgan Chase Bank – an account only he had access to,” the Department of Justice (DOJ) said. “He then allegedly wired much of the money from the Chase account to his personal bank accounts.” The DOJ also alleged that Kirchner wired $20 million directly from Slync’s SVB account into his personal checking account. The government says Kirchner used the funds to “fund a splashy lifestyle,” including the purchase of a private jet for $16 million. When Slync failed to pay employees over a number of weeks in the spring of 2022, the US Attorney’s Office says Kirchner attributed the company’s lack of funds to false reasons. “He first claimed that the company’s cash was invested in illiquid assets that were difficult to divest,” DOJ said. “Later, (Kirchner) said that the US government had frozen the company’s accounts because he had transacted in his personal capacity with sanctioned entities in Russia. Neither explanation was true.” DOJ also alleges Kirchner fired two Slync employees in June 2022 who expressed concern to investors about his management of the company’s finances. A month later, he allegedly “removed certain IT administrator privileges from key Slync employees, preventing the employees from accessing Slync’s computer systems,” DOJ said. “He then allegedly attempted to delete approximately 18 gigabytes of Slync data, including emails.” Slync’s board of directors fired Kirchner last August and replaced him in October with logistics technology veteran John Urban. Slync’s investors recapitalized the company in February, backing the company’s technology and Urban’s ability to move Slync past the Kirchner legal saga. If convicted, Kirchner faces up to 20 years in federal prison for each count of wire fraud and up to 10 years in prison for each count of money laundering. Kirchner also faces a separate SEC complaint on charges brought on the same day in February he was arrested and charged by the DOJ. title: US warehouse vacancy rose in first quarter as demand waned
content: Builders are slowing down on new projects, potentially leading to a more balanced warehouse market in 2024. Photo credit: Roman Vyshnikov / Shutterstock.com. While still below long-term averages, industrial real estate vacancy in the US has crept up to the highest level in 14 years as more warehouses face less demand for distribution space. Builders are responding to the downturn with fewer new projects, so rents have yet to fall. Commercial real estate services firm CBRE’s first-quarter industrial real estate report showed nationwide vacancy reached 3.5%, up 50 basis points from the fourth quarter of 2022. That is the highest vacancy rate since the second quarter of 2009, CBRE said Wednesday, but remains below the 10-year average of 5%. The vacancy rate ticked up as 89 million square feet of warehouse space became available in the first quarter, which CBRE said was the highest quarter-on-quarter increase on record. Newly built warehouses are also adding to the vacancy rate. CBRE said new construction completions totaled 144.1 million square feet, the second-highest amount on record. But lessees only occupied 43% of the new supply, down from a 73% occupancy rate for quarterly completions in 2022. While the amount of both new and existing warehouse space leased remains positive over the last 13 years, the 54.2 million square feet of net absorption during the first quarter was the lowest since the second quarter of 2020 and below the 10-year average of 87.6 million-square feet. With the new warehouse openings in the first quarter, total US industrial space increased 2% from a year ago to 18.3 billion square feet, CBRE said, adding that as “the urgency to increase inventories has waned,” warehouse demand will be uneven through 2023. “A large amount of new construction scheduled for delivery this year will cause some spikes in vacancies across the US but should be fully absorbed by late 2024,” CBRE said. Regional markets, especially near ports, have also been seeing a slowdown as the import surge of the past two years has waned and shippers reevaluate their warehousing needs. The New Jersey warehouse market saw its vacancy rate tick up to 3.3% in the first quarter, its highest since the second quarter of 2022. Even with the weaker demand in the first quarter, other indicators of warehouse supply and demand remain healthy. Average rents rose 3% quarter over quarter and 11% year over year to $9.91 per square feet, a record level. In response to higher interest rates and greater supply, builders appear to be pulling back on new warehouses. CBRE said projects under construction declined for the first time in more than four years to 620 million square feet, down 7% from the fourth quarter, which should bolster the market in 2024. “Q1 was the second consecutive quarter with a noticeable decline in construction starts, which should lead to a sizeable drop in deliveries in [the second half of] 2024,” CBRE said. title: Target has tracked down nearly all of its palm oil supply
content: Target traced 96% of its palm oil supply down to the mill level in 2022 and is working to trace the remaining volumes, according to a recently updated company webpage about its supply chain transparency. That level of traceability is up from 76% in 2021 for Target’s owned brands, which the company reported in its latest ESG report from July. At the time, the retailer had set a goal to track its entire palm oil supply by the end of the year. To track palm oil origins, the company is working with the nonprofit Earthworm Foundation, which works to improve sustainable sourcing around numerous commodities including cocoa, cotton, wood and several others. Palm oil is widely used in consumer products, including food and cosmetics. Concerns about deforestation and human rights have cast a shadow over the commodity and its use for years. Indonesia and Malaysia — countries rich in biodiversity — produce over 85% of the global supply, according to the Yale Center for Business and the Environment. Target sourced 7,542 metric tons of palm oil in 2021, up from 7,095 the year before. The company has worked to increase use of palm oil certified by the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, which aims to encourage more sustainable production practices and markets. Target’s procurement of RSPO-certified palm oil increased by 37% between 2019 and 2021. By the end of 2021, use of RSPO-certified palm oil spanned 3,000 products in Target’s owned brands. Along with palm oil, Target said it is accelerating its traceability initiatives in other commodities as well. It has of late focused on cotton, because of the material’s prevalence in its product assortment as well as regulatory requirements around the fiber. The retailer has said it aims for full visibility in its cotton supply but has not laid out a timeline yet.

title: Evergreen pushed contracted cargo to spot market: FMC shipper complaint
content: In addition to seeking undisclosed monetary relief, importer CertiFit is asking the FMC to ensure Evergreen cannot refuse its contracted cargo in the future. Photo credit: Sheila Fitzgerald / Shutterstock.com. A Utah-based auto parts importer says Evergreen Marine failed to provide contracted vessel space and then forced the shipper to pay higher spot market rates to get its cargo on the carrier’s vessels, according to a new complaint filed with the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC). Sometimes, that involved the shipper paying spot rates for space on the very same ship it had contracted. CertiFit Inc. inked a one-year contract with Evergreen in April 2020 for a minimum quantity commitment (MQC) of 1,000 TEU, but the carrier only provided 353 TEU, the shipper alleged in the complaint, filed Thursday. CertiFit says it was forced to pay $750,000 in spot market rates for vessel space, some of which was provided on Evergreen and OOCL vessels; both are members of the Ocean Alliance. In addition to seeking undisclosed monetary relief, CertiFit is asking the FMC to ensure Evergreen cannot refuse its contracted cargo in the future. “Respondent’s conduct suggests a deliberate practice of entering into service contracts based on quoted rates while expecting not to fulfill the service commitments in those contracts at the contracted rate, but instead, failing to provide carriage of complainant's cargo in favor of shippers willing to pay higher prices,” CertiFit wrote in its complaint. Taiwan-based Evergreen did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Evergreen Marine last December was ordered by the FMC to refund more than $500 to a trucking company for detention fees it was charged on a container over Memorial Day weekend in 2020 when the Port of Savannah was closed. Under the Ocean Shipping Act of 2022 (OSRA-22), the FMC is mandated to provide rulemaking that would define what is considered unreasonable refusal by an ocean carrier take on a shipper’s cargo. That rulemaking is still in progress. In the meantime, complaints from shippers continue to be filed with the FMC. On April 27, bankrupt Bed Bath & Beyond accused OOCL of falling short of space commitments and is seeking $31.7 million in damages. Yang Ming, HMM and Maersk also have had cases brought against them within the last year for alleged unreasonable denial of space. title: China to remain top for logistics investment despite regional sourcing shift
content: A planned Maersk logistics center in China would be built in a free trade zone in Shanghai’s Pudong district close to the bridge linking Shanghai with the Yangshan deepwater port (pictured). Photo credit: Weiming Xie / Shutterstock.com. China will remain the top destination for growing investment in new logistics-related facilities in Asia even as some leading manufacturers seek to shift production to other countries in Asia, real estate investment officials say. That comes as logistics and industrial investment in the region was estimated at about $50 billion last year, down from a record $72 billion in 2021, but still the second-highest level recorded. “Current estimates of full-year investment in Asia-Pacific last year stand at $45 billion, though this is likely to be revised upwards,” said Dominic Brown, an analyst focusing on the Asian market for real estate services company Cushman & Wakefield. “[Last year] still looks like it will exceed the total volume recorded in 2020, and so sit second to the 2021 peak.” China accounted for between 25 to 33% of that total. By comparison, investment in logistics and industrial premises in the US topped $142 billion last year, down 17% from 2021, according to real estate company CBRE. Brown said Cushman & Wakefield’s recent China investor intentions survey showed 65% of respondents indicated interest in logistics assets in “Tier 1” cities and 40% in major “Tier 2” cities. “Given the survey was done in Q4 2022 prior to China’s reopening announcement, we expect investors interest in the logistics sector will be further strengthened this year,” he said. Tier 1 cities include Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Chongqing, Hangzhou, Dalian and Ningbo, while Tier 2 cities include Xiamen, Kunming, Guiyang and Nanchang. The Singapore government’s sovereign wealth fund has led the total investment volume in logistics and industrial facilities in Asia, according to Dennis Yeo, Cushman & Wakefield’s head of investor services, logistics and industrial, for Asia-Pacific Corporate investors plus owner-occupiers such as Maersk, Cainiao and SF Logistics have also become more active in the logistics and industrial sector as they target both growth and defensive opportunities. Maersk said in January it would build its first green and smart logistics center in China that would start operation by September 2024. The $174 million, 1.6 million-square-foot complex will be built in the Lingang free trade zone in Shanghai’s Pudong district close to the bridge linking Shanghai with the Yangshan deepwater port. John Geng, Maersk’s head of contract logistics in Greater China, said the facility will be in a good location to serve China’s domestic market with import cargoes handled through the Yangshan terminals. “It also operates as a regional or global fulfilment center through export cargo, while providing the possibilities for customers to hold inventory in the complex as part of domestic, regional or global fulfilment solutions,” he said. Geng added the complex will serve as a regional and global hub targeted at customers in the retail lifestyle, tech, auto and fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sectors, providing them with ocean and air connectivity. title: Renewed focus on purchase order management leads to tech vs. service dilemma
content: Some experts believe upstream visibility into purchase orders and supplier management will one day resemble what’s been built on the final-mile side. Photo credit: Rawpixel.com / Shutterstock.com. Pandemic-induced demand for containerized goods in 2021 and early 2022 brought back in vogue a software category — purchase order (PO) management — that had long been considered by shippers to be important, although somewhat dusty amid shinier new objects on the market. PO management is not a new concept, having first emerged in the 1990s. But extended lead times on products sourced abroad during the pandemic reinvigorated the idea that importers needed to better manage the connection between an order to an overseas supplier and the logistics legs once products had been produced. “Cargo owners needed to be more particular about which containers they need,” said Grant Sernick, director of sales at Toronto-based logistics management software vendor 3rdwave. “It isn't sufficient to assume that goods were flowing and would arrive in time. They need to be prescriptive. But most companies do not have visibility into what product is in which container. For the most part, once a PO is issued, visibility is lost until it is received at a warehouse or distribution center.” Sernick said PO management systems solve this issue, but that PO management is a “poorly defined product set and varies wildly between software vendors.” He suggested shippers that recognize supply and demand shocks are likely to more frequently “require a new class of software that understands the entire inbound supply chain, organized around product or SKU,” and not containers. Graham Parker, CEO of Singapore-based logistics technology provider Gravity Supply Chain Solutions, said the pandemic “showed the divorce between the suppliers and the buyers when they needed 100% visibility inside, and especially at the first mile.” “They had an accurate understanding of what they had ordered but no idea where it was in the manufacturing cycle, at origin ports or en route,” Parker said. “They could see a container but were scrambling to understand what was inside these containers, not only at the order level but at the SKU, or item, style or part level. When they needed to be agile, they were anything but.” Parker said shippers lacking the visibility that PO management can enable are still paying the price in terms of margin compression. “The ever-increasing freight rates [from 2020 through the first half of 2022] meant to try and meet the demand they were paying over the odds,” he said. “Then the inevitable downturn in demand meant they had tremendous stock volumes all over the place and no idea where it was and how best to manage the flow, or whether to slow it down or cancel. The burden of managing product flows, paying suppliers and managing cash flow was greater than ever, yet the various business departments had no end-to-end collaboration. So, essentially, they were blind.” Bryn Heimbeck, CEO of Seattle-based logistics management software vendor Trade Tech, said the importance of PO management software has risen in tandem with stronger linkages between finance and supply chain. “Twenty or 30 years ago, [chief financial officers] were not as closely tied to supply chains,” he said. “The focus was on point of sale and restocking store shelves. Inventory carrying costs were not a key financial factor in the market's understanding at the time. Now, we are looking at full replenishment models, incorporated into just-in-time, and the CFO has a major focus on the supply chain and is working with supply chain executives, who themselves have a far greater breadth of responsibility.” But even as international transit times have now normalized, the scars of the pandemic have yet to wane. Beyond shippers focusing once again on PO management is a secondary dilemma: Do they use a PO management system from a third-party logistics provider (3PL), or do they use one from a software vendor? “It depends,” Rob Garrison, CEO of PO management software vendor Mercado, said at the TPMTech conference in Long Beach in late February. “There are benefits to both models.” Garrison said the pure technology approach provides neutrality in terms of which providers a shipper uses. But it can also depend on the person within the importer organization that wants to manage purchase orders. “A typical product is manufactured for three months, shipped for one month and then sold,” Garrison said. “Depending on where you’re at in the customer continuum on that journey, what’s going to be most important to you? For some, they want to optimize for logistics, and so that combination of service and technology is exactly what they’re looking for. But if I'm on the purchasing side of the organization, and that provider doesn’t have a purchasing solution, maybe it’s not the best option.” Sernick said PO management “isn't a 'throw-in' service.” “So shippers need to ask themselves how wedded they are to their 3PL,” he said. “PO management is really hard to do well. Most 3PLs don't have their own PO management software. They have bought a third-party software application and what cargo owners will find is that they cannot affect any meaningful changes with that third-party software.” Heimbeck said finance will play a determining role in whether a beneficial cargo owner (BCO) goes with a 3PL’s PO management solution. “The real question is whether a BCO has, or wants to have, the staff and logistics expertise to manage the supply chain overseas,” he said. “Decisions on setting up, controlling and expediting the origin supply chain process is still grounded in local staff. Previously, BCOs relied primarily on their 3PLs’ systems, but this is changing with the attention to information flow demanded by the CFO and others within the BCO. And this trend will probably continue.” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: NY-NJ terminals alter free time tariff as FMC rule on closed gates looms
content: APM Elizabeth is the only NY-NJ facility to recently offer Saturday gates as open weekends will soon be considered allowable free time. Photo credit: rblfmr / Shutterstock.com. Marine terminals at the Port of New York and New Jersey that open on weekends and holidays will be able to use those gate hours as part of their free time calculation for container storage under a tariff change due to take effect June 1. Under current rules, terminals do not count weekends and holidays as part of free time, whether they are open or not. The rule changes will not have much of an initial cost impact on shippers as almost all New York-New Jersey terminals are closed on weekends and holidays, thereby not counting toward free time, and containers are now moving off the port faster. But APM’s recent decision to open its Elizabeth, N.J., terminal on Saturdays has left truckers and shippers concerned about the risk of being charged more demurrage at that facility as available free time effectively ends more quickly with its open Saturday gates. A tariff issued in April by the New York Terminal Conference, which comprises five of the six New York-New Jersey marine terminals, said Saturdays, Sundays and longshore worker holidays will not be included in the five-day period allowed for free time before import demurrage kicks in “except where terminal gates are open.” The sixth terminal, Maher, issued its separate tariff last year that changed its free time policy to include in that period weekends and holidays altogether. The new changes take effect June 1. The length of free time does not change. Along with the exclusion of working weekends and holidays from free time calculations, the new tariff also increases demurrage rates for periods when containers linger past their free time. Depending on the length of that time, demurrage costs will range from $186 to $400 per day, up from a previous range of $172 to $384 per day. In addition, a new daily rate of $568 will be assessed on containers lingering 30 days or more past free time. Giovanni Antonuccio, a director at APM Terminals who sits on the NYTC, said in a statement to the Journal of Commerce that the group, which has typically raised demurrage rates along with other tariff items as part of normal general rate increases (GRI) every October, held off such increases for the last two years due to the severe constraints shippers faced in retrieving containers during the pandemic-era surge. The tariff changes come as the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) is looking into a rulemaking, expected to be completed in mid-June, that includes whether free time given to shippers for their import containers should include days when a terminal is closed or inaccessible to truckers. In anticipation of that ruling, several ocean carriers have decided to stop charging detention, demurrage and per diem on days when terminals are closed due to weekends, holidays or port closures. Marine terminal operators also face the possibility they may not be able to charge demurrage for days when a terminal is closed, yet still need a financial incentive to move boxes off their facilities to prevent congestion. The Port of Houston approved a new tariff that excludes gate closures from free time periods but does raise the fees shippers face once free time ends. Speaking in general about the ongoing changes to demurrage policies, Matthew Leech, president of Ports America, the operator of the Port Newark Container Terminal, told the Journal of Commerce that if the FMC will eventually not allow terminals to collect demurrage on days when they are closed or otherwise limit free time policies, rates will need to rise to offset those changes. “We’re going to still collect the same amount of revenue, but we’re just going to do it differently as a response in the end,” Leech said. “We’re simply going to change the charge on the days we can collect, and not charge on the days we can’t and protect the revenue.” “If a container sits in an off-dock depot instead of a terminal, it would pay the facility for storage,” he added. “It doesn’t get free storage on the weekends.” It’s unlikely that most, if any, New York-New Jersey shippers are even incurring demurrage currently. The average dwell time for a container at the port at the end of April was just under three days, according to data from the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey (PANYNJ), well down from dwell times that ranged from one to two weeks and, in some instances, more than 30 days over the course of the last two years. New York-New Jersey marine terminals were open on many Saturdays during 2021 and 2022 to handle the volume surge. But only about 4% of the port’s freight moved on Saturdays, according to PANYNJ estimates. Marine terminals dropped Saturday gate openings last year given the low activity and a port-wide cost to open on those days of over $1 million. Even so, Maersk subsidiary APM has recently opened its terminal for three Saturdays in a row from April 23 through May 6 due to a “customer request,” according to a notice viewed by the Journal of Commerce. The company has not indicated publicly whether the Saturday gate hours will be implemented on a regular basis. With NY-NJ import volumes through March down 27% from the year-earlier period, shippers and truckers have questioned APM’s need for Saturday gates, especially because the terminal would be able to include that day in the period before demurrage is charged after June 1. In a poll conducted by the Association of Bi-State Motor Carriers, all 40 respondents said they will not be using APM’s Saturday gates. Bi-State President Lisa Yakomin said that APM’s Saturday gates have raised concerns among her group’s members that more per diem fees will be levied against truckers and shippers starting next month. “There’s just no reasonable explanation for a terminal to open on a Saturday with import numbers like these, and when you consider the tariff changes that were just announced,” Yakomin said. “It’s hard not to conclude that this is a strategy to decrease free time and increase the risk of incurring detention and demurrage charges.” Peter Friedmann, executive director of shipper advocacy group Agriculture Transportation Coalition (AgTC), told the Journal of Commerce that many truckers run out of their hours of service by the weekend and warehouses that would receive cargo are closed, so opening for a few hours on the weekend “doesn’t really do you much good.” “You can ask, then, why are they doing it because it’s expensive to open,” Friedman said. “But if for every container they can be charging demurrage, that’s the way they’re going to be paying the money to make it work.” Contact Michael Angell at michael.angell@spglobal.com and follow him on Twitter: @michael_angell. title: Top US Shippers: Continued poor service threatens budding ag export recovery
content: US agriculture exports spiked 10.5% in the second half of 2022, wiping out a 4.7% decline in the first half. Photo credit: KAMONRAT / Shutterstock. US agriculture exports rebounded in the second half of last year as port and inland congestion eased and vessel reliability improved, but exporters say lingering service issues continue to hamper overseas sales in early 2023, while tensions with China threaten to derail growth in shipments to the largest importer of US foodstuffs. Dismal ocean carrier schedule reliability over the last two-plus years of surging imports from Asia caused significant delays for agricultural exports, resulting in lost sales, according to shippers. A 10.5% year-over-year spike in containerized US agriculture exports in the second half of 2022 offset a 4.7% first-half decline, leaving overall volumes 0.8% higher for the full year at 1.53 million TEU, according to PIERS, a sister product of the Journal of Commerce by S&P Global. The relatively flat growth in annual agriculture exports followed a 2021 in which volumes tumbled 10.4% amid pandemic-induced capacity and equipment shortages. Shippers are confident agriculture export volumes will be healthier in 2023 as growing demand, specifically in East Asia, allows for expansion in both existing and newer markets, but they warn that a continued lack of vessel schedule reliability — as well as a stronger US dollar that’s making US exports more expensive abroad — could jeopardize those gains. Through February, US agriculture exports are down 6.6% compared with the first two months of 2022. “Customers overseas, who can only afford to have so much inventory, are relying on shipments to come in on time as they estimate, and that’s a constant conversation,” Thomas Mershon, profit center manager of international carriers at US agribusiness The Andersons, told the Journal of Commerce. Schedule reliability for vessels arriving at US West Coast ports from Asia rose to 42.3% in March from 30.1% in February and 19.6% in March 2022, while Asia–US East Coast on-time performance reached 44.5%, up from 39.1% in February and 19.8% in March 2022, according to data from Sea-Intelligence Maritime Analysis. Even with the improvement, however, trans-Pacific vessel reliability remains well below the averages of 66.7% to the West Coast and 58.3% to the East Coast in 2019. When eastbound ships arrive late on the fronthaul from Asia, backhaul cargoes are delayed. And when it comes to agricultural goods, even short delays of just a few days can make or break sales. “The biggest issue is then when you have foodstuff and you’re talking about a commodity, we are losing that sale, that demand,” Mershon explained. “Think of it like a soybean that’s going to be eaten in Asia. People are going to eat that soybean for lunch, and if your serving is not there for lunch today, they will go somewhere else and eat it, and you missed that sale forever,” unlike non-perishable items such as a pair of shoes or a book that a consumer can still purchase the next day. Peter Friedmann, executive director of the Agriculture Transportation Coalition (AgTC), said the relative improvement in schedule reliability has increased the competitiveness of US agricultural products in overseas markets, but he cautioned that the overall outlook is still uncertain. “It’s much better,” Friedmann said of ocean carrier service levels. “But at the same time, we’re all depending on the global economy, the economy of the importing country, the wealth of that importing country, and the weather production among our competitors.” Despite rising political tensions between the US and China that range from import tariffs and intellectual property rights to Beijing’s tacit support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, China has become an increasingly important destination for US agricultural products. Last year, shipments to mainland China accounted for 23.9% of overall US agriculture exports, up from 19.9% in 2021 and 9.9% in pre-pandemic 2019, according to PIERS. By comparison, the next largest destination for US agriculture imports in 2022, Japan, accounted for 11.7% of the total. However, any further increase in political tensions could cause demand growth to slow, according to Mike Steenhoek, executive director of the Soy Transportation Coalition (STC), a group that includes the United Soybean Board, the American Soybean Association and twelve state soybean boards. “Every year, we’re helping supply China’s nutritional and protein needs, and that creates a lot of stability to that relationship, and that needs to be built upon,” Steenhoek told the Journal of Commerce. “It would be really unfortunate if that were to be curtailed because then all of a sudden, there’s a greater likelihood of us being at odds with China.” Contact Teri Errico Griffis at teri.griffis@spglobal.com. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Forwarders’ digital journey not complete yet: Magaya survey
content: Competition from digitally native forwarders, Amazon and even shipping lines has increased the motivation for logistics services providers to invest in technology. Photo credit: Rawpixel.com / Shutterstock.com. Nearly a quarter of logistics services providers (LSPs) surveyed by forwarding technology provider Magaya in February and March have no specialized forwarding software or operating system, while approximately half are not completely reliant on cloud-hosted software. Those findings, taken from a survey of 70 forwarders, third party logistics providers (3PLs) and non-vessel-operating common carriers (NVOs), published Monday, paint a picture of an LSP industry still in the market for technology to better serve shippers and connect with carriers across modes. “The results of this survey reinforce our vision for the future of digitization in freight forwarding and confirm opportunities abound for maximizing the benefits of technology in the industry,” Magaya CEO Gary Nemmers said in a statement. While half of forwarders surveyed have completely migrated to cloud-based solutions, meaning they don’t self-host any systems, the other half still rely wholly or partly on systems they need to host themselves. The benefit of cloud-hosted software is primarily about removing the cost and maintenance burden of running a system from the user. The survey also found that nearly three-quarters of respondents offered a digital portal to connect with customers, but that the features within those portals vary. “Most did have the capability of booking and tracking shipments,” Magaya said. “Fewer than half were able to view schedules, accept online payments and interact via chat with customers. Lack of budget and not wanting to change back-end systems were the biggest blocking factors holding back the companies that did not currently have an online customer portal.” In terms of the impact of technology on quoting, Magaya found that the respondents’ average time to respond to an request for quote (RFQ) was 3.5 hours, with a median time to respond to quote requests of 30 hours. The spread of response times ranged widely, from one minute to two days. Among digital priorities, tracking and visibility ranked the highest, followed by a investing in general forwarding operating system. Rate management and trade compliance tools tied for third. The top priorities from a broader business perspective were customer retention, customer acquisition and lower costs and overhead. Also of note, 44 percent of respondents said the market wasn’t offering adequate artificial intelligence tools to support forwarding operations. title: Top US Shippers: Price inflation pulls the plug on surging US electronics imports
content: Electronics accounted for 6% of overall US containerized imports in 2022. Photo credit: ECLIPSE PRODUCTION / Shutterstock.com. US consumers dialed back demand for electronics imports last year amid growing concerns about the US economic outlook and the worst price inflation since the 1970s. Containerized imports of televisions, mobile phones, computers, gaming consoles and a variety of other devices and gadgets sold under the electronics banner declined 2.1% to 1.66 million TEUs in 2022, according to PIERS, a sister product of the Journal of Commerce within S&P Global. That decline, however, followed a 4% increase that boosted electronics imports to a record high of 1.7 million TEUs in 2021. Last year’s dip in containerized electronics imports — although more of a small step down from the top of a tall staircase than a head-over-heels fall — is a sign that US consumers were holding back on some discretionary purchases, including higher-cost items, after two years of heightened spending across the consumer goods spectrum during the COVID-19 pandemic. The monthly US inflation rate averaged 8% in 2022, rising as high as 9.1% last June. From 2015 through 2020, inflation averaged 1.5% on an annual basis. Unadjusted price inflation was up 5% year over year in March, and 5.6% if the food and energy segments are excluded, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index. Food prices were up 8.5% on average. Despite continued strong demand for certain electronics, such as televisions and home automation devices, US consumer technology sales fell about 8% in 2022 and will drop another 5% in 2023, according to the NPD Group. The market research firm expects sales to flatten in 2024 before ticking up 2% in 2025 as the replacement cycle for certain technology products kicks into higher gear. “Even during challenging economic times, the consumer electronics industry tends to perform well,” Ben Arnold, executive director and consumer technology industry analyst for NPD, said in the firm’s latest technology forecast. Purchases of large-screen TVs, for example, can replace other spending as products progressively become less expensive. “Despite near-term economic headwinds, consumer electronics sales will remain above 2019 levels and industry average selling prices are expected to grow by the end of the forecast period in 2025 — a sign that tech remains a household spending priority,” Arnold said. Same-store US sales at electronics retailer Best Buy fell 10.3% in 2022, as growth in gaming and tablets failed to offset declines in computing, home theater, appliances and mobile phones, according to company reports. Best Buy, which is restructuring its stores and distribution network to match demand, is hoping for a rebound late 2023 or 2024, as consumers begin to upgrade and replace electronics purchased during the initial COVID-19 outbreak. “On average, US households now have twice as many connected devices as they did in 2019, and consumers indicate that more of their tech purchases are need-based than want-based,” CEO Corie Barry said in a March 2 earnings call. “We believe there will be a desire from our vendor partners to stimulate replacement cycles or build completely new categories going forward.” Still, Best Buy’s best-case scenario called for flat comparable sales in the current fiscal year. “The low end of our guidance reflects a scenario where consumer spending regresses even further from our current levels and lasts longer into the year,” CFO Matt Bilunas said during the call. In addition to consumers tightening their belts, ongoing supply chain disruptions and a shortage of microchips also dragged down import volumes as there were fewer products to ship. Labor shortages caused by the COVID-19 pandemic also crimped production in Asia for many manufacturers and importers, particularly in China. COVID-19 restrictions temporarily impacted the primary iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 14 Pro Max assembly facility located in Zhengzhou, China, in November and December. During those months, Apple “had significantly less iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 14 Pro Max supply than we planned, causing ship times to extend far beyond what we had anticipated,” CEO Tim Cook said during the technology giant’s Feb. 3 earnings call. That situation lasted through most of December, he said. But like many high-value electronics products that need to meet tight release deadlines, Apple’s iPhones are more likely to arrive in the US by air than in ocean containers. Electronics imports have seen significant diversification of sourcing away from China in recent years, but analysts warn that reshoring or nearshoring these products is much more difficult than moving production of less complicated, lower-priced goods. “You have to be sure you have the production capacity you need in the target market,” Laurence Allan, S&P Global director of economics and global risk, said at the Journal of Commerce’s Breakbulk & Project Cargo Conference in April. Mainland China’s share of containerized US electronics imports fell to 50.8% last year from 63.6% in 2018, according to PIERS. Vietnam picked up most of the slack, increasing its share of the market to 12.8% in 2022 from just 3% in 2018. Taiwan-based TMSC, one of the world’s largest semiconductor makers, is expanding production in the US, with plans to spend $40 billion on two US sites that will begin production in 2024 and 2026. “We’re all in, in terms of being the largest customer for TSMC in Arizona,” Apple’s Cook told investment analysts. title: EY Americas leader: 70% of supply chain digital transformation efforts fail
content: ORLANDO, Fla. — The exhibition floor of the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium is annually marked by rows of providers of technology solutions operating out of booths adorned with buzzwords: AI, transparency, resiliency. “Transform” and “transformation” also make frequent appearances. But what Sumit Dutta of EY Americas knows is that the success rate on true supply chain digital transformation isn’t good: 70% of them fail. Dutta, whose formal title is EY Americas’ supply chain and operations field of play leader, offered up that number and knows that when EY is leading the type of transformation that his company gets hired to implement, he’s pushing up against odds that are stacked against success. Dutta, in an interview with FreightWaves at the Gartner event, said of digital transformations of company supply chains, “There are several things which clients continue to deal with and they’re getting better at it. But the industry continues to struggle.” Dutta ticked off some of the key issues that are undercutting the possibility of a successful digital overhaul. — “No. 1,” he said, is the data itself. “How do I get the right information, the quality information into these digital platforms?” — Another issue is visible just in the sheer number of exhibitors at the symposium. “The number of options down there is also a bit of an issue with clients trying to figure out the right solution,” Dutta said. “How do you cut through a lot of this clutter?” — The need to “stay back.” That was the term Dutta used to describe the risk of his clients “getting besotted with the next shiny object” instead of saying, “‘What is the business problem that I’m trying to solve?’” He cited a current client whose initiative was focused on compliance with negotiated container rates through the supply chain. Compliance rates climbed from about 25% to 80% as a result of the technology effort. It wasn’t “shiny” but by improving compliance it saved money. — The need to “get out of a pilot,” Dutta said. “Everyone’s very good at piloting.” But a lot of companies involved in a pilot of transformative technology “don’t know when to draw a line and say, yes, it’s successful.” At a certain point, the decision needs to be made to either go ahead with the technology or drop it and move on. The in-between is a condition that Dutta referred to as “pilot purgatory.” — A technology transformation cannot just be about the software. Dutta said he has seen companies introduce “an end-to-end digital platform, which spanned across logistics and manufacturing and they rolled out one of the top solutions.” And in some cases, “not a single person used it. … The process hadn’t been properly defined, people hadn’t been trained and people hadn’t been coached on why they should use it. Some of the technology solutions “just become idle things on the side.” Another key point that Dutta raised: The companies hired to make the changes need to be straight with the clients. “We tell them, ‘Listen, you should be aware and we should be aware together,’” he said. “‘Just because you’re embarking on a transformation journey doesn’t guarantee success.” And part of that blunt chat involves noting the 70% failure rate. Dutta agreed with one observation: The functionality of those software solutions on display at the Gartner event heavily overlap and success comes from finding that sweet spot that differentiates one offering of supply chain software from another. How that happens, according to Dutta, has several possible pathways. One key is to provide “best practices” rather than trying to fix the existing system. “You can’t just automate an existing workflow,” Dutta said. Ensuring the transformation relies on best practices makes it “so that that is not just a renovation but a reimagining.” Part of that, Dutta added, is that whatever technology solution is designed is targeted at a company’s needs rather than any sort of “one-size-fits-all” approach. And even after the solution is implemented, Dutta said it needs to be “future proofed” so that after the 12 to 18 months that might be the length of the implementation process, a client doesn’t need to realize that it’s already obsolete. “You need to make sure that what you have is not the best solution of yesterday.” Dutta has seen the importance of supply chain issues soar post-pandemic, citing data that before COVID, supply chain issues were mentioned on just 1-in-6 earnings calls. Today, it is above 70%. Even internally at EY, Dutta said the consultancy’s management “has declared that supply chain is among our top two priorities across all of our competencies,” which number about a dozen. It isn’t just an issue of making sure supply chain problems are avoided, according to Dutta. There’s a realization among companies that a broken or inefficient supply chain is going to crimp growth. “What you can do as a business is now informed by what a supply chain can enable you to do.” That replaces what Dutta described as the previous view toward the supply chain: It was a “lights on” function, meaning that it was an activity that was needed just to keep the lights on rather than providing a route to expansion. “It was like you just had to make sure you didn’t screw up.” He’s seen that in the recall of some of his former colleagues and friends who were supply chain managers and thought they had retired. Instead, they’re getting called back into action, often by private equity companies looking to invest in logistics and tapping into their knowledge base and experience. ‘Quiet quit’ product of disengaged supply chain workforce Truck transportation jobs aren’t afraid of heights; they rose again in April Wall Street greets e2open’s tough forecast with a stock plunge Past the hype. title: Top US Shippers: US toy imports ‘normalizing’ after slipping from record 2022
content: A spike in US demand for toys and games in 2021 shifted import volumes into the typically slower first half in 2022. Photo credit: Cholpan / Shutterstock.com. US toy imports came down slightly from record levels last year but remained well above the historical average amid excess inventories prompted by unusual consumer buying patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to toy manufacturers. Even with a 4.6% year-over-year decline, the 1.26 million TEUs of toys and games brought into the country in 2022 was still the second-highest volume ever, according to data from PIERS, a sister company of the Journal of Commerce within S&P Global. The slowdown in demand aligned with a broader fading of US import demand in the fourth quarter of 2022, largely due to an inventory overhang that didn’t spare toy makers and their retailer customers. “Holiday results [in 2022] were heavily skewed by the volatility and timing of retail inventory movement throughout the year, not by the underlying marketplace performance of our business, with growth in [point of sale] for both the fourth quarter and the year,” Ynon Kreiz, chairman and CEO of Mattel, said in a Feb. 8 earnings call. A surge in demand for toys and games in late 2020 and throughout 2021 reverberated in “unusual sales patterns” in 2021 and 2022, as Hasbro CEO Chris Cocks put it, resulting in a year in which volume was heavily front-loaded in the first half. “Retailers were buying much earlier in the year [in 2021],” Cocks said in a Feb. 16 earnings call. “We were playing catch-up from 2020, particularly in Q1, in terms of fulfilling orders, and we don’t see that happening this time. Actually, we see retail inventory [as] not unhealthy but still having a little bit of an overhang given the slowing consumer demand that we saw in Q4.” Cocks said Hasbro expects US toy demand to begin to “normalize” by the fourth quarter of 2023. He also said the company’s sales pattern will return to a more typical seasonal cadence; Hasbro is projecting that 60% to 65% of its sales will come in the second half in 2023, a “more historically normal” ratio than the 57% of sales the company reported for the second half last year. Smaller toy manufacturers have felt the impact of volatile and unusual sales patterns even more acutely, especially those that rely more predominantly on spot ocean freight rates, as opposed to direct contracts with container lines. Total ocean freight spend for USAOPOLY, for example, spiked to $4.2 million in 2022, up from $3 million in 2021 and $1.2 million in 2019, according to Vice President Paul May. “Volumes for us went up a bit last year, but not to the extent that it came close to offsetting the cost of freight,” May told the Journal of Commerce. “From a cashflow perspective, it was super painful.” The licensed games and puzzles maker, which procures capacity exclusively on the spot market, is projecting a spend of $2.1 million this year after trans-Pacific spot rates plummeted in late 2022 and early 2023. As of May 4, the average spot rate from Asia to the US West Coast of $1,825 per FEU was down 78.7% year over year and 85.3% from its September 2021 peak, according to data from Drewry’s World Container Index. May said excess stock “is still an issue” for USAOPOLY’s customers after a “weird” year in 2022. “There was still an appetite for product and space on ships was still a problem in the first half,” he said. “We knew the economy would take a turn at some point. But we have a much better feeling for this year and a pretty good feeling for next year.” USAOPOLY is intent on lowering its own inventory levels in 2023 and into 2024, May said. “We tried to keep it under control, but this past year, we had the most inventory we’ve ever had rolling into a new year,” he said. “That puts pressure on the warehousing side, because that’s also coming at a premium.” Hasbro had reduced its on-hand inventory levels at the end of 2022 by $168 million from the third quarter, but they were still up $125 million (23%) from the end of 2021, Debbie Hancock, vice president of investor relations, said in the Feb. 16 earnings call. Although much has been written about US importers attempting to diversify sourcing away from China in the wake of the pandemic and strained trade relations with Beijing, China remained the dominant source of toy imports in 2022, according to PIERS. Even with a marginal drop in share — from 84.9% in 2021 to 84.4% last year — mainland China still exported more than 17 times more toys and games to the US than Vietnam, the second-largest source of US toy imports by volume. May said USAOPOLY now sources about 70% of its volume from Asia and the rest domestically in the US, up from about 60% in years past, further evidence — albeit anecdotal — that the nearshoring of manufacturing and sourcing has been slow, at best. title: FMC adds oversight heft by naming first director of enforcement program
content: Since OSRA-22 became law last June, US shipping interests who sought relief from the FMC over disputed fees have won back just over $1 million. Photo credit: Avigator Fortuner / Shutterstock.com. The US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) has appointed the first director of its widening enforcement program, putting new muscle behind its oversight of ocean shipping amid a growing number of shipper complaints in the aftermath of broad reform measures that are almost a year old. Former US immigration judge John G. Crews II will head up FMC’s Bureau of Enforcement, Investigations and Compliance (BEIC), another step in fulfilling the agency’s staffing requirements under the Ocean Shipping Act of 2022 (OSRA-22). Crews will oversee the BEIC’s three departments that were reorganized under one umbrella last July, FMC said in a statement Monday. He previously worked as an attorney advisor at the Department of Justice, an assistant US attorney, a law clerk to a US district judge and a police officer. “The commission is fully committed to meaningful and effective enforcement of its statutes,” FMC Chairman Daniel Maffei said in the statement. “I am confident Mr. Crews will provide effective leadership of BEIC and his efforts will be instrumental in achieving deterrence through enforcement.” FMC’s workforce has risen to 132 as of this month, including three new attorneys. The agency’s goal is 163 full-time employees by 2024. FMC has been rebuilding its enforcement program “to suit the needs and requirements of today's international ocean shipping industry,” Managing Director Lucille Marvin said at the agency’s bi-monthly meeting last week. “We’re a specialized agency and we serve a very niche area of the supply chain, and you can’t just hire any old person off the street,” Marvin said. “We have very specific skills that we’re looking for.” Since OSRA-22 became law last June, US shipping interests who sought relief from the FMC over disputed fees have won back just over $1 million. The agency has also collected nearly $3.2 million in civil penalties from Wan Hei, Hapag Lloyd and Ocean Network Express. The FMC last week announced it had created a new geographic structure that will allow investigators to oversee regulated entities in specific regions. Region one includes New York, New Jersey, Chicago and Norfolk; region two includes Atlanta, Charleston, Savannah, Miami and Houston; and region three comprises Los Angeles, Long Beach, Oakland, Seattle and Salt Lake City. title: UPS, Teamsters kick off high-stakes national contract negotiations
content: UPS and the Teamsters union kicked off national contract negotiations this week, commencing a bargaining process with immense stakes for both parties and the customers who send millions of packages daily through the company’s network. National bargaining began after the two sides exchanged initial proposals Monday, and talks “continued in earnest on Tuesday,” according to updates from the Teamsters. The start of the talks came three weeks after the originally planned date of April 17, as the Teamsters pushed the company to reach agreements on region-specific supplemental contracts before national bargaining could commence. Two supplemental agreements affecting workers in Kentucky and Northern California still haven’t been finalized, but union leaders handling those negotiations urged national talks to get underway, the Teamsters said Tuesday. The current five-year contract expires July 31, and Teamsters leadership has made clear that a strike will occur if a deal is not reached by then, an event that would cause immense disruption for shippers. “Teamsters will not be working beyond the expiration date of that contract unless there is a new contract that our members deserve, endorse, embrace, and vote on,” General President Sean O’Brien said in April. “We are prepared to work seven days a week to get it done.” UPS has expressed optimism that a contract agreement can be reached in time. But experts say the risk of a strike is higher this year than in previous bargaining cycles due in part to the leadership of O’Brien, who successfully campaigned as an outspoken critic of previous contract negotiations during his campaign for Teamsters general president in 2021. “There’s an unpredictability about this year that hasn’t been there for the last few contracts,” said Alan Amling, distinguished fellow at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville’s Global Supply Chain Institute and former VP of corporate strategy for UPS. Inflationary pressures provide added motivation for O’Brien and the rest of the Teamsters to push for wage increases in the next contract. The union is also fighting to address concerns such as scheduling issues and pay discrepancies between certain positions. The negotiations between UPS and the Teamsters have two facets, according to UPS. One is the National Master Agreement, covering topics like wages, healthcare and pensions. The other is the various supplemental agreements that address local topics in specific regions. UPS CEO Carol Tomé said in an April 25 earnings call that the company and the Teamsters have established five subcommittees at the national bargaining table to focus on key areas of the contract, enabling the negotiation process to move faster. Tentative agreements have already been reached on five issues, including more opportunities for union members to fill job vacancies prior to UPS hiring external workers, according to the Teamsters. “What’s most critical about these early hours of national negotiations is that big gains are already being made and the Teamsters have made zero concessions to get them,” General Secretary-Treasurer Fred Zuckerman said in a statement Tuesday. “The progress made since yesterday at the national table has been hugely consequential for the rest of the bargaining process.” Once an agreement is tentatively reached between the company and union representatives, workers will vote on whether to ratify. It needs a simple majority vote for approval. Around 330,000 UPS employees in the U.S. are represented by the Teamsters. That number is primarily made up of package delivery drivers, tractor-trailer drivers, package handlers, clerks and mechanics, according to UPS. Union membership at UPS has also grown in recent years, with 72,000 Teamsters-represented jobs added between August 2018 and February 2022. Other parcel delivery companies are poised to see increased business in the event of a strike as shippers divert their packages elsewhere. Top competitor FedEx, for example, called on its customers earlier this year to onboard their volumes by March 31 in order to avoid strike-related disruptions. Fast-growing regional carriers also stand to gain from the uncertainty. “There’s more competition than ever,” Jeremy Tancredi, a partner in West Monroe’s Operations Excellence practice, said of the parcel delivery space. Tomé said diversion activity “wasn’t very much” in Q1. However, as the contract expiration date draws near, the company has assigned executives to top customers to keep them updated on negotiations and minimize volume loss. The company expects an agreement will help bring any diverted volume back. “Customers say, ‘We’d like to ship with you, we’re just going to sit on the sidelines till you’re done,’” Tomé said. “So we just need to get it done, and we will.”

title: Even CPG volumes are slowing for brokers
content: An unusually broad-based downturn in goods flows that has affected even the most resilient of customer segments — consumer packaged goods and food and beverage — has freight brokers scrambling to differentiate themselves and compete for less available freight. Tyson Foods’ stock plunged by more than 16% after it announced that it lost money in the first quarter of 2023, couldn’t manage to grow beef and pork volumes even after cutting prices and lowered its estimates for revenue growth to “flat to 1%” for the year. According to one broker who spoke to FreightWaves, a large food conglomerate is moving 8-10% fewer loads just by consolidating smaller shipments into full truckloads; a decrease in vendor order flow was responsible for a further 5-7% reduction in volume. Another freight broker said that many of the shippers who led the charge to push contract rates down in 2022 are now slowing the pace of their RFPs and looking to lock in their savings long term. “I look at the bid cycle like an accordion,” said Pat Gillihan, chief revenue officer at Transportation One, a Chicago-based freight brokerage. “It completely contracted from annuals to semiannuals to quarterlies in order to capture the market movements on the upswing and now on the downswing. Now that accordion is being tremendously extended: Quarterlies are now semis, semis are now annuals. It suggests that the shippers have realized they’ve captured the bottom of the market and are looking to extend those low rates.” Typically, spot rates stay within about 25 cents per mile of the prevailing contract rate. If spot rates exceed the contract rate by much more than that, shippers start to feel the bite of tender rejections and raise their rates to ensure compliance. Historically, if spot rates dropped below contract rates by much more than 25 cents per mile, shippers would save money by moving their freight on the cheaper spot market until they contracted carriers lowered rates. Today, spot rates are an incredible 72 cents per mile below contract rates, when including a fuel surcharge of $1.20 per mile. That means that shippers should be able to extract further concessions from their contracted carriers if they so choose. Some shippers are still frequently rebidding their freight down, but others have moved on to other priorities, including service. Gillihan said that shippers are enforcing the highest service standards they can — and dinging their carriers and suppliers with fines more frequently when shipments don’t go exactly according to plan. “If you’re not executing at a 98.5% service level or above, you’re being ousted from the network,” Gillihan said. “It’s not even a topic of conversation, just an expectation. The application of fees has also increased. We see more $250 chargebacks and $500 fees [for late or incomplete shipments]; things that big box retailers would have let slide previously are now triggering fees.” Demand softness has started working its way up the supply chain from the retailers to their food and beverage vendors to the companies that make packaging like cardboard boxes. Packaging Corp. of America, the third-largest containerboard/box producer in North America, which experienced a 13% year-over-year decline in box shipments in the first quarter, announced Tuesday that it was idling its containerboard plant in Wallula, Washington, indefinitely, and laid off hundreds of employees. To the extent that CPG and food and beverage shippers are looking for new transportation providers, they’re focused on asset-based trucking carriers, not necessarily third-party logistics providers. That’s changed the way some freight brokers sell their services. Gillihan said that at Transportation One, he goes to market with a “strategic capacity-based sales model.” He works closely with the best small and midsized trucking carriers that he can find and tries to plug the holes in their networks where they need freight. That strategy lowers Transportation One’s cost to serve its customers and makes its capacity stickier in those lanes. Gillihan said leading with the best carriers helped Transportation One hit 24.7% year-over-year volume growth in the first quarter of 2023, numbers that many larger 3PLs would struggle to put up in this market. Echo Global Logistics, a Chicago-based 3PL with $4.4 billion in 2022 gross revenue, has leaned even further into assets in a bid to differentiate itself. Echo, now a private company since its acquisition by The Jordan Co. in November 2021, is in the process of rethinking itself as a supply chain solutions provider. That includes purchasing real assets. In May 2022, Echo bought Roadtex Transportation, which operates a nationwide network of 32 cold chain warehousing facilities and a dedicated less-than-truckload fleet. Roadtex’s main hubs are in New Jersey, Indianapolis and Chino and Sacramento, California. Roadtex’s Indianapolis presence includes more than 1 million square feet of temperature-controlled warehousing. That allows Echo to get in even deeper with midsized food and beverage and pharmaceutical shippers. In January of this year, Echo hired Frank Hurst, a longtime LTL veteran, from Roadrunner to run LTL and now temperature-controlled logistics at Echo. Hurst’s vision is for Echo to integrate its services and become a single-source solution provider for temperature-controlled logistics. “When talking to customers, COVID is in the rearview mirror for them, [in terms of] the supply chain disruptions and service impacts,” Hurst said. “Their expectation is that their service providers get back to providing the highest level of service, and we talk about this with our LTL carriers, focusing on on-time service and quality. Our customers don’t want the excuses of driver shortages and supply chain disruptions — they want fluidity and on-time delivery.” Less-than-truckload rates have come down some as customers rebid freight but LTL pricing is “more rational” than truckload pricing, Hurst said, explaining that LTL carriers are tied to physical real estate like cross-dock facilities and the workers in them, which also constrains where their fleets can build density. That means that LTL rate increases can be more tied to macroeconomic inflation than the boom-and-bust cycles of a volatile market like truckload freight. Hurst said that Echo’s ability to provide critical aspects of the storage and distribution of temperature-controlled freight helps its CPG customers meet the demands of big box retailers. “That linkage is critical,” Hurst said. “Retailers are the distribution channel for CPG and food and bev, and shipping into mass merchants requires a heightened level of service, planning, details and flexibility. That’s why shippers that have temperature-controlled needs partner with a Roadtex or Echo — understanding those requirements can be daunting.” Past the hype. title: Top US Shippers: Supply chain bottlenecks put cork in US alcohol imports
content: Shifting shipping patterns and consumer habits caused US wine imports to rise 2.2% last year, while beer imports fell 10.4%. Photo credit: Paolo Paradiso / Shutterstock.com. Shipments of alcoholic beverages to the United States took a dip last year as port congestion, poor schedule reliability, changes in vessel services and the limited supply of refrigerated containers combined with a continued shift in consumption patterns that saw more consumers drinking at home, rather than at bars and restaurants. US imports of wine, beer and distilled spirits slipped 1.3% to 477,162 TEUs last year, following a particularly strong 2021 in which volumes rose 4.4%, according to PIERS, a sister product of the Journal of Commerce within S&P Global. Those volumes could have been higher in both years, if not for widespread port congestion that severely hampered vessel reliability and, in turn, crimped available capacity and equipment, according to Alison Leavitt, managing director of the Wine and Spirits Shippers Association (WSSA). “Both 2021 and 2022 were incredible years for the wine and spirits industry,” Leavitt told the Journal of Commerce. “We would have seen more growth except for the supply chain challenges.” The surge in trans-Pacific imports that began in mid-2020 prompted carriers to pull ships out of service in the trans-Atlantic trade between Europe and North America, the industry’s busiest lane, starting in March 2021. Leavitt said Mediterranean Shipping Co.’s decision to deploy additional vessel capacity on the trans-Atlantic trade was a “savior” for wine and spirits shippers. But the trans-Atlantic wasn’t alone in this, as carriers also redeployed vessels from north-south lanes serving on other major wine- and spirits-producing regions to the then-booming trans-Pacific. The remaining ships then had to contend with chronic congestion at major US ports, which dragged down on-time performance and, in turn, raised the risk of spoilage at sea. “Trade lanes were challenged the whole year,” she said. “We weren’t getting any relief on congestion and vessel space until the end of 2022.” Container ships sailing from South America to North America, for example, arrived within one day of their scheduled arrival time on just 33% of sailings in 2022, down from 53% in 2021 and 85% during pre-pandemic 2019, according to data from Sea-Intelligence Maritime Analysis. Average on-time performance from Australia and New Zealand to the US was just shy of 42% last year compared with 43% in 2021 and 76% in 2019. During the height of the disruptions, transit times from the West Coast of South America to the Port of Oakland rose as high as 100 days, compared with 20 days prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Leavitt said. “Sitting in the sun off the coast of Southern California for 40 days is not good for wine,” added Robert Tobiassen, president of the National Association of Beverage Importers (NABI). Tobiassen said wine and beer importers also struggled to procure enough refrigerated (reefer) shipping containers to satisfy demand. In some instances, carriers were using reefers to carry dry cargo to take advantage of record-smashing rates for dry cargo, which is also easier to handle from a carrier perspective. “Reefers were very hard to get for our members,” he said. As if that wasn’t enough, containerized shipments of alcoholic beverages encountered further delays after being discharged from vessels. Tobiassen cited an example in which one NABI member had a container of wine get lost in the stacks at the Port of Los Angeles for two months back in 2021. The box was discharged in September and placed at the bottom of a stack of six other containers, but the terminal’s inventory system could only record data for a six-high container stack, so longshore workers had to comb through the stacks manually to find it. “Wine is very perishable stuff,” Tobiassen said. “They finally found it in November because the computerized inventory locator wasn’t designed for more than six containers.” Similar to their dry cargo counterparts, alcoholic beverage importers also faced delays in receiving products at inland destinations via rail, Tobiassen said. Average rail container dwell times at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach peaked at 16.5 days in August 2022, compared to just 3.3 days in December 2021, according to data from the Pacific Merchant Shipping Association (PMSA). Shifts in shipping methods and consumer tastes are also affecting wine and beer imports in different ways, Tobiassen said. Some wine importers have been using large plastic bladders stowed within reefers to move wine in bulk and then blending and bottling the product domestically, rather than bottling at the source. This process can significantly reduce shipping costs; a single bladder-equipped container can hold 24,000 liters of wine compared to approximately 9,900 bottles (7,425 liters) via the traditional method. But Tobiassen said many wine drinkers are eschewing the low-cost brands that come in bladders in favor of wine bottled at the source because of their appellation. That shift contributed to a 2.2% increase in wine imports last year, according to PIERS data. Beer imports, meanwhile, slumped 10.4% in 2022, as the slow reopening of restaurants and bars hindered demand for kegged beer from overseas and ongoing steel and aluminum tariffs increased the cost of kegs themselves. “The beer people had the biggest problem last year as keg beer sales plummeted,” Tobiassen said. Leavitt said more people are still drinking at home compared with before the pandemic, which means “slightly less volume of containers,” but resurgent demand for dining out, live entertainment and cruises could help boost alcoholic beverage imports. “The grocery store surge has died down, but we’re getting back to more on-premises drinking,” she said.
