title: US shippers expanding private fleets in uncertain truck market
content: US retailer Walmart increased the size of its private fleet 41% between December 2020 and June 2023, according to Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration data. Photo credit: William B. Cassidy / Journal of Commerce. US shippers are increasingly putting control of their freight into their own hands, boosting the use of their own privately operated fleets despite a truckload market favorable to them. The trend underscores the growing importance of stability, consistency and predictability in increasingly integrated, time-dependent and complex supply chains, shippers and logistics executives told the Journal of Commerce. But the shift of more freight to private fleets isn’t universal. Dedicated trucking is a popular alternative, and many shippers have distribution networks that may make using company-owned trucks less economical. Some of the largest private fleets are operated by retailers, including Walmart, Dollar General and Amazon. But the growth of private fleets appears to be affecting capacity in the broader truckload market and may help to keep pressure on rates, with less freight tendered to for-hire carriers. “I believe we are seeing a shift of focus beyond cost to providing control and enhanced visibility in the supply chain,” Tom Moore, executive vice president of the National Private Truck Council (NPTC), an industry association, told the Journal of Commerce. Shippers are seeking “a new balance among dedicated, private and one-way services,” the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals (CSCMP) said in its 2023 State of Logistics report. From 2020 through 2022, shipper spending on private fleets and dedicated trucking rose 30%, according to the report, released in June. The report didn’t separate private fleets from dedicated spending. The CSCMP study pegged the five-year compound annual growth rate for that spending at 8%, and the annualized growth rate was 6% in 2022, it said. The pandemic forced shippers to become more flexible in terms of the services they buy and what they offer their customers. One customer “might want a dedicated fleet with gold-plated trailers, while the other wants a low-budget option,” said one food shipper who did not want to be identified. That shipper does not operate a private fleet but agreed that company-owned trucks are one more option a shipper can offer in pursuit of that “new balance” cited by CSCMP. Data filed by companies with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) tracks the growth of private carriage since 2018 and through the COVID-19 pandemic. Since 2018, the number of private fleets registered in the US has climbed almost 19% to 898,932 as of September, according to the FMCSA. Those carriers include 160,672 shipper-owned fleets with both private and for-hire authority. The data suggests private fleets now account for 44% of existing motor carriers, by registration, although that doesn’t mean they haul a similar percentage of existing tonnage. The number of private fleets increased 1.5% from December 2022 through September, even as the number of registered for-hire interstate motor carriers dropped 1.8%, FMCSA data shows. Ongoing private fleet expansion may also be inferred from strong heavy truck sales in a weak trucking market. “Private fleet growth is evident as Class 8 tractor retail sales are on pace to set a record this year, yet for-hire fleets are by and large demonstrating capital discipline,” Tim Denoyer, vice president and senior analyst at ACT Research, said in a statement. S&P Global expects US North American heavy-duty truck production to increase 5.1% in 2023, despite a weak US for-hire trucking market. Expanded use of private fleets could explain a portion of that increase, along with the completion of backlogged orders. Denoyer believed shippers were increasing the volume they ship in their private fleets by mid-single-digit percentages. That’s supported by NPTC annual benchmarking surveys that showed private fleets increased shipments 10.3% in 2020, 9.7% in 2021 and 4.6% in 2022. Some of the largest US shipper-owned fleets are getting much larger. Over the past three years, Dollar General has expanded the size of its private fleet 238%, from 368 trucks in December 2020 to 1,242 trucks this June, according to FMCSA’s motor carrier safety measurement system (SMS). In the same 2020-2023 period, Amazon has built its in-house fleet from a base of 4,578 trucks to 15,125 vehicles, a 234% increase, the FMCSA data shows. Walmart grew its private fleet from 8,507 to 12,023 trucks in the same time frame. And these shippers plan to add more trucks to their in-house operations. “We plan to have more than 2,000 tractors in our private fleet by the end of 2023,” Jeff Owen, the former CEO of Dollar General, said during a second-quarter earnings call in August. Todd Vasos replaced Owen as CEO in October. The private fleet is one tool Dollar General is using to attain that stability, alongside increased distribution center capacity. In addition, “we save approximately 20% of associated costs every time we replace a third-party tractor with one from our private fleet,” Owen said. Shippers are working hard to draw more truck drivers to their private fleets, too. Walmart last year launched a private fleet development program that gives employees a company-paid path toward earning a commercial driver’s license (CDL) over 12 weeks. This year, Walmart expanded the program to 25 transportation centers within 50 miles of 439 Walmart stores. The retailer also pays new drivers up to $110,000 a year. Those moves underscore the importance of in-house control over trucking, alongside external partnerships with for-hire carriers, at one of the nation’s largest retailers. Private fleets are not a panacea for shipper transportation ills, however. They tend to be used in outbound delivery of finished goods, NPTC’s Moore points out. Dollar General in August said its private fleet handled 50% of its outbound shipments from distribution centers to stores, for example. “It’s this control over outbound distribution that has spurred many companies to establish or re-establish a private fleet after previously outsourcing such movements,” Moore said. NPTC’s latest benchmarking study found 70% of respondents used their private fleets for outbound distribution. For-hire fleets accounted for 17% of their outbound shipments. But the models that led many shippers to deploy private fleets in the past appear to be changing. For decades, private fleets were seen as cost centers that were needed to provide a level of guaranteed service for certain customers. Shippers struggled to utilize them effectively, often gaining for-hire authority to pursue backhauls. Dedicated contract carriage grew as a result. The volatility shippers have seen in truckload rates over the past several years, with shorter cycles, higher peaks and lower valleys, is pushing more companies to include the tactical use of private fleets in more holistic transportation strategies, Moore said. “In the face of capacity constraints through much of the pandemic, shippers responded by expanding private fleets,” he said. “The results proved a tonic for many corporations, providing a viable hedge against fluctuations in service and price in the outside carrier market.” Contact William B. title: Carbon tax needed to spur real action on maritime emissions
content: At current prices, using biofuel would double the cost of an Asia–Europe transit from $1,000 to $2,000 per container, according to one forwarder. Photo credit: GreenOak / Shutterstock.com. SINGAPORE — Without a sufficiently high price on carbon, the maritime industry will lack the needed incentive to make the transition to zero-carbon fuels, slowing the process of decarbonization. But it’s an open question whether that will ever happen, leaving it as an open question how the industry will progress down the path toward achieving net-zero emissions by or around 2050, the revised goal of global regulators. Today, there is no carbon pricing mechanism in place on a global level, and despite low carbon fuel products offered to beneficial cargo owners (BCOs) by carriers and forwarders, there has thus far been minimal uptake outside of a few early adopters. As a result, the costs of making such fuels available are being borne largely by carriers who say they can’t fund the energy transition forever. According to a global forwarder, about 200 BCO tenders that it saw for the 2023–24 contract year contained requirements for CO2 mitigation such as biofuel, but none of the final contracts contained these clauses. As one forwarder explained, using a biofuel formula at current prices doubles the cost of an Asia–Europe transit from $1,000 to $2,000 per container. In other words, despite public commitments by some 4,000 companies globally to reduce Scope 3 emissions, according to S&P Global Sustainable1, those commitments are not trickling down to ocean shipping given that shippers, at least currently, are unwilling to pay higher-than-market freight rates to achieve those goals. S&P Global is the parent company of the Journal of Commerce. Many believe the only way to change this scenario is through implementation of a global enforceable tax on carbon. It can’t be just any tax, though; it must be high enough to neutralize the price of traditional bunkers and zero-carbon fuels, or at least close the gap significantly. Otherwise, the playing field will remain uneven, and the market will remain dependent on individual companies to take the first steps. But that might be out of reach. The regulatory wheels that would potentially result in a carbon tax with sufficient teeth to force adoption at a global scale were put in place in July, when the member states of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) agreed to a more ambitious revised greenhouse gas (GHG) policy. The goal is now for the maritime industry to reach net-zero GHG emissions “by or around” 2050, with checkpoints that call for reducing total GHG emissions 20% relative to 2008 levels — and striving for 30% — by 2030, and 70%, although striving for 80%, by 2040. To ensure that was not simply an idle pledge, the IMO agreed to formulate a GHG emissions pricing mechanism, also called a “market-based measure,” by 2027, as well as a marine fuel standard. But some believe it will be too difficult politically for the IMO member states to agree to a sufficiently high carbon price due to concerns that transport costs will skyrocket, particularly for remote economies such as the Pacific islands. For example, some believe an ambitious price of $250 to $300 per ton of carbon would be needed to effectively decarbonize, given the cost of producing alternative fuels such as ammonia. “What I am absolutely sure that is going to happen is that there is not going to be a solution that is going to make everyone happy,” Susana Germino, general manager of sustainability and decarbonization at ocean carrier Swire Shipping, told the recent Project Cargo Conference in Singapore organized by maritime news outlet Heavy Lift and Project Forwarding International. That is leading some to focus instead on the potential for a fuel standard, similar in theory to the low-sulfur fuel requirement the IMO imposed in 2020, as the most viable path forward. “The fuel standard, similar to previous IMO rules like the IMO 2020 sulfur cap, has the potential to become the main demand driver for green shipping fuels,” Rico Salgmann, Washington-based transport specialist at the World Bank, told the Journal of Commerce. But the issue with a fuel standard is that, as with other costs, the ability of ocean carriers to pass the cost of compliance on to their customers depends in part on market conditions. For example, some believe that in the current depressed ocean container freight market, carriers won’t be able to pass on costs related to shipping’s inclusion in the European Union Emissions Trading System (ETS). This is no different to how carriers won’t pass along detention and demurrage costs or will extend credit terms during down markets. That flies in the face of a point carriers have made all along: they can’t fund the industry’s energy transition alone. If forced to do so, it could lead to further consolidation and less competition among carriers — an outcome that could be even more detrimental to shippers than helping to bear the additional cost burden of decarbonization. title: CBP increases scrutiny of skyrocketing low-value international shipments
content: Brokers and consignees can voluntarily participate in a data-sharing program with US Customs and Border Protection on shipments valued at less than $800. Photo credit: FOTOGRIN / Shutterstock.com. PROVIDENCE, RI — US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is asking customs brokers to ensure they have better insight into customers using a CBP program involving low-value international shipments. The increase in scrutiny comes as CBP is processing a rising number of such shipments, part of the agency’s “Type 86” pilot program on de minimis shipments valued at no more than $800. “We’re now seeing almost 2.5 million small packages come in through all of our international mail facilities and hubs, through maritime cargo as well, and in trucks going across the border,” John Leonard, deputy executive assistant commissioner at CBP’s Office of Trade, said at the CONECT Northeast Cargo Symposium in Providence Wednesday. “De minimis is exploding, it really is becoming a huge part of our trade landscape.” Under the de minimis rule, a consignee can import one package per day worth $800 or less without filing a formal customs entry with CBP. The Type 86 pilot is a voluntary program in which a consignee can have its broker provide CBP with data filed through the agency’s automated broker interface (ABI). “What we’re hoping to do, especially with customs brokers who do file Type 86 [entries], is get them more aware of who the customer is, who the client is and what is actually in the shipment,” Leonard said. Leonard said importers or their brokers do have to file a “harmonized tariff system” (HTS) number with the Type 86 entry, giving a better sense of the product being shipped. “It’s very similar to a formal entry in some respects, except there’s no bond,” he said. “But a lot of the key data elements are very, very similar to what’s on the formal entry. But our fear is that brokers are not tracking as closely who the client is and what is in the parcel.” Raised expectations of the knowledge customs brokers should possess about their customers’ shipments will likely rankle a broker community that has long highlighted to CBP the inherent dangers of increased de minimis shipments. Those shipments, outside of the ones imported under the Type 86 program and another initiative, called the Section 321 data pilot, don’t require customs entries. Customs brokers at the CONECT conference told the Journal of Commerce that they already endeavor to understand their customers’ shipment activity, but can’t possibly know what is inside every small, low-value package moved. One broker, who did not want to be identified, said an increased onus on brokers is especially difficult considering the fee they receive for filing a Type 86 entry isn’t enough to justify a “know what’s in the parcel” process on every shipment. The ambition to screen de minimis shipments to a greater degree is not just about ensuring that shippers overseas are adhering to US customs regulations, but mostly about prohibiting illicit goods from entering the country via the low-value goods provision, with Leonard emphasizing fentanyl as a key target for CBP. “That's the message, that we want to work in partnership with brokers,” he said. “Let's get better visibility [as] to what is coming in into the country.” The issue of enforcing compliance with forced labor regulations is a related activity, with CBP jointly tracking country of origin on low-value shipments to ensure products aren’t tied to suppliers using forced labor. A CBP dashboard on enforcement of the Uyghur Force Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) shows that Malaysia, not China, was by far the largest country of origin for violations this year as of Oct. 10. “If you start looking at, what do we produce or what do we import from China, that’s actually not the risk that Customs is looking at,” trade attorney Mollie Sitkowski, a partner at Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath, told the conference. “You need to then look at what you're importing from Malaysia and Vietnam and then ask those suppliers [about their ties to forced labor]. So it makes understanding compliance for a supply chain very difficult.” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@spglobal.com. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: ILA looking for local ports to bring in more union foremen
content: ILA leadership, which has traditionally supported Democratic presidential candidates, is considering Donald Trump for 2024. Photo credit: ILA. NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Battles over the role of union longshore workers are spreading beyond the Port of Charleston, according to the leadership of International Longshoremen’s Association (ILA), who say dockworkers are underrepresented in supervisory jobs at many marine terminals along the East and Gulf coasts. The local disputes are unfolding against broader talks on a coastwide master contract and come at a time when the ILA is looking to shore up political support during the upcoming 2024 election year. For the past two years, the ILA has claimed that ocean carriers calling Charleston’s new Leatherman terminal are violating terms of the union’s current master contract with maritime employers due the terminal employing non-union, state workers to operate cranes. The ILA’s ability to sue ocean carriers to enforce that provision is now before the US Supreme Court for a possible hearing. However, work jurisdiction issues, such as what’s occurring at Charleston, are hitting other East and Gulf coast ports, ILA Executive Vice President Dennis Daggett said at a meeting of union locals from Southeast and Gulf Coast ports. The bulk of those disputes are over who oversees dockworkers and the union’s role in back-office work, he added. “Right now, we have jurisdictional or technology disputes in Boston, Virginia, Charleston, soon-to-be Savannah, Miami, New Orleans and Mobile,” Daggett said at the conference in Nashville. He said many East and Gulf coast marine terminals “have no foremen, no union supervision at all.” “The way it should go is that [marine terminal] management do the thinking, come up with a plan and turn it over to a union foreman who takes it to the ILA rank-and-file to execute the plan,” he said. “That’s not happening.” The role of foremen and union supervisors is not outlined in the current master contract but instead left to the ILA locals and port-specific employers. The master contract, however, does outline that clerical work at marine terminals should be performed by union dockworkers if they have done that work in the past. Daggett pointed to the local agreement the ILA struck with marine terminals at the Port of New York and New Jersey as an example for other East and Gulf coast locals to follow. There, the local agreement includes a role for a union “master foreman ... involved in operational and supervisory functions at a marine terminal.” While other dockworkers are paid on an hourly basis, the master foreman receives a weekly salary and receives some of the wage increases outlined in the master contract. The master foreman also has a part-time role mediating disputes between labor and management. Rather than using union foremen and supervisors, Daggett said marine terminals are using assistant managers to oversee daily operations and do the types of clerical work that had been done by ILA members. “When I go into these ports and see only three or four clerks, but six or seven assistant managers, that tells me they are doing our work and they are limiting our access to terminal operating systems,” he said. “When I see that they don’t even have 20% of the manning that we have in New Jersey, something is wrong.” “You can’t use the word ‘New Jersey’ in front of management, it’s taboo,” Daggett added. “But it shouldn’t be. New Jersey should be the model.” ILA President Harold Daggett told the Journal of Commerce there “should be a foreman for every longshore gang,” adding that ports in the Southeast and Gulf states rely too heavily on management for dockworker supervision. “We had 15 superintendents on the pier in one place and no foreman,” Daggett said. “They want to control everything. In the south, [union foremen] have been picked on for years and years and been suppressed. Now, we’re going try and change all that.” Ahead of next year’s contract talks — the current master contract expires on Sept. 30, 2024 — the ILA is also considering a big switch in its political allies. Harold Daggett told attendees at the Nashville conference that he plans to meet former president Donald Trump in Florida, who is looking for the union’s support in his upcoming bid for a second term. Daggett said Trump’s support of right-to-work laws during his term was the reason that most unions backed President Joe Biden in 2020. But Trump is now “looking to take care of things for the unions,” Daggett said. Daggett faulted Biden, who provided a video address to the ILA at its July meeting, for not giving more support to the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) during its protracted talks for a new contract. Instead, the White House acceded to maritime employers by sending in Labor Secretary Julie Su to help mediate those talks. “When the ILWU was going through talks, you’d think he would have picked on the foreign companies out there that are setting up automation and getting rid of American jobs, but he didn’t do that,” Daggett said. “He went after the ILWU, telling them to get this contract signed. What the hell is that? They are fighting for their jobs.” “Biden’s a nice man, don’t get me wrong,” Daggett said. “But I am going to go sit and talk to Trump and see what he’s got to say.” Contact Michael Angell at michael.angell@spglobal.com and follow him on X: @michael_angell. © 2026 S&P Global.
